conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain that all local boards advocated and attribute the legislative stall solely to Senate leadership refusing local bills for teacher housing.
side_b_arguments: Sen. Mike Woodard pushed back, stating Durham County, DPS, and City officials all advocated for SB 203/HB 231 and that the Senate President Pro Tem's office simply blocked local bills while county staff already hold general-law authority to partner on restricted-use land.
conflicts.resolution: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby was directed to consult the UNC School of Government and DPS counsel to confirm whether existing statute enables restricted-use conveyance without special legislation.

conflicts.issue: School Board Public Criticism of BOCC Over Teacher Pay ($5,000 Raises) and Affordable Housing
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Brenda A. Howerton rebuked public statements by School Board members blaming the BOCC for blocking teacher affordable housing and $5,000 pay raises without ever contacting commissioners.
conflicts.side_a_position: Demand direct inter-board communication and condemn public misrepresentations blaming the five women commissioners for stalling housing and teacher supplements.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted she received zero direct outreach prior to weekend remarks claiming School Board members had lobbied all five commissioners on affordable housing and teacher raises.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stated BOCC has not refused teacher housing or youth support and called for the boards to communicate directly rather than assign blame publicly.
conflicts.side_b_position: Note earlier multi-year history underlying the School Board's perspective while continuing legal review of surplus property conveyance.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted the School Board chair referenced earlier historical conversations predating newer members while Interim Attorney Willie Darby awaited a legal mechanism from DPS counsel.
conflicts.resolution: No formal action; commissioners requested that elected peers cease public finger-pointing and engage the Board directly alongside legal staff.

conflicts.issue: Scope, Bylaws, and Public Messaging of the Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force
conflicts.summary: During the six-month Task Force update, county commissioners and city officials clashed over whether task force members were exceeding their advisory mandate by organizing public opposition campaigns against the Youth Home and criticizing Bull City United staffing, versus fulfilling their charge to engage residents on non-carceral safety alternatives.
conflicts.side_a_position: Task Force members should adhere strictly to bylaws by submitting vetted formal recommendations to elected boards rather than running public advocacy campaigns or claiming BOCC failed to fund prevention leadership.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Brenda A. Howerton objected to public campaigns accusing commissioners of prioritizing youth 'cages' when BOCC already funded a CISS department director, data statistician, and My Brother's Keeper initiatives.

Commissioners and Council Member DeDreana Freeman cited a missing Q1 report, unclear board-liaison notification of public forums, and the need to respect bylaws limiting official action to recommendations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Task Force town halls, public dialogue, and critiques of Youth Home detention spending and BCU oversight reflect legitimate community-led exploration of non-carceral safety strategies.
side_b_arguments: Task Force Co-chair Marcia Owens questioned expanding Bull City United into more neighborhoods before hiring a dedicated director and voiced community concern over Youth Home funding.

Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson defended the task force's public town halls and focus on non-carceral recommendations, noting elected bodies retain final authority to adopt or reject proposals (while Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton urged an inclusive approach that does not exclude law enforcement).
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken; committee members concluded discussion by emphasizing clearer liaison communication and submitting written recommendations to the City Council and BOCC in 2022.

conflicts.issue: Property Tax Reappraisal Schedule: Immediate Commitment to 2025 vs. Waiting for 2022 State Data Under Current 2026 Plan
conflicts.summary: Following Tax Administration's report that Q1 2021 sales ratios dropped to 79.6% (below the 85% statutory trigger) while Farragut software conversion remained on schedule, commissioners disagreed on whether to move toward formally scheduling a 2025 reappraisal now or await state Department of Revenue confirmation under the February 2021 compromise delaying to 2026.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prepare and consider formally scheduling a 2025 general reappraisal rather than waiting until 2026–2027, minimizing cumulative homeowner sticker shock and maintaining shorter assessment cycles.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs warned a seven-year gap before 2026–2027 exposes homeowners to severe property tax jumps even under a revenue-neutral rate, while shorter 3- to 4-year cycles improve equity.
Commissioner Heidi Carter welcomed Tax Administration's readiness to conduct a 2025 reappraisal ahead of the earlier 2026 schedule.
conflicts.side_b_position: Respect the February 2021 compromise setting 2026 and avoid changing the board's reappraisal date repeatedly until February 2022 trends and April 2022 NCDOR notice clarify whether advancement to 2025 is legally mandated.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns urged colleagues not to pressure Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson again after the board already compromised from 2027 down to 2026 in February.
Interim Manager Claudia Hager recommended returning in February 2022 with additional sales-ratio data and software conversion progress rather than revising the formal schedule prematurely.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton and commissioners agreed to await Tax Administration's February 2022 follow-up update and April 2022 NCDOR statutory notice.

conflicts.issue: Board Training Consultant Selection Process and Open vs. Closed Session Venue
conflicts.summary: Commissioners disagreed over whether discussions of board training consultants and prior RFP policy handling should occur in open or closed session, as well as the propriety of using open-ended commissioner comments for unscheduled policy topics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Discuss RFP policy context and consultant options openly in public session since no statutory closed-session exception applies to board training, and use commissioner comments to inform the public.
side_a_arguments: County legal guidance indicated there is no North Carolina statutory exception allowing closed session for board training.
Publicly clarifying section 5 of the RFP policy prevents half-truths about prior consultant outreach.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep sensitive personnel/consultant commentary in closed session where appropriate, avoid using open-ended comments as unscheduled agenda items, and establish a formal scope of work for an attorney-led RFP.
side_b_arguments: Open-ended commissioner comment placeholders risk turning unscheduled remarks into de facto agenda items.
Consultant and legal discussions tied to agenda items are more appropriately handled in closed session or through a formal scope-of-work RFP process.
conflicts.resolution: Commissioners agreed by informal consensus at 04:43:50 to submit scope-of-work input for board training to Attorney Darby by Friday so an RFP could be issued.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
conflicts.issue: Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Prioritization Criteria and Surplus Property Strategy
conflicts.summary: Commissioners challenged staff to establish objective prioritization criteria for the $2B+ CIP pipeline and to reconsider major property commitments like the Boys and Girls Club and old DSS building.
conflicts.side_a_position: Urged an objective, facility-condition-driven priority list, coordinated city-county-DPS infrastructure planning, and re-evaluating Boys and Girls Club and surplus parcels.
side_a_arguments: Urgent aging-infrastructure repairs (mold, leaks) should rank ahead of individual commissioner pet projects.
Land use rezonings drive EMS, sewer, and school capital demands and must be coordinated via a tripartite infrastructure committee.
Selling or repurposing former school sites, surplus downtown lots, and rethinking the Boys and Girls Club site could relieve CIP debt pressures.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff noted that many CIP projects have been queued for decades and emphasized balancing capital construction with ongoing operating costs and staff capacity.
side_b_arguments: Staff capacity and Durham's AAA bond rating constrain how quickly projects can be delivered.
Worst-case placeholders (like $15M for the old DSS building and $18M for homeless infrastructure) are needed while public-private options are explored.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to send a prioritization feedback template and return in November with refined sequencing, Gant timelines, and affordability scenarios.

conflicts.issue: Legal Authority for a School Adequate Public Facility Ordinance (SAPFO) vs. Advisory Task Force
conflicts.summary: During discussion of DPS's projected 4,800-student growth from approved developments, commissioners and BOE members expressed interest in pursuing an Orange County-style SAPFO or growth controls, while County Attorney Curtis Massey cautioned against assuming the County has legal authority to enact one.
conflicts.side_a_position: Explore an intergovernmental Growth & Education Task Force alongside studying Orange County's SAPFO and UDO revisions to manage school overcrowding.
side_a_arguments: Each newly approved development creates unfunded school seat costs ($100,000 per seat) that fall on county taxpayers without developer concurrency.
Consulting Orange County officials could clarify how their SAPFO and task force operate to see what tools Durham can adapt.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution that Durham County's prior adequate public facility ordinance was struck down as exceeding county authority and that Orange County relies on a special local act.
side_b_arguments: Under the 2006 Durham Landowners precedent, North Carolina counties lack general statutory authority to impose education impact fees or concurrency denials without state enabling legislation.
Any enforceable growth coordination also requires City Council participation since municipal rezonings drive residential approvals.
conflicts.resolution: County Attorney Curtis Massey agreed to consult Orange County Attorney John Roberts on how Orange County's SAPFO was authorized, while commissioners directed Deborah Craig-Ray to consider adding developer school impact fee authority to the state legislative agenda.

conflicts.issue: Codifying Pre-K Expansion Funding Commitments in the BOE–BOCC MOU
conflicts.summary: BOE Chair Rogers suggested revising the BOE–BOCC Memorandum of Understanding to lock in multi-year Pre-K expansion targets and timelines, prompting differing perspectives among commissioners.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support revisiting the BOE–BOCC MOU to ensure alignment and institutionalize support for Pre-K expansion and the new data-sharing MOA.
side_a_arguments: Board compositions change over time, and an updated MOU can ensure the data-sharing agreement and long-term Pre-K priorities remain consistent.
Shared alignment strengthens joint advocacy to the state and business community.
conflicts.side_b_position: Caution that codifying funding figures in an MOU could inadvertently cap or reduce commissioners' otherwise aggressive annual Pre-K investments.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners have repeatedly pushed staff to invest more in Pre-K each year—reaching roughly $8–10 million—without needing a contractual floor.
An MOU has different perceived weight across boards and may not be necessary to sustain funding.
conflicts.resolution: No formal action taken; commissioners agreed to stay engaged on the Pre-K data-sharing MOA and future MOU discussions.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session #4 - Wednesday, June 4, 2024
conflicts.issue: Scheduling Non-Budget Zafiqo Temple Presentation During Budget Work Session
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton sought to schedule a future September presentation on a Zafiqo Temple land deal at the close of the final budget work session, prompting pushback that non-budget items were inappropriate in the current financial climate and budget session.
conflicts.side_a_position: Place the Zafiqo Temple land deal community presentation on a September agenda
side_a_arguments: Community members undertaking the land deal between Raleigh and Durham requested an opportunity to present to the Board.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer non-budget presentation requests out of the budget work session to board leadership
side_b_arguments: A presentation involving a land deal is unrelated to the FY 2024-25 budget and inappropriate given the tight financial climate.
conflicts.resolution: Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns noted the request would be discussed in leadership/agenda planning and adjourned the budget work session.

conflicts.issue: EOC and Backup 911 Call Center Investment vs. Primary City-County 911 Unification
conflicts.summary: During consent review of a $5 million LOBs appropriation and design contract for a new Emergency Operations Center and shared backup 911 center, commissioners questioned moving forward before resolving primary 911 consolidation and consulting the Sheriff and state regulators.
conflicts.side_a_position: Expressed frustration that emergency lease deadlines are forcing a major 911 backup investment before resolving the long-stalled policy issue of consolidating City and County 911 call centers, and questioned whether Sheriff Birkhead and state DIT were consulted.
side_a_arguments: The County is being forced into the investment because Duke is ending the City's backup 911 lease rather than resolving primary 911 unification first.
Sheriff Clarence Birkhead publicly stated no one has spoken directly with him about consolidation.
State DIT regulates 911 VoIP compliance and has not been consulted on a merger.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff maintained the EOC/backup 911 facility is an urgent, jointly funded (53%/47% City/County) necessity that leaves primary consolidation open for future discussion.
side_b_arguments: Duke University requires the City to vacate its leased backup 911 space by December 2026.
The existing EOC on Broad Street was inadequate for social distancing during COVID-19.
The new facility provides a shared City-County backup 911 center while keeping separate primary centers for outage redundancy as requested by the Sheriff.
conflicts.resolution: Item remained on the consent agenda for future regular-session action; staff committed to convening stakeholders around primary 911 coordination separately.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session #3 - June 3, 2024
conflicts.issue: Funding Board of Education's Late $1.39 Million Hard-to-Fill / EC Teacher Supplement Request
conflicts.summary: Commissioners differed over whether to include the Board of Education's late $1.39 million addition (carrying a $278,000 charter school surcharge, ~$1.67 million total) for hard-to-fill positions in the county budget.
conflicts.side_a_position: Remove or deprioritize the late $1.39 million addition to reduce the tax-rate burden and prioritize core County/school obligations
side_a_arguments: The $1.39 million addition was added late at the quarterly retreat and was not in the original budget request.
Removing it saves roughly $1.67 million including the 20% charter surcharge before the Board has even addressed County staff compensation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Emphasize the critical need for competitive Exceptional Children (EC) teacher supplements
side_b_arguments: Exceptional Children teaching positions are very difficult work and highly competitive to fill, causing DPS to lose staff.
conflicts.resolution: Deferred to June 4 budget work session; staff noted it could be reconsidered later if not included in the initial adopted budget.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - FY 2024-25 Budget Work Session #3 - June 3, 2024
conflicts.issue: County Funding for Hayti Reborn Justice Movement ($1.45 Million) Amid Employee Benefit Cuts
conflicts.summary: Commissioners disagreed on whether Durham County should fund Hayti Reborn's $1.45 million reduced budget request in a year requiring property tax hikes and County employee health benefit reductions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose $1.45 million in County funding for Hayti Reborn
side_a_arguments: Hayti Reborn is already slated to receive $1 million from the City (half of its prior $2 million budget) and was originally understood as one-time funding.
Most of the $1.4 million request goes to salaries while Durham County is cutting health benefits for its own staff.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain County financial support for Hayti Reborn for at least two years
side_b_arguments: The County helped launch Hayti Reborn and it makes no sense to undercut a young organization serving youth connected to Durham Tech before the City's contribution is even certain.
conflicts.resolution: Remained unresolved on the add/delete list pending further budget balancing on June 4.

conflicts.issue: Urban Ministries Expanded Shelter and Day Center Feasibility Study Timing vs. Joint Housing Task Force
conflicts.summary: During the ARPA update, commissioners and county leadership differed on whether to move forward rapidly with a local shelter/day center feasibility study or wait for alignment at the joint City-County-DPS housing table.
conflicts.side_a_position: Advance funding for an Urban Ministries expanded shelter and day center feasibility study promptly rather than delaying for broader multi-body coordination.
side_a_arguments: Local homelessness and shelter capacity needs are urgent and would benefit from accelerating site and feasibility analysis now.
Remaining unallocated ARPA funds or local dollars could be positioned sooner if planning begins immediately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Coordinate shelter and day center planning through the Combined City-County-DPS Housing Initiative before committing additional study resources.
side_b_arguments: The joint City-County-DPS table is actively aligning intergovernmental homelessness and housing priorities to avoid duplicated efforts.
The Homeless Day Center RFP closing June 5 will provide direct provider proposals to evaluate alongside joint plans.
conflicts.resolution: No formal action taken; County Manager Kimberly Sowell and Deputy Manager Claudia Hager noted staff would coordinate around the pending RFP and joint housing discussions.

conflicts.issue: City-County Cost-Sharing for $120,000 Emergency Rental Assistance Shortfall and FY25 Eviction Diversion
conflicts.summary: City and County leaders disagreed over whether the City should split the emergency $120,000 DSS rental assistance shortfall 60/40 with the County given historical funding divisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Split the urgent $120,000 FY24 gap proportionally—60% County ($72,000) and 40% City ($48,000)—aligned with property tax rate shares rather than leaving the County to cover an unbudgeted emergency alone.
side_a_arguments: Emergency funding needed between April and June 30 sits outside regular annual budget allocations.
Both jurisdictions face shared constituent eviction pressures and should share the bridge cost proportionately.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain the historical division in which the City funds Forever Home Durham ($8.2M dedicated tax) and Legal Aid eviction defense ($500k–$1M annually) while the County handles DSS rental assistance.
side_b_arguments: City Manager Wanda Page and Councilmember Javiera Caballero noted the City already commits major dedicated tax dollars to housing supply and tenant legal representation under a 2018/2019 division of labor.
Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton requested three concrete funding options before City Council takes up the request.
conflicts.resolution: No committee vote; staff was directed to present funding options for the City Council work session ahead of the County's April 22 regular meeting.

conflicts.issue: Prioritizing Community Safety & Wellness Task Force Budget Requests and Presentation Inclusion
conflicts.summary: During the Community Safety & Wellness Task Force presentation, commissioners pressed for fiscal prioritization among seven costly requests and criticized internal exclusion of task force member Muffin Hudson.
conflicts.side_a_position: The task force must narrow its seven broad funding requests to a realistic top-three priority list for FY25 and ensure all members—especially community representative Muffin Hudson—are permitted to speak fully.
side_a_arguments: The County faces tight FY25 revenue constraints and cannot fund all seven multi-million-dollar requests simultaneously.
Vice Chair Burns objected that task force leadership failed to allow Muffin Hudson to present her sections earlier in the briefing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Present the full seven-part interconnected safety and wellness package as adopted by the task force rather than pre-cutting community recommendations.
side_b_arguments: Harm reduction, diversion, detention reform, DSS family support, and HEART expansion address mutually reinforcing root causes of justice involvement.
conflicts.resolution: Discussion continued into the afternoon session (Part 2) with staff directed to price options such as FTIR drug checking and countywide HEART tiers.

conflicts.meeting_title: BOCC - Work Session for Tuesday, January 2, 2024
conflicts.issue: Structure of County Participation in Affordable Housing Loan Fund (Direct City Contribution vs. County-Specific RFP)
conflicts.summary: During discussion of the Affordable Housing Task Force's first recommendation, commissioners expressed differing preferences on whether to contribute non-ARPA county funds directly into the existing City of Durham loan fund or issue a separate county RFP to establish a distinct county revolving housing fund.
conflicts.side_a_position: Contribute non-ARPA county funding directly to the existing City of Durham loan fund for governmental efficiency while reserving ARPA/RFP funds for distinct models like community land trusts.
side_a_arguments: Creating a separate county fund duplicates an existing City/Self-Help mechanism.
Community land trusts are a distinct model that permanently protects against gentrification and warrants their own RFP.
conflicts.side_b_position: Launch a new county RFP and distinct revolving housing fund scaled toward $20 million rather than simply folding into the City's existing fund.
side_b_arguments: The task force white paper identified nuances in county priorities—such as supporting both builders and individuals—that justify a separate county RFP.
Wake County launched its own $61M fund via RFP, and Durham County should aim for a $20M fund rather than remaining at $500,000.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; staff committed to returning in February 2024 with Self-Help Credit Union and detailed funding options.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
conflicts.issue: Magnitude and Oversight of APS Shelter Funding Increase (23% / $201,958 vs. Flat / 10%)
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split over whether to fully grant the Animal Protection Society of Durham's 23% ($201,958) funding increase given its 30-year non-competitive sole-source contract and capacity pauses, or honor its full operating/wage request.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support full $201,958 funding in light of APS's 33-year partnership, heavy private fundraising, 650+ volunteers, and overdue staff wage increases.
side_a_arguments: The County covers only ~34% ($841,000) of the shelter budget while APS fundraises nearly three-quarters of total costs and provides immense volunteer labor value.
APS's requested 3% wage adjustment is modest given county employees are moving to a $19.22/hr living wage floor.
conflicts.side_b_position: Question an immediate 23% increase without recent competitive RFPs, clearer reserve/profit-and-loss separation, and operational review of intake capacity pauses.
side_b_arguments: Holding a sole-source shelter contract for roughly 30 years without competitive RFPs warrants stronger financial audit review and performance transparency.
At points when the shelter hit capacity, intake stalled; requested clearer operational reporting before committing permanent increases.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved via informal work-session poll at 03:13:00 with three commissioners giving thumbs-up to add the $201,958 APS increase to the FY24 budget subject to follow-up data on shelter hours and peer benchmarks; subsequently enacted in the June 12 budget.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
conflicts.issue: Conditioning Future School Capital Funding on DPS Reuse Plans for Surplus Campuses
conflicts.summary: During the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan briefing, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Heidi Carter disagreed over whether the board should leverage county bond/capital approvals to force DPS reuse plans for vacated Northern High School and Durham School of the Arts sites.
conflicts.side_a_position: Withhold support for new school capital allocations unless DPS produces concrete reuse plans for vacated public school facilities.
side_a_arguments: Escalating bond costs (such as DSA rising toward $200 million) require joint city-county-school discipline so aging campuses are not left vacant or underutilized.
Commissioners control capital funding and must demand coordinated multi-agency planning.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer to the elected Board of Education's statutory governance over school facility disposition and reuse decisions rather than imposing capital vetoes.
side_b_arguments: School board members are separately elected officials accountable to voters for managing DPS property decisions.
Capital funding decisions should support joint student needs without undermining school board autonomy.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken during the CIP briefing; County staff noted ongoing multi-agency coordination ahead of the 2026 bond cycle.

conflicts.issue: Adding a $40 Million DPS Green Energy Bond Request Before Energy Audits Are Completed
conflicts.summary: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs pressed for clarity on whether DPS's $423.5M bond package adequately funded its renewable energy goals and green-bond line items, while Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and DPS Director Frederick Davis II cautioned against adding an unvetted $40M figure prior to energy audits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Wait for DPS's funded internal energy audits before adding another $40M onto taxpayers beyond the hard-won reduction to a 2.5-cent bond tax rate.
side_a_arguments: No board or school-board advocate could explain what the $40M green-bond email campaign specifically covered, and installing solar before upgrading windows and insulation is inefficient.
Staff worked hard to bring the CIP bond tax impact down from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents for residents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Ensure DPS's modernization and energy-efficiency/generation commitments are explicitly tracked and adequately funded through clear CIP or audit-backed line items.
side_b_arguments: County staff created a transparent dedicated renewable-energy line item, and DPS should confirm its 2030/2050 carbon-reduction goals are similarly resourced.
Once DPS completes its energy audit, future two-year CIP updates can incorporate vetted renewable energy projects.
conflicts.resolution: Budget staff and DPS clarified that $3M in 2016 bonds was already allocated for Lyons Farm solar and a districtwide energy audit, leaving future green-energy allocations for the subsequent CIP update once the audit concludes.

conflicts.issue: In-House Transportation Attorney FTE vs. Outside Legal Consultants
conflicts.summary: Commissioners differed during the Add/Delete list review on whether to fund a dedicated $140,000 in-house transportation attorney FTE or rely on outside consultants / an existing proposed attorney position.
conflicts.side_a_position: Prefer using outside consultants or recruiting transportation expertise within the already-planned new attorney position to minimize ongoing FTE costs.
side_a_arguments: Adding another permanent FTE increases recurring County personnel costs when specialized transportation advice might be procured more cost-effectively via consultants or combined into the general attorney hire.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hire a dedicated in-house transportation attorney FTE to advise the County on GoTriangle and complex transit matters.
side_b_arguments: Ongoing GoTriangle issues are creating problems because Durham County government currently has no internal legal counsel with transportation expertise to advise the Board (Howerton).
General Manager Claudia Hager noted that hiring part-time or contractual legal talent at that level can be difficult compared to a full-time role that could later be re-evaluated through attrition.
conflicts.resolution: No decision was made during the open work session; Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs agreed to defer the personnel discussion to closed session ahead of the June 6 work session and June 13 budget vote.

conflicts.issue: 1% for Public Art Starter Allocation ($500,000) in the Capital Improvement Plan
conflicts.summary: Commissioners questioned whether a proposed $500,000 allocation in the FY 2022-23 CIP to establish a 1% Public Art Fund was an appropriate priority given inflation-driven capital cost overruns.
conflicts.side_a_position: Oppose or scrutinize dedicating $500,000 to a new Public Art program during high inflation and tight debt-service fund balance reserves.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs expressed surprise at the $500,000 allocation when other urgent needs lack funding and projects like the 300 E. Main parking deck face $4M cost overruns.
Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned who requested the allocation and whether commissioners had aligned on spending half a million dollars on public art while human-service needs go unmet.
conflicts.side_b_position: Include the $500,000 starter placeholder based on prior CIP discussions for board review during budget markups.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Kimberly Sowell and GM Claudia Hager explained the line item reflected prior Board policy interest in a 1% art policy for capital projects and could be adjusted through the Ad/Delete budget process.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted the $500,000 CIP placeholder remained subject to Board removal or modification during upcoming budget work sessions.

conflicts.issue: 2025 Tax Reappraisal Burden, Residential Displacement, and Homeowner Relief Eligibility
conflicts.summary: Commissioners debated how to mitigate rising tax burdens on longtime, lower-income residents ahead of the 2025 reappraisal and 2022/2026 bond referenda within statutory limits.
conflicts.side_a_position: Expand local Low-Income Homeowner Relief access (e.g., shortening the 10-year ownership rule to 5–7.5 years) and transparently present cumulative multi-year tax impacts to protect residents from gentrification and displacement.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns warned rapid gentrification in Black and brown neighborhoods plus stacked tax rate increases (2016, 2019, and upcoming bonds) threatens displacement once 2025 values reset after a six-year gap.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs pushed lowering the 10-year residency rule in the county's DSS grant program and tracking multi-year household bill impacts alongside legislative relief advocacy.
conflicts.side_b_position: Statutory uniformity rules prevent Durham County from unilaterally altering property exemptions or deferrals beyond existing state circuit-breaker laws without General Assembly action.
side_b_arguments: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson noted North Carolina General Statutes strictly govern property exemptions and homestead deferrals ($719M already exempt countywide), requiring grant-based local workarounds or Raleigh legislation.
conflicts.resolution: Staff noted pending DSS Board recommendations to revise the local homeowner grant tenure rule and agreed to provide clearer historical tax-impact graphics for taxpayers.

conflicts.issue: GoTriangle DOLRT $157M Consultant Expenditures and Local Durham HUB Inclusion
conflicts.summary: Commissioners pressed GoTriangle over $131 million spent on national prime consultants and sparse Durham-based HUB participation prior to DOLRT's 2019 cancellation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Criticize disproportionate consulting spending with large national engineering firms and inadequate participation by local Durham-based HUB businesses.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged GoTriangle's DBE summary, noting that the bulk of prime contracts went to national corporations and DBE subs were concentrated in Wake County or out-of-state rather than Durham's 347 registered HUBs.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton pressed GoTriangle on accountability and financial transparency to restore public trust.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend federal FTA procurement compliance, DBE target attainment (8.8%–18.5%), and necessary 30%-to-final engineering work required before any federal grant award.
side_b_arguments: GoTriangle CFO Saundra Freeman and CDO Katharine Eggleston stated FTA rules prohibit federal reimbursement until a Full Funding Grant Agreement and mandate DBE (not local HUB) caps, while 2019 cancellation halted final subcontracting payouts.
conflicts.resolution: GoTriangle pledged continued detailed expense transparency and coordination on land-banked property disposition and future transit governance.

conflicts.issue: Protocol for Pulling Sheriff's Office Consent Agenda Items and Clarifying Security Roles (Item 21-0706)
conflicts.summary: Following Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs's decision to pull Item 21-0706 from consent for public discussion, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the lack of prior direct outreach to Sheriff's staff, prompting an exchange over transparency versus interagency courtesy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Commissioners should contact the Sheriff's Office directly with operational questions before pulling a consent item so Sheriff staff are not blindsided and lobby screeners are not conflated with detention officers.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted the Sheriff's Office received no heads-up prior to the item being pulled from consent.
Burns emphasized that private security vendors guard public entrances rather than replacing certified detention officers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Pulling the item allows transparent public explanation that the $412,303 amendment funds lobby weapons screening out of the Sheriff's existing budget rather than expanding detention custody.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs stated she contacted Interim Manager Claudia Hager beforehand and wanted the public to clearly hear why the amendment was needed amid Sheriff staffing vacancies.
conflicts.resolution: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead confirmed the contract funded entrance screening posts due to roughly 50 detention vacancies, and all five commissioners voted 5-0 to approve Item 21-0706.

conflicts.issue: 2104 & 2112 Ellis Road Rezoning (Case Z2000042): Self-Storage vs. Multi-Family Housing & Transit-Oriented Development
conflicts.summary: Resident Todd Paton and commissioners debated whether rezoning residentially zoned land along Ellis Road to Commercial General for a self-storage facility undermined Durham's urgent multi-family housing needs and future commuter rail transit-oriented development.
conflicts.side_a_position: Preserve residential zoning for multi-family housing and transit-oriented development near the proposed regional passenger rail stop rather than approving another self-storage facility.
side_a_arguments: Written commenter Todd Paton argued Durham faces skyrocketing rents and needs 40,000 new housing units, making a 100+ unit apartment complex the highest and best use.
Commissioner Heidi Carter noted it felt counterintuitive to upzone residential land to commercial given Durham's housing shortage and proximity to a proposed commuter rail station.
Commissioner Nida Allam requested transportation staff input on potential impacts on the planned regional passenger rail line.
conflicts.side_b_position: Approve CG(D) zoning for climate-controlled self-storage because site geometry and median traffic restrictions make residential use unviable and RTP firms and nearby apartments need local storage.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and Robert Schunk stated the 4.86-acre lot is only 200 feet wide with right-in/right-out median restrictions on Ellis Road, which would force excessive residential U-turns.
Byker noted the site is over a half-mile walk outside the core transit-station area and would serve RTP life-science startups and CROs needing off-site climate-controlled storage.
Ellis Crossing developer Eric Rifkin testified that his 1,800-unit mixed-use project across the street supports the facility as a needed amenity for residents.
conflicts.resolution: The public hearing was left open for 24 hours (through September 14) for transportation staff follow-up and additional comment; the board unanimously approved the rezoning 5-0 on September 27.

conflicts.issue: Process and Timing for Placing ARPA Funding Discussion on the BOCC Agenda
conflicts.summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs clashed over Jacobs's request to schedule a 15-minute ARPA funding discussion during the May 10 regular session.
conflicts.side_a_position: Place a 15-minute high-level ARPA process discussion on the May 10 regular session agenda (or use commissioner comments time) pursuant to the board's March 22 directive.
side_a_arguments: The March 22 minutes reflected a board directive for Claudia Hager to bring ARPA back at the April/May sessions.
Any three commissioners can request an agenda item, and a 15-minute high-level process discussion required no staff preparation.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer ARPA agenda placement to the Chair/Vice Chair agenda-prep meeting until staff prepares materials and U.S. Treasury guidelines are released.
side_b_arguments: Sending emails late Sunday night and mid-day Monday bypassed established agenda-prep procedures and left board members and staff unprepared.
General Manager Claudia Hager advised that the School of Government and State Treasury urged local governments to wait for official U.S. Treasury ARPA guidance before formal discussions.
conflicts.resolution: Chair Howerton declined to place the item on that day's or May 10's agenda without agenda-prep review and moved forward with the agenda.

conflicts.issue: Motion to Require Commissioner Heidi Carter to Recuse Herself from the County Manager's Contract
conflicts.summary: Chair Howerton moved that Carter recuse herself from comments and involvement in the County Manager's contract citing prior meeting precedent; Burns seconded while noting she had been unaware of the motion. Carter stated she would not recuse herself regardless of the vote, Allam cited legal advice/communications received, and the motion failed 2-3.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-3)

conflicts.issue: 10% Employee Hazard Pay Continuation and Pre-Retreat Cost Visibility
conflicts.summary: Commissioners differed on whether to keep committing funds to the 10% frontline employee hazard pay ahead of the budget retreat without complete multi-item cost totals, versus committing unconditionally to hazard pay for burned-out pandemic staff.
conflicts.side_a_position: Maintain 10% hazard pay unconditionally for frontline workers enduring severe pandemic burnout, supported by strong revenue collections and fund balance growth.
side_a_arguments: County revenue collections and expense management grew the fund balance, leaving the county financially solvent to support hazard pay.
Staff working daily on pandemic programs face severe burnout and put themselves and their families at risk.
Commissioners were elected to make hard choices for the most vulnerable, and no budget retreat will change support for paying workers.
conflicts.side_b_position: Require full cost estimates across proposed start and end dates and weigh all competing funding requests together at the upcoming budget retreat.
side_b_arguments: Budget documents arrived around 5:00 PM just before a 6:00 PM meeting, leaving insufficient time for review.
The board needs a complete picture of total costs to ensure funding is sustainable across all competing county priorities.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; Chair Brenda A. Howerton affirmed appreciation for county staff and deferred detailed budget deliberations to the upcoming board retreat.

conflicts.issue: 10% Employee Hazard Pay Commitment vs. Budget Retreat Cost Review
conflicts.summary: Commissioners expressed differing approaches to continuing 10% pandemic hazard pay versus holding spending commitments until complete cost projections could be weighed at the budget retreat.
conflicts.side_a_position: Stand firmly behind 10% hazard pay for burned-out frontline pandemic workers regardless of budget retreat debates.
side_a_arguments: County employees working daily on pandemic response experience severe burnout and put themselves and their families at risk.
The county saved money and maintains a triple-A bond rating because of staff hard work, and no budget retreat will alter support for hazard pay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Obtain clear start-to-end cost projections and evaluate overall budget affordability across competing needs at the board retreat.
side_b_arguments: Complete cost numbers are needed to understand how the county will afford all requested priorities.
The board should take adequate retreat time—potentially an additional retreat—to examine the full financial picture.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; Chair Brenda A. Howerton affirmed staff appreciation and deferred further discussion to the budget retreat.

conflicts.issue: Funding 10% Employee Hazard Pay and Potential Department Budget Cuts (DSS Impact)
conflicts.summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs questioned the fiscal sustainability of funding ongoing 10% hazard pay through lapsed-salary reserves while departments were asked to model budget cuts that could affect DSS assistance, whereas County Manager Wendell Davis and Chair Brenda A. Howerton maintained that hazard pay was covered without threatening DSS funds.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question reliance on April 2020 lapsed-salary strategies for unbudgeted hazard pay until full costs and downstream impacts on mandated DSS programs are clear.
side_a_arguments: Hazard pay was not included in the original April 2020 budget-management blueprint.
Departments are simultaneously being asked to examine conservative budget cuts, which in DSS could threaten mandated rental, emergency, and food assistance.
Commissioners need complete hazard-pay cost totals before making fully informed spending choices.
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue 10% hazard pay using FY 2020 fund balance savings, departmental cash-flow management, and federal reimbursements, with no cuts to DSS assistance.
side_b_arguments: Expenditure mitigation strategies produced $8.9 million in FY 2020 fund balance growth without spending budgeted reserves.
In 30 years of disaster management, federal emergency reimbursements have consistently covered eligible response costs; pressures are isolated to public safety cash-flow timing.
Chair Howerton urged staff to clarify publicly that funding hazard pay will not eliminate any DSS assistance funds.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; County Manager Wendell Davis committed to returning with detailed hazard-pay cost figures and budget clarification.

conflicts.issue: 10% Employee Hazard Pay Funding Sustainability and DSS Budget Impact
conflicts.summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs challenged funding ongoing 10% hazard pay from lapsed-salary reserves while departments faced potential budget reductions, whereas County Manager Wendell Davis and Chair Brenda A. Howerton defended hazard pay funding and rejected suggestions that DSS funds would be cut.
conflicts.side_a_position: Hold on committing unbudgeted hazard pay via lapsed-salary reserves until complete cost figures and impacts on other county priorities and DSS are provided.
side_a_arguments: The April 2020 budget-management blueprint did not contemplate hazard pay.
Asking departments to identify conservative budget cuts raises concerns about maintaining DSS assistance and other community needs.
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain 10% hazard pay backed by $8.9 million in fund balance growth, departmental cash-flow management, and federal disaster reimbursements, without reducing DSS funds.
side_b_arguments: Cost-mitigation strategies generated $8.9 million in FY 2020 fund balance growth without drawing down budgeted reserves.
Federal emergency reimbursements are expected to cover eligible hazard pay costs, with budget pressures limited to public safety cash-flow timing.
Chair Howerton requested explicit public clarification that DSS assistance funds would not be eliminated.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; County Manager Wendell Davis agreed to bring back detailed hazard-pay cost figures and budget clarification.

conflicts.issue: Timing and Retroactivity of $950,000 DPS Classified Staff $15/Hour Pay Funding Ahead of Bond Rating Calls
conflicts.summary: Commissioners and county staff differed over whether to appropriate the full $950,000 for retroactive $15/hour DPS classified employee pay immediately on January 11 or defer action until late January so staff could finalize year-end projections for bond rating agencies.
conflicts.side_a_position: Willingness to take a calculated fiscal risk to act sooner on DPS classified pay and exercise elected policy authority even when differing from cautious staff recommendations.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter argued the disagreement reflected differing 'risk budgets' and supported taking full action on January 11 rather than delaying.

Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized that elected officials must make decisions aligned with community priorities and values even when differing from staff recommendations, and sought clarity on July 1 versus August 2020 retroactivity.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid rushing financial commitments before delivering accurate year-end fiscal projections to bond rating agencies within three weeks.
side_b_arguments: County staff noted that rating agency calls require accurate, non-speculative year-end outlooks for the current and prior fiscal years.
Deferring the full remaining $950,000 review until January 24/25 allows finance staff to complete projections without rushing rating-agency prep.
conflicts.resolution: Compromise direction reached without a formal vote: move forward at the January 11 meeting with pay retroactive to January 2021 and return later in the month to consider the remaining $950,000 retroactive to August 2020 (subsequently approved on January 25, 2021).

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham County Government BOCC Live WorkSession Dec 7 2020
conflicts.issue: Election of Vice Chair — Nomination of Nimasheena Burns
conflicts.summary: Chair Howerton nominated Commissioner Burns citing racial equity and community emails; County Attorney Siler noted three votes are required and no second is needed for a nomination.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 2-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-3)

conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (2-3)

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
conflicts.issue: Policy Concerns Over $472,500 Detention Facility Food Pass Doors Contract (Item 24-0424)
conflicts.summary: During consent agenda review, Commissioner Wendy Jacobs questioned a surprise $472,500 contract to install 238 food pass doors at the Detention Facility, asking whether it would increase detainee cell confinement time.
conflicts.side_a_position: Questioned why the $472,500 food pass door installation appeared on consent without prior board briefing and sought assurance it would not lengthen cell confinement.
side_a_arguments: The board had not previously heard about this issue before seeing the $472,500 contract on the consent agenda.
Needed policy clarity on whether installing food pass doors for meals, documents, and tablets would increase the amount of time detainees remain confined in cells.
conflicts.side_b_position: Staff and Sheriff's Office defended the project as a phased safety/security upgrade identified in a 2001 facility assessment that does not alter detainee out-of-cell time.
side_b_arguments: About 100 doors were already installed in earlier phases over five to six years.
Food pass doors limit staff exposure when passing food, documents, or swapping tablets without changing how long detainees spend in their cells.
conflicts.resolution: Staff committed to providing additional background information to commissioners prior to the regular session consent vote; no vote was taken at the work session.

conflicts.issue: School Impact Fees, Developer Proffers, and City-County Legislative Alignment on Growth Concurrency
conflicts.summary: Following DPS's projection of $480M+ in new school seat construction needs, elected officials and attorneys examined whether the City or County could require developer impact fees or concurrency while debating how to align joint lobbying in Raleigh.
conflicts.side_a_position: Questioned the legal basis prohibiting local school impact fees and suggested challenging infrastructure definitions and accepting City voluntary proffers while coordinating joint City-County lobbying.
side_a_arguments: School buildings are essential public infrastructure driven directly by residential rezonings.
The City has not faced legal claims over voluntary proffers accepted on behalf of the school system.
Joint City-County legislative alignment is needed in the upcoming General Assembly long session.
conflicts.side_b_position: Legal counsel advised that North Carolina's Dillon's Rule and the 2006 Durham Land Owners Association decision strictly prohibit county-mandated school impact fees or concurrency without state enabling legislation.
side_b_arguments: Under Dillon's Rule, counties lack statutory authority to impose school impact fees or taxes without General Assembly authorization.
Orange County / Chapel Hill had to reimburse developers after a lawsuit over adequate public facilities fees.
Only voluntary proffers or new state enabling legislation are legally viable.
conflicts.resolution: BOCC had already referred the issue to its legislative liaison (Deborah Craig-Ray) for County legislative goals, and Chair Nida Allam committed to placing a joint City-County legislative priorities alignment presentation on the next meeting agenda.

conflicts.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Jun. 26, 2023
conflicts.issue: Equity Guarantees, HBCU/School Access, and MWBE Benchmarks for Proposed Regional Multi-Sport Complex
conflicts.summary: Following Discover Durham and the Durham Sports Commission's presentation on a major 250,000-sq-ft indoor and 37-acre outdoor sports complex, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged staff to replace broad promises with binding equity, local access, and MWBE commitments before seeking county funds.
conflicts.side_a_position: Do not advance county support without written details on MWBE inclusion, affordable local resident/youth access, hotel coordination, and consultation with HBCU (NCCU) and high school athletic leadership.
side_a_arguments: Local programs such as NCCU basketball lack adequate practice courts and local youth are often priced out of tourism-driven facilities.
The board's equity standards require concrete written access, minority/women-owned contracting plans, and community stakeholder outreach—not general assurances.
conflicts.side_b_position: Continue feasibility scoping toward a fall funding and site recommendation centered on sports tourism economic impact and the 2029 World University Games.
side_b_arguments: Durham lacks competitive indoor/outdoor tournament capacity compared with peer communities, missing out on youth access and sports-tourism revenue.
Staff welcomed the feedback and pledged to return in the fall with expanded equity, access, and facility-sharing details.
conflicts.resolution: Informational update concluded with no vote; presenters committed to incorporating Burns's MWBE, HBCU, and local access benchmarks into the fall recommendation.

conflicts.issue: Extending Application Period for RDU Airport Authority Board Appointments
conflicts.summary: Commissioners split 4-1 on Commissioner Nida Allam's motion to reopen and extend the application window for any RDU Airport Authority Board vacancy that did not receive majority support on the night's ballot, following procedural clarification over acting after ballots were cast.
conflicts.side_a_position: Extend the application period for any RDU Airport Authority seat without a majority ballot winner to broaden the applicant pool.
side_a_arguments: Encourages more applicants to seek appointment to the RDU Airport Authority Board.
Still allows a candidate who wins a majority of Board votes on the current ballot to be appointed immediately while extending only the unfilled seat.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed extending the application window (one dissenting vote; procedural concern raised about intervening before ballot results were read).
side_b_arguments: Procedural clarification noted that commissioners had already submitted ballots and were awaiting the clerk's announcement of the results.
conflicts.resolution: Motion passed 4-1; Yesenia Polanco-Gautam was appointed to the first vacancy by majority ballot vote, and the second vacancy was held open for re-advertisement.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham Delegates Meeting with County Commissioners and Staff
conflicts.issue: Strategic Risk of Advancing Emergency Powers Amendments (G.S. 166A-19.24/19.31) in 2022 Short Session
conflicts.summary: County legal staff requested statutory fixes for remote emergency meetings and civil enforcement, whereas Durham lawmakers cautioned against opening Chapter 166A in a polarized General Assembly.
conflicts.side_a_position: Seek legislative clarity during the 2022 short session allowing local governing boards to meet remotely during local declarations of emergency and use civil/equitable remedies.
side_a_arguments: Senior Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey argued current statutes ambiguously limit remote meeting flexibility to gubernatorial emergency declarations rather than local crises like cyberattacks or local disasters.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer or avoid opening Chapter 166A emergency-powers bills during the May 2022 short session to prevent counter-amendments.
side_b_arguments: Rep. Vernetta Alston and Sen. Mike Woodard warned that pandemic-era hostility toward emergency powers among legislative majorities could lead to restrictive counter-measures rather than helpful local clarifications.
conflicts.resolution: Staff and delegation agreed to coordinate through NCACC and legislative counsel on whether to defer the proposals to the 2023 long session.

conflicts.issue: Freezing Unfilled Law Enforcement Positions to Fund Unarmed Behavioral Health Crisis Responders
conflicts.summary: During the behavioral health infrastructure presentation, an unidentified commissioner and the Durham County Sheriff disagreed over whether unfilled Sheriff's Office positions should be frozen to fund behavioral health crisis response specialists versus using federal ARPA/CARES funds while keeping law enforcement centered in co-responder models.
conflicts.side_a_position: Freeze unfilled law enforcement positions and reallocate duties to behavioral health specialists for non-armed crisis response.
side_a_arguments: Communities are asking to decriminalize behavioral health challenges, poverty, and homelessness and reduce racial bias in crisis response.
Reorganizing unfilled positions rather than cutting filled roles avoids punitive action against officers while scaling non-armed response such as paramedicine.
conflicts.side_b_position: Do not freeze Sheriff's Office positions or cut 10% of the Sheriff's budget; fund behavioral health response with ARPA/CARES dollars and include law enforcement at the center of co-responder models.
side_b_arguments: The Sheriff's Office is already short-staffed amid nearly 1,000 shootings and over 129 shooting victims in Durham's Black and brown communities.
Ample federal CARES and American Rescue Plan funds are available for behavioral health initiatives, and established models like CAHOOTS operate in coordination with law enforcement.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote was taken during the work session; both sides agreed on continuing collaboration around crisis response models.

conflicts.issue: Non-Renewal of County Manager Wendell Davis's Contract (Termination June 29, 2021)
conflicts.summary: Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns strongly opposed the non-renewal, calling it non-merit-based, racially motivated retaliation for Davis's 2020 concerns regarding racial bias and pointing to the absence of a performance appraisal or board training.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 3-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (3-2)

conflicts.issue: Relieve County Manager Wendell Davis of Duties Effective Immediately
conflicts.summary: Motion relieved County Manager Davis of his duties immediately and stated the board would appoint an interim county manager.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 3-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (3-2)

conflicts.issue: Extend Contract of Outside Attorney Denise Smith Klein to Execute Board Decisions
conflicts.summary: Jacobs clarified the motion as an extension of Klein's existing contract at her existing hourly rate; Howerton and Burns objected that no total cost or rate confirmation for expanded execution work had been established.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 3-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (3-2)

conflicts.issue: Authorize Outside Attorney Denise Smith Klein Engagement Letter to Review County Manager's Contract
conflicts.summary: Authorized Acting County Attorney Willie Darby to finalize an engagement letter with attorney Denise Smith Klein to review the County Manager's contract and hold individual consultations with each commissioner. Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns opposed hiring outside counsel for contract interpretation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 3-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (3-2)

conflicts.summary: Authorized Acting Attorney Darby to finalize an engagement letter with outside counsel Denise Smith Klein to review the County Manager's contract and consult individually with each commissioner; Howerton and Burns dissented.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioner Meeting Nov 25, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam presided over the November 25, 2024 regular session, which served as the final meeting for outgoing Commissioners Nimasheena Burns, Heidi Carter, and Brenda A. Howerton—marking the conclusion of Durham County's historic first all-female Board of County Commissioners. Following the unanimous approval of minutes and ceremonial plaque and video tributes alongside emotional farewell addresses from the three departing commissioners, the board unanimously adopted its consent agenda, which included a land transfer for Durham Tech campus expansion and a $2 million affordable housing agreement with Housing for New Hope. The board also appointed Stephen Artaban to the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, Land Acknowledgment, Pledge, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam opened the meeting with the public charge, followed by Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns reading the land acknowledgment and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton leading the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Wallace read county announcements covering Thanksgiving closures, Kids Voting Durham participation (over 18,000 youth), the holiday parade, the NAIA football championship, and a new restaurant in Admin II. Vice Chair Burns added an urgent appeal for residents with driver's licenses to apply for paid CDL training to alleviate Durham Public Schools' bus driver shortage.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (November 4, 2024 Work Session and November 12, 2024 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter moved and Commissioner Wendy Jacobs seconded approval of the November 4, 2024 work session and November 12, 2024 regular session minutes. The motion carried unanimously without discussion.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognition and Farewell Tributes for Outgoing Commissioners
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Claudia Hager recognized dignitaries in attendance and celebrated the legacy of Durham's historic 2020–2024 all-female board before presenting appreciation plaques to Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns (2020–2024), Commissioner Heidi Carter (2016–2024), and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton (2008–2024), followed by a video tribute. Each outgoing commissioner delivered farewell remarks reflecting on accomplishments such as Black maternal health investments, veteran services, MWBE disparity goals, Hayti Reborn, living wage increases, single-use plastics and TNVR ordinances, and school funding, while urging the incoming board to stay committed to equity and public education. Chair Allam, Commissioner Jacobs, and Clerk Wallace also offered heartfelt tributes to their departing colleagues.

agenda_items.title: Adoption of Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: No items were pulled from the consent agenda, though Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns highlighted several major investments included in the package, specifically a land transfer to enable new building construction at Durham Tech, a $2 million agreement with Housing for New Hope under the revolving Affordable Housing Trust Fund, and additional youth funding. The board then unanimously approved the consent agenda.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam presided over the October 7, 2024 Board of County Commissioners work session, which opened with reflections on the one-year anniversary of October 7th and an initial closed session on personnel. In open session, the board reviewed consent agenda items—including a $472,500 detention facility food pass door contract that prompted policy questions from Commissioner Wendy Jacobs—and suspended the rules to approve a contract amendment for uniform security services with Nighthawk Security and Consulting LLC. Commissioners then received major work session updates on the Public Art Program, the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) prioritization and debt modeling, the USDA-funded Farm Campus community engagement report, revisions to the Business Recruitment and Expansion incentive policy, and ARPA obligation deadlines ahead of the December 31 federal cutoff before entering a second closed session and adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, Land Acknowledgment, and October 7th Anniversary Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam opened the work session with the public charge and Commissioner Wendy Jacobs read the land acknowledgment. Chair Allam and Commissioner Jacobs both offered remarks marking the one-year anniversary of the October 7, 2023 attacks, grieving the loss of Israeli and Palestinian lives, remembering a Durham community member held hostage, and calling for a ceasefire, return of hostages, and a political two-state solution.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Personnel) and Report Out
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board recessed into closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) to consider a personnel matter. Upon returning to open session at 01:36:00, Chair Nida Allam reported that no action was taken and that the board unanimously voted to seal the closed session minutes.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Claudia Hager reviewed twelve items proposed for the upcoming regular session consent agenda, including a $472,500 contract with CML Security LLC to install 238 food pass doors at the Detention Facility, EMS SAMHSA opioid grant funding ($307,251), Central Pines Regional Council MOA, HIPAA risk assessment, Public Health grants, utility sanitary sewer extension contracts, Queen Street garage lighting, and a DHHS charge-master rate letter. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs questioned whether the 238 food pass doors would increase cell confinement times; Sheriff's Office staff clarified it was a phased safety upgrade from a 2001 assessment that would not change confinement hours. Jacobs also requested EMS overdose reduction data, and staff confirmed opioid overdoses dropped from 90 per month during COVID to 56 in July.

agenda_items.title: Other Business: Suspension of Rules and Contract Amendment with Nighthawk Security and Consulting LLC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board was requested to suspend its rules to take immediate action authorizing the County Manager to execute a contract amendment for uniform security services with Nighthawk Security and Consulting LLC. Commissioners voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and 5-0 to approve the contract amendment.

agenda_items.title: Update Presentation on the Durham County Public Art Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy Director Perry Mans, Project Manager Brenda Hayes-Bright, and Public Art Coordinator Sarah Martin presented completed and upcoming public art installations funded under the 2019 up-to-1% public art policy, noting 75% MWBE participation and 11 of 12 selected artists residing in North Carolina. Highlights included murals at the Youth Home, Innovation Lab, 300 East Main parking deck, Stanford L. Warren Library, 500 East Main, and DecO on the Go mobile outreach panels. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns praised the community engagement and discussed converting Martin's contract position to permanent, supporting local artist studio space, and exploring private-sector art partnerships.

agenda_items.title: Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Update and Prioritization
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Claudia Hager, Budget Director Keith Lane, and Deputy Director Perry Mans reviewed Phase 2 of the 10-year CIP update, detailing revised cost estimates, affordability constraints, and major projects including the Animal Shelter, Sheriff's Training Facility, Project Build at Hope Valley, Fire/EMS Station 19, Parkwood Fleet Maintenance, an $18 million homeless services center placeholder, and Admin II. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs urged coordinated city-county-DPS infrastructure planning, rethinking the Boys and Girls Club property, and evaluating surplus county/school parcels and Museum of Durham History options. Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns requested an objective infrastructure prioritization list driven by urgent building conditions rather than commissioner preferences.

agenda_items.title: USDA-Funded Farm Campus Feasibility Study: Community Engagement Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt presented the interim community engagement report prepared with Co-Inspire Consulting for the proposed Farm Campus on Orange Factory Road, centering BIPOC, immigrant, women, and young farmers. Key insights emphasized inclusive community governance, addressing historical distrust, transit access barriers, shared commercial kitchen and cold-storage needs, and phased cohort incubator programming. Commissioners discussed agritourism opportunities and ensuring presentation of the final HR&A feasibility study to advisory boards like DOST.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of Updated Business Recruitment and Expansion Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Economic Development Director Andy Miracle and Manager Matt Filter presented proposed revisions to the 2019 business incentive policy ahead of an October 28 vote. Changes include adding a special lane for corporate headquarters projects, allowing hybrid work schedules, tying job wage verification to Durham County's living wage standard, removing the unused $1,000-per-job option, organizing Community Partnerships and Benefits into six buckets as a living attachment, shortening default 10-year terms where appropriate, and streamlining clawbacks and MWBE reporting. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs praised the living-document benefits approach and requested adding support for hiring justice-involved individuals via Justice Services, emphasizing job pathways across education levels, and formalizing annual public compliance reporting.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Update: Obligation Deadlines, DPS ILAs, and Reallocation Options
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Claudia Hager and staff reported that all 49 ARPA projects are on track to meet the December 31, 2024 federal obligation deadline, highlighted the October 23 groundbreaking of the first joint City-County ARPA affordable housing project ($2.7M ARPA gap funding out of $13.5M total), and reviewed draft capital and Pre-K/Title I ILAs with Durham Public Schools. Staff outlined Treasury flexibility to amend contracts or shift unspent balances after December 31 into priority areas like Slater Road sewer infrastructure, childcare subsidies/Pre-K, and food security. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs asked about planning for the 2026 fiscal cliff when $10.8 million in ARPA community grants expires.

agenda_items.title: Second Closed Session (Personnel, Opioid Litigation, Attorney-Client Privilege) and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) and (a)(3) for two personnel/attorney-client matters and national opioid litigation. disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
disagreements.issue: Policy Concerns Over $472,500 Detention Facility Food Pass Doors Contract (Item 24-0424)
disagreements.summary: During consent agenda review, Commissioner Wendy Jacobs questioned a surprise $472,500 contract to install 238 food pass doors at the Detention Facility, asking whether it would increase detainee cell confinement time.
disagreements.side_a_position: Questioned why the $472,500 food pass door installation appeared on consent without prior board briefing and sought assurance it would not lengthen cell confinement.
side_a_arguments: The board had not previously heard about this issue before seeing the $472,500 contract on the consent agenda.
Needed policy clarity on whether installing food pass doors for meals, documents, and tablets would increase the amount of time detainees remain confined in cells.
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff and Sheriff's Office defended the project as a phased safety/security upgrade identified in a 2001 facility assessment that does not alter detainee out-of-cell time.
side_b_arguments: About 100 doors were already installed in earlier phases over five to six years.
Food pass doors limit staff exposure when passing food, documents, or swapping tablets without changing how long detainees spend in their cells.
disagreements.resolution: Staff committed to providing additional background information to commissioners prior to the regular session consent vote; no vote was taken at the work session.

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Oct. 7, 2024
disagreements.issue: Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Prioritization Criteria and Surplus Property Strategy
disagreements.summary: Commissioners challenged staff to establish objective prioritization criteria for the $2B+ CIP pipeline and to reconsider major property commitments like the Boys and Girls Club and old DSS building.
disagreements.side_a_position: Urged an objective, facility-condition-driven priority list, coordinated city-county-DPS infrastructure planning, and re-evaluating Boys and Girls Club and surplus parcels.
side_a_arguments: Urgent aging-infrastructure repairs (mold, leaks) should rank ahead of individual commissioner pet projects.
Land use rezonings drive EMS, sewer, and school capital demands and must be coordinated via a tripartite infrastructure committee.
Selling or repurposing former school sites, surplus downtown lots, and rethinking the Boys and Girls Club site could relieve CIP debt pressures.
disagreements.side_b_position: Staff noted that many CIP projects have been queued for decades and emphasized balancing capital construction with ongoing operating costs and staff capacity.
side_b_arguments: Staff capacity and Durham's AAA bond rating constrain how quickly projects can be delivered.
Worst-case placeholders (like $15M for the old DSS building and $18M for homeless infrastructure) are needed while public-private options are explored.
disagreements.resolution: Staff agreed to send a prioritization feedback template and return in November with refined sequencing, Gant timelines, and affordability scenarios.

meetings.executive_summary: Resuming in open session on October 7, 2024, the Board of County Commissioners reviewed consent agenda items covering Detention Center food-pass doors, EMS SAMHSA opioid grants, public health grants, and sanitary sewer extensions, and voted unanimously 5-0 to suspend the rules and authorize a security contract amendment with Nighthawk Security & Consulting LLC. Commissioners received comprehensive updates on the Public Art Program, the County's $2.2 billion requested 10-year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), the USDA-funded Farm Campus feasibility community engagement study, revisions to the Business Recruitment and Expansion incentive policy, and ARPA project obligations ahead of the December 31, 2024 deadline. Commissioner Wendy Jacobs questioned item 24-0424 ($472,300 with CML Security LLC for 238 Detention Facility food-pass doors) to confirm it would not increase cell confinement time, and sought outcome data on item 24-0589 ($370,261 SAMHSA EMS opioid grant), where staff reported 3,000+ Narcan kits distributed and monthly overdoses dropping from ~90 during COVID to 56 in July. Hager also walked through solid waste planning (24-0596), HIPAA risk assessment (24-0597), Public Health grants (24-0600, 24-0601), electrical and chemical contracts (24-0612, 24-0613), Detention Center fire pump assessment (24-0616), sanitary sewer extension contracts generating net county consumption revenue (24-0617), Queen Street garage lighting (24-0621), and DHHS chargemaster rates (24-0624).

agenda_items.title: Durham County Public Art Program Update

Warren Library, 500 East Main parking deck, Board of Elections, Sheriff's Training Facility, and Emergency Operations Center.
