meetings.title: BOCC - Regular Session for Monday, January 8, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam presided over the January 8, 2024 regular session, which featured ceremonial recognitions alongside two land-use public hearings. The board introduced Durham County's new Early Childhood Coordinator, adopted proclamations and resolutions for National Mentoring Month and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Day, congratulated Sheriff Clarence Birkhead on a 100/100 ACA jail reaccreditation audit score, and approved prior minutes and the consent agenda 5-0. Following public hearings, the board voted 5-0 to adopt UDO Text Amendment TC23003 creating the Eno River Critical District A2 (EA2) watershed overlay around the new Teer Quarry water intake and its consistency statement, and voted 5-0 to approve Street Closing SC220008 closing portions of Electra Road, Exum Road, and an unimproved 30-foot lane to expand the Sheriff's firing range buffer after clarifying to a resident that no algae scrubber was planned on the site. The board concluded with a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6), taking no action.

agenda_items.title: Opening Ceremonies, Announcements, Sheriff Re-Accreditation Recognition, and Approval of Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter led the Pledge of Allegiance and Clerk Wallace read published announcements including the Justice Resources resource fair, FY24 Q3 Durham Transit Work Plan comment period, and vaccine clinics. Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns congratulated Sheriff Clarence Birkhead on achieving 100 out of 100 compliance during the detention center's American Correctional Association three-year reaccreditation audit, and the board approved the November 27, 2023 and December 4, 2023 minutes.

agenda_items.title: Introduction of New Durham County Early Childhood Coordinator
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff introduced Durham County's newly hired Early Childhood Coordinator (former Book Babies leader at Book Harvest with an M.Ed. in early intervention and family support) to lead implementation of the Early Childhood Action Plan alongside the county's $6 million-plus investment in Durham Pre-K. Commissioners welcomed her and emphasized early childhood brain development and family support.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation: National Mentoring Month (January 2024)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter read a proclamation declaring January 2024 National Mentoring Month. DeWarren Langley of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation and representatives from El Centro Hispano, Bull City Bulldogs, Wall Street Juniors, Inspiring Minds, and MBK Durham shared updates on youth mentoring, financial literacy, and violence-prevention programs.

agenda_items.title: Resolution Celebrating and Honoring Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns read a resolution honoring the life and service of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. DeWarren Langley accepted the resolution on behalf of the MLK Steering Committee and announced upcoming observance ceremonies, $1,000 student scholarships, and Keeper of the Dream awards.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam noted the items had been reviewed during the prior work session and asked if any commissioner wished to pull an item. Seeing none, the board unanimously approved the consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: UDO Text Amendment — Teer Quarry Intake (TC23003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff Aaron Cain and Sarah Young presented staff-initiated UDO Text Amendment TC23003 (revising Articles 4, 8, and 12) required by state watershed regulations for a new Eno River water intake at Teer Quarry, creating the Eno River Critical District A2 (EA2) overlay within a half-mile of the intake while exempting existing lots unless redeveloped. Water Management's Sid Miller noted construction and regular supplemental water withdrawal are roughly three to four years away; with no public speakers, the board adopted the ordinance and its N.C.G.S. 160D-605 consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing (24-0002): Street Closing Request — Electra Road, Exum Road, and 30-Foot Lane (SC220008)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented County-initiated street closing SC220008 (filed by Jose Torres on behalf of Durham County) to permanently close a 1,112-foot section of Electra Road, a 694-foot unimproved portion of Exum Road, and a 1,168-foot unimproved 30-foot lane so adjacent county parcels could recombine into a 90.2-acre parcel providing a larger, safer buffer for the Sheriff's firing range. meetings.title: BOCC - Work Session for Tuesday, January 2, 2024
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam presided over the January 2, 2024 BOCC work session, opening with citizen comments from Durham County library staff opposing a proposed Sunday hours expansion without first conducting an independent staffing audit, ending 7-day work rotations, guaranteeing comp time, and recognizing workers' right to organize; County Manager Dr. Sowell replied that no decision had been made and an external consultant and internal operational assessment were underway. Commissioners reviewed upcoming consent agenda items including separating the Public Information Office into its own fund center ($175,000), expanding a Durham Center for Senior Life navigator to full time ($40,000), increasing Freese and Nichols's Snow Hill Road pump station contract (+$416,360), and switching 17 Sheriff hybrid vehicles to EcoBoost due to supply availability ($159,000 savings). Under discussion items, the board suspended the rules and voted 5-0 to approve statutory public official bonds, and reviewed an ARPA update showing 71% of $62.4 million encumbered across 57 projects alongside Affordable Housing Task Force recommendations before entering closed session on litigation (Anthony DiBrosky v. Durham County).

agenda_items.title: Citizen Comments: Library Sunday Hours, Staffing, and Labor Protections
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Library workers Kyle Lampert, John Davis (whose Zoom audio dropped, prompting the clerk to invite written submission), and Larkin Coffey urged the board to perform an independent staffing audit, fill vacant positions, end 11-month terminations of substitute workers, prohibit 7-day work rotations, guarantee full comp time for Sunday shifts, and recognize workers' right to organize before opening libraries on Sundays. County Manager Dr. Sowell responded that no decision had been made, any proposed rotation would involve only 3-4 Sundays per year without 7-day stretches, and both an external consultant and the Office of Strategy and Performance were evaluating library operations and culture.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review for Next Regular Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Sowell reviewed items slated for the regular session consent agenda, including creating a dedicated PIO fund center ($175,000, Item 23-0762), renewing Accela for Durham One Call ($42,770.82, Item 23-0911), expanding a Durham Center for Senior Life food/benefits navigator to 1 FTE ($40,000, Item 23-0920), increasing Freese & Nichols engineering services for the Snow Hill Road pump station (+$416,360 to $821,360, Item 23-0924), and substituting 17 Ford EcoBoost interceptors for unavailable hybrids for the Sheriff's Office (Item 24-0015, saving $159,000). Commissioners asked about city cost-sharing and Cabin Branch failing septic systems on Snow Hill Road and thanked retiring food security coordinator Mary Oxendine.

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item: Approval of Public Official Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Andrews presented statutory performance bonds required by North Carolina General Statutes—held over from December due to new personnel in the CFO ($1M cap) and Tax Administrator roles and covering the Register of Deeds and Sheriff as well—while noting dated statutory language like 'chairman' and 'his' would be updated where permissible. The board suspended the rules and unanimously approved the bonds for all four officials.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Implementation Update and Affordable Housing Task Force Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager reported that 71% of the county's $62.4 million ARPA funds were encumbered or committed across 57 projects ahead of the December 21, 2024 encumbrance deadline, with ~$500,000 remaining uncommitted alongside $3.5 million in revenue replacement flexibility and pending RFPs for youth, digital equity, arts, senior home repair, and land trusts. Hager and engineering staff presented three Affordable Housing Task Force white-paper recommendations: investing in an affordable housing loan fund, reviewing post-pandemic housing support services, and establishing an affordable housing scorecard. Commissioners debated contributing directly to the existing City/Self-Help fund versus running a county RFP for a $20M revolving fund, stressed 30-year affordability and right-of-first-refusal safeguards, and discussed transit/planning representation and homelessness shelter needs ahead of a February deep-dive.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session: Attorney-Client Privilege (Anthony DiBrosky v. Durham County, N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 5-0 to adjourn into closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) to consult with counsel regarding Anthony DiBrosky v. Durham County. After returning at 02:24:38, the chair reported no action was taken and direction was given to staff, and adjourned the meeting.

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend Rules for Approval of Public Official Bonds
votes.notes: Chair Allam announced 'Ayes have it 5 to 0.' Mover and seconder were not named aloud.
votes.discussion_detail: Because timely filing with the Clerk of Court was required for newly appointed CFO and Tax Administrator performance bonds alongside the Register of Deeds and Sheriff bonds, the board voted to suspend the rules at the work session.

votes.item_title: Approval of Public Official Bonds (CFO, Tax Administrator, Register of Deeds, and Sheriff)
votes.notes: Chair Allam announced 'Ayes have it 5 to 0.'
votes.discussion_detail: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs moved approval of the public official bonds for all four statutory officers (CFO, Tax Administrator, Register of Deeds, and Sheriff) to meet statutory requirements, and Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton seconded.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session (N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3))
votes.notes: Chair Allam announced 'the ayes have it five to zero.'
votes.discussion_detail: Commissioner Heidi Carter moved and Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns seconded entering closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) to consult with the county attorney regarding Anthony DiBrosky v. Durham County.

disagreements.meeting_title: BOCC - Work Session for Tuesday, January 2, 2024
disagreements.issue: Structure of County Participation in Affordable Housing Loan Fund (Direct City Contribution vs. County-Specific RFP)
disagreements.summary: During discussion of the Affordable Housing Task Force's first recommendation, commissioners expressed differing preferences on whether to contribute non-ARPA county funds directly into the existing City of Durham loan fund or issue a separate county RFP to establish a distinct county revolving housing fund.
disagreements.side_a_position: Contribute non-ARPA county funding directly to the existing City of Durham loan fund for governmental efficiency while reserving ARPA/RFP funds for distinct models like community land trusts.
side_a_arguments: Creating a separate county fund duplicates an existing City/Self-Help mechanism.
Community land trusts are a distinct model that permanently protects against gentrification and warrants their own RFP.
disagreements.side_b_position: Launch a new county RFP and distinct revolving housing fund scaled toward $20 million rather than simply folding into the City's existing fund.
side_b_arguments: The task force white paper identified nuances in county priorities—such as supporting both builders and individuals—that justify a separate county RFP.
Wake County launched its own $61M fund via RFP, and Durham County should aim for a $20M fund rather than remaining at $500,000.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; staff committed to returning in February 2024 with Self-Help Credit Union and detailed funding options.

meetings.title: BOCC - Dec 11, 2023 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nida Allam presided over her first regular session following her December 4 election, with Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton granted an excused absence (4-0). The board approved the November 6 work session minutes (4-0), passed the ARPA-heavy consent agenda (4-0), and heard a Department of Social Services presentation on North Carolina's Medicaid expansion rollout. Commissioners then held four Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) public hearings, unanimously approving (4-0) the annual UDO Omnibus Text Amendment, the Pedestrian Malls amendment (23-0894 / TC-2304), and the Conservation Subdivisions clarification (23-0895). On the fourth public hearing—the contentious, privately initiated Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD, 23-0896) amendment—the board voted 3-1 to adopt the City Council-modified ordinance and consistency statement, with Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns dissenting.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Excused Absence of Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nida Allam opened the meeting, read the public charge, and invited Commissioner Heidi Carter to lead the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Wallace read announcements including the December 18 Board of Elections Phase One and MWBE outreach session and the DCHC MPO / CAMPO Destination 2055 transportation survey. Chair Allam announced that Commissioner Brenda A. Howerton requested an excused absence, which the board approved.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Presentation: Eno River Association 2024 Calendar
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Eno River Association Executive Director Jessica Sheffield presented the organization's 2024 calendar to the board. Commissioners thanked the association for its ongoing conservation partnership with Durham County.

agenda_items.title: Approval of November 6, 2023 Work Session Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: At Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns's reminder, the board returned to the minutes item before taking up the consent agenda. Commissioners approved the November 6, 2023 work session minutes without edits.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Including ARPA Equity Framework Allocations)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Nimasheena Burns highlighted that the consent agenda included roughly 20 items advancing ARPA funding through an equity framework prioritizing rural, diverse, and urban communities, and praised County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell and Deputy Managers Maurice Jones and Claudia Hager. Chair Nida Allam echoed the recognition of staff's work before calling the vote.

agenda_items.title: Presentation on Medicaid Expansion Implementation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Department of Social Services Director Maggie, COO Kelly Inman, and Assistant Director Margaret Faircloth briefed the board on North Carolina's Medicaid expansion launch, explaining online applications via epass.nc.gov as well as in-person and phone intake. Staff reported keeping wait times under 30 minutes while coordinating with partner groups such as Urban Ministries and serving approximately 70,000 existing Medicaid enrollees.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 1: UDO Omnibus Text Amendment (Comprehensive Plan & Technical Revisions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planning Manager Alexander Cahill presented the annual UDO Omnibus Text Amendment, combining technical updates with early Comprehensive Plan implementation measures. Proposed changes expanded mailed public hearing notice from 600 to 1,000 feet, required sign postings for multifamily properties when mailing addresses are unavailable, aligned childcare definitions with state law, allowed Durham Public Schools to seek residential-area school sites via rezoning rather than special use permits, permitted two driveways for duplexes, removed the infill tree-coverage exemption for single-family and duplex lots, and added a 0.6 opacity county-line buffer. No speakers signed up for the public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 2 (23-0894 / TC-2304): UDO Text Amendment — Pedestrian Malls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a privately initiated text amendment (TC-2304) modifying Article 16 Design District streetscape, right-of-way, and block/lot standards for pedestrian malls. Commissioners noted the process worked smoothly and no members of the public signed up to speak.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 3 (23-0895): UDO Text Amendment — Conservation Subdivisions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Curtis Massey presented a UDO text amendment to Section 6.2.4 / Article 6 clarifying that the 12 general purpose statements for conservation subdivisions are not all mandatory criteria, addressing pending litigation against the county while preserving the 50% open-space requirement. Two public speakers testified during the hearing, and staff noted that recently adopted phased-development and tree-preservation rules apply to conservation subdivisions and residential districts would be prioritized in the UDO rewrite.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 4 (23-0896): UDO Text Amendment — Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the privately initiated SCAD text amendment as modified and adopted by Durham City Council, noting that the Planning Commission had recommended denial 6-6 in March and that Council removed provisions opposed by staff. Twenty-two speakers addressed the board, with critics raising concerns over inadequate community engagement, developer loopholes, rural/unincorporated impacts, and disability parking accessibility, while supporters urged approval to expand housing supply, ADUs, and walkability. Commissioners voted 4-0 at 04:11:30 to extend the meeting by 15 minutes until 11:00 PM; in final deliberation, Commissioners Carter, Jacobs, and Chair Allam supported adopting the revised SCAD text to maintain a single City-County UDO and expand ADUs and parking-minimum removal, while Vice Chair Burns opposed passing private text amendments prior to the UDO rewrite.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Andrews announced the results of the board's written ballots for two advisory bodies: an appointment to the City-County Appearance Commission and an appointment to the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission.

disagreements.issue: Adoption of Privately Initiated SCAD UDO Text Amendment (23-0896)
disagreements.summary: Commissioners split 3-1 over adopting the City Council-amended Simplifying Codes for Affordable Development (SCAD) UDO text amendment, debating joint City-County UDO uniformity, ADU and parking rules, and whether privately initiated text amendments should wait for the comprehensive UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the City Council-modified SCAD amendment to keep a unified City-County UDO, expand ADUs and remove parking minimums, and monitor impacts during the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Voting no would split the shared UDO into separate City and County ordinances for the first time.

City Council removed the provisions Planning staff flagged as problematic, and remaining items like larger ADUs (above 800 sq ft) and ADUs on church property help county residents and aging family members.
Removing parking minimums reduces car dependency and supports walkability and transit, while staff will monitor unintended impacts ahead of the UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose adopting the privately initiated SCAD amendment prior to the comprehensive UDO rewrite.
side_b_arguments: As chair of the Joint City-County Planning Committee, Burns recalled near-unanimous agreement to limit private text amendments until the comprehensive UDO rewrite was completed.
Most provisions primarily affect the City rather than unincorporated Durham County, and ADU amendments had already been passed previously.
Rejected political pressure from external advocates and argued the amendment did not meaningfully guarantee affordable housing.
disagreements.resolution: Both the ordinance (23-0896) and its statutory consistency statement passed 3-1 (Allam, Jacobs, Carter aye; Burns nay).

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for December 4, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The December 4, 2023 Work Session opened with the annual board leadership elections, in which the board elected Nida Allam as Chair (majority voice vote) and Nimasheena Burns unanimously as Vice Chair (5-0). Commissioners then reviewed consent agenda items for the December 11 regular meeting, including public health grants, a $50,000 county share for a joint City-County crisis communications plan, $600,000 in LOBs for the new Emergency Operations Center and backup 911 center, and the 2024 meeting calendar (moved to December 11 after flagging a Passover conflict on April 22). In work session presentations, Research Triangle Foundation staff presented proposals for a 100-acre Hub RTP social district and the long-range RTP 3.0 land-use and Urban Research Service District (URSD) tax-district framework. Deputy Manager Claudia Hager concluded with an ARPA update covering remaining project timelines through September 2026, school nurse funding, pre-K, cultural arts, and $2 million for homelessness planning and infrastructure.

agenda_items.title: Annual Election of Board Chair and Vice Chair
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Andrews presided over the statutory annual election of the Board Chair; Commissioner Heidi Carter nominated Nida Allam, who was elected Chair by a majority vote. Newly elected Chair Allam then presided over the Vice Chair election, where Commissioner Wendy Jacobs nominated Nimasheena Burns, who was unanimously elected Vice Chair. Both new leaders and outgoing Chair Brenda A. Howerton—who noted she would not seek reelection—offered remarks on community priorities.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Chair elected by majority; Vice Chair elected 5-0

agenda_items.title: Public Charge and Citizens' Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Allam read the public charge. DeWarren Langley, Executive Director of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation, spoke during public comment to urge board investment in youth programming and services.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review for December 11, 2023 Regular Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell walked commissioners through consent items including public health grants (230808 $1,200 RJCM pilot; 230809 $100,000 NACCHO COVID-19 access; 230851 $59,743 Guilford training; 230853 fee schedule), an interlocal agreement with the City of Durham for a Joint Crisis Communications Plan up to $50,000 (230832, with commissioners requesting school stakeholder inclusion), a McKim & Creed utilities contract amendment (230845), Emory Cemetery relocation (230854), tax administration software/authority (230870, 230871, 230872), $600,000 in LOBs for the new EOC and backup 911/Sheriff's Call Center (230882, where Commissioner Jacobs urged pursuing integrated City-County 911 operations), and the 2024 BOCC calendar (230901, deferred to December 11 to check a Passover conflict on April 22).

agenda_items.title: Hub RTP Social District Proposal Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Maurice Jones and Research Triangle Foundation Senior Director of Placemaking Amanda Ronan presented a request to establish a social district across the 100-acre Hub RTP site, launching initially in Phase 1 around the retail/food-and-beverage horseshoe, stream, stage, lawn, and splash pad. Vice Chair Burns asked about Research Triangle High School across the street, >35% MWBE construction participation, private security (Cain Security), and transit capacity for future Davis Drive job growth.

agenda_items.title: RTP 3.0 Framework and Urban Research Service District (URSD) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: RTP leadership and County staff presented the RTP 3.0 long-term vision introducing enhanced corporate campuses, missing-middle residential neighborhoods, and mixed-use density nodes, which would require covenant votes by park landowners and tenants. County staff explained the existing RTP special tax district and statutory Urban Research Service District (URSD) sub-district mechanism—capped at Durham City's 55-cent tax rate—to finance infrastructure and debt service, while commissioners stressed integrating workforce/affordable housing, transit, the Comprehensive Plan, and Durham Tech partnerships.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners Work Session for November 6, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: During the six-hour November 6, 2023 Work Session, Chair Brenda A. Howerton and all five commissioners heard public comments thanking the board for $3 million to preserve Carver Creek Apartments and urging stronger Juvenile Crime Prevention Council (JCPC) data reporting. The board reviewed a slate of consent agenda grants, then suspended the rules (5-0) and approved a resolution (5-0) granting an expedited hearing for UDO conservation-subdivision amendment TC23005 (23-0828). Commissioners also received detailed presentations on the Durham Transit Plan FY24 Q2 Work Program amendments ($139,550 net for GoTriangle mobile ticketing and the FAST 2 study) and Bus Speed & Reliability / BRT study, the 2025 General Reappraisal (23-0821), public health harm reduction and opioid settlement funding, JCPC monitoring ($701,001 state allocation), and Durham County's blasting permit process (23-0827), before discussing commissioner comments and adjourning after closed session.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Comments (Carver Creek Apartments and JCPC Data)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Housing for New Hope leader Russ Pierce thanked the board for $3 million in matching funding alongside the City of Durham to acquire and preserve 48 affordable units at Carver Creek Apartments as part of an expanding ~120-unit supportive housing campus. DeWarren Langley of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation urged the board to ask JCPC for actionable risk-and-needs and juvenile complaint trend recommendations rather than only an annual funding plan.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Public Health, Justice Grants, Utilities, and Capital Projects)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Sowell presented upcoming consent agenda items including $862,450 for public health infrastructure (230746), $1.404M for school health teams (230748), $265,113 for COVID-19 immunization (230750), $150,000 for Triple P (230751), $199,106 JAG grant (230760), Homeland Security and DOJ grants (230780, 230781), Northeast Creek sewer modeling ILA (230793), $400,000 for the Shoppes of Hope Valley pre-development study (230797), $237,000 for Stagville Memorial (230799), and a $21.3M capital project amendment (230824). Public Health Director Rod Jenkins answered Commissioner Carter's questions on recruiting environmental health specialists and school nurses.

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 23-0828: Expedited Hearing Request for UDO Amendment TC23005 (Conservation Subdivisions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Curtis Massey and Planning Director Sara Young requested suspending the rules to approve an expedited public hearing schedule for UDO Section 6.2.4 / Paragraph 6.4 (TC23005) due to pending litigation challenging whether general purpose statements are mandatory subdivision standards. The board voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and 5-0 to adopt the expedited-hearing resolution.

agenda_items.title: Durham Transit Plan FY24 Q2 Work Program Amendments and Bus Speed & Reliability Study
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Administrative Officer Brandy Minor, DCHC MPO Executive Director Doug Plachcinski, and GoTriangle Assistant Finance Director Steven Schlossberg presented two FY24 Q2 Transit Plan amendments totaling $139,550 net: GoTriangle's mobile ticketing open-payment upgrade ($75,550 gross, $29,550 net) ahead of July 1, 2024 fare return, and Durham County's $110,000 share of the $850,000 regional FAST 2 BRT/highway transit study. Staff also briefed the board on the countywide Bus Speed and Reliability Study, with commissioners stressing outreach after zero public comments, rider education, and coordination with the Comprehensive Plan and UDO.

agenda_items.title: Presentation 23-0821: Durham County 2025 General Reappraisal Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Introduced by Assistant County Manager Dwayne Brinson, newly appointed Tax Administrator Keyar Doyle and Deputy Assessor Starlin Beatty provided an update on the January 1, 2025 general reappraisal. They reviewed Durham County's rapid population growth past 350,000 residents, the transition to a four-year reappraisal cycle, and how comparable market sales drive tax value adjustments.

agenda_items.title: Harm Reduction and Opioid Settlement Funding Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health staff presented outcomes from syringe-services, naloxone, and xylazine test-strip distribution, noting federal grant restrictions against purchasing naloxone or sterile syringes and proposing opioid settlement funding for a dedicated harm-reduction specialist, supplies, peer outreach, and a library naloxone vending machine pilot. Commissioners asked about youth overdose prevention and naloxone availability in schools.

agenda_items.title: Juvenile Crime Prevention Council (JCPC) Annual Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: JCPC Chair Kevin McIver, NC DPS consultant Eddie Cruz, and Justice Services manager Mark Strange reviewed the $701,001 state allocation (with a 15% county match), monthly and annual monitoring of funded youth programs, waitlists, and unspent-fund reversions caused by staffing vacancies. Commissioners discussed school attendance ties, evening/night offense timing, and the recent state pay-raise resolution for detention workers and court counselors.

agenda_items.title: Presentation 23-0827: Durham County Blasting Permit Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OES Director Jim Groves, Assistant Fire Marshal Greg Bowden, and City Fire Marshal Chief Joey Morton and Deputy Chief Chris Wilcox explained statutory authority under NCGS 153A and NC Fire Code Chapter 5607, noting that 24-hour resident notification currently applies only to buildings within 500 feet—leaving rural sites with repeat blasting unnotified. Commissioners expressed support for exploring a stronger local blasting ordinance and closer City-County coordination.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners addressed public emails regarding the October 23 joint statement by Allam and Burns on rising Islamophobia and anti-Semitism, discussed new homelessness tiny-home and Justice Services data-sharing committees, and reviewed planning for Sunday library hours. Commissioner Carter questioned keeping undefined commissioner comment slots on work-session agendas before the board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under GS 143-318.11(a)(5) and adjourned at 06:11:54.

meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and all five commissioners convened on October 23, 2023, approving prior minutes (5-0) and voting unanimously (5-0) to appoint and swear in Keyar Doyle as Durham County Tax Administrator. disagreements.issue: UDO Text Amendment TC2302 (23-0783) Aligning Ordinance with Comprehensive Plan and Urban Growth Boundary Procedures
disagreements.summary: The board split 4-1 on adopting UDO Text Amendment TC2302 following public outcry over urban growth boundary expansions, Lick Creek and Falls Lake environmental impacts, and confusion over how the Comprehensive Plan had been approved on consent.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt TC2302 as the minimum procedural alignment needed to implement the adopted Comprehensive Plan while pursuing the UDO rewrite and blasting-permit reforms.
side_a_arguments: TC2302 only updates UDO references (Future Land Use Map to Place Type Map, biennial assessment reporting, and Downtown Design District boundaries) to match the already-adopted Comprehensive Plan.
Residents were heard on both sides of the urban growth boundary, and the Comprehensive Plan guarantees utility access and affordable housing policies in new growth areas.
Deeper zoning and conservation protections will be addressed during the upcoming UDO rewrite and City-County blasting permit review.
disagreements.side_b_position: Dissent against adopting TC2302 (1 nay vote; individual dissenter unnamed in voice vote), reflecting public concerns over overdevelopment and lack of transparency.
side_b_arguments: Public speakers opposed expanding subdivisions bisecting Lick Creek and threatening Falls Lake and Perry Farms.

Commissioners acknowledged residents did not realize they could request pulling the Comprehensive Plan from the prior consent agenda and expressed concern about missing markup/maps in the earlier packet.
disagreements.resolution: Both TC2302 (23-0783) and its NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 4-1 on voice votes.

disagreements.issue: Phased Grading Acreage Limits, Tree Preservation Tiers, and Enforcement in UDO Text Amendment 23-0687 (TC2200004)
disagreements.summary: The board split 3-2 over UDO Text Amendment TC2200004, debating whether a 50-acre phase cap and tiered tree-preservation rules went far enough to curb mass grading, buffer clearing, and sediment runoff into Lick Creek.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve TC2200004 as an immediate step forward that prevents unphased clear-cutting, avoids high-density loopholes, and can be strengthened during the UDO rewrite.
side_a_arguments: Requiring tree preservation within each phase prevents developers from clear-cutting an entire 50+ acre tract at once and clustering saved trees on one edge.
Unlike Cary's three-tier rule that exempts developments above 8 dwelling units per acre from grading limits, Durham's rule applies across all applicable projects.
City Council already passed the amendment unanimously, and rejecting or delaying it would postpone environmental protections while staff prepares the UDO rewrite.
disagreements.side_b_position: Dissent against adopting TC2200004 as drafted (2 nay votes on voice vote), arguing the 50-acre phase cap and enforcement mechanisms fail to match stricter peer limits or stop developer damage.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Burns questioned why Durham allowed 50-acre phases rather than adopting the 20–25 acre mass-grading limits used by Cary, Raleigh, or Wake Forest.
Critics and public speakers pointed to continued sediment runoff into Lick Creek, utility/buffer disturbance exceptions, and perceived delays in enforcement despite added county inspection positions.
disagreements.resolution: Both TC2200004 (23-0687) and its NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement passed 3-2 on voice votes.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners - Work Session for Sep. 5, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 5, 2023 Board of County Commissioners work session, with all five commissioners reviewing proposed regular-session consent items ranging from Double Bucks ARPA funding and HHS HVAC repairs to public health grants, Triangle Wastewater Treatment Plant rehabilitation, and a Durham-to-Roxboro Rail Trail grant support letter. Work session briefings covered Unified Development Ordinance text amendment TC22004 on phased development and tree preservation, Durham Open Space and Trails Commission interlocal updates, DSS eviction diversion and Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) gaps, opioid harm reduction, strategic planning, and a major $15.8 million ARPA realignment toward joint City-County affordable housing, homelessness services, and water/sewer infrastructure. Under an added action item moved from August 28, the board voted 4-0 to suspend its rules and shorten the Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees appointment to a two-year term before appointing Dr. Tara Fikes via ballot, followed by a brief closed session on real property acquisition and employment negotiations.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order, read the public charge, noted no speakers had signed up for Citizens' Comments, and guided the board through consent agenda review. Commissioners questioned Detention Center maintenance technical budget adjustments, EMS Operative IQ fleet software versus RTA compatibility ($46,200), Farmer Foodshare's selection over Bellwoods Residential Solutions as Double Bucks ARPA fiscal sponsor ($483,972), and GAP certification barriers for local farms selling to Durham Public Schools. Staff also reviewed HHS HVAC split-system upgrades ($421,500), five NCDHHS Public Health epidemiology/communicable-disease grants, a $1,263,635 Triangle WWTP rehabilitation package, a $400,000 Whispering Pines stream restoration grant, a $500,000 Durham-to-Roxboro Rail Trail planning grant support letter, and moved the Farmland Preservation Board presentation to the upcoming regular agenda.

agenda_items.title: 23-0658: UDO Text Amendment (TC22004) on Phased Development and Tree Preservation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Robin Schultz and Planning Director Sara Young presented UDO text amendment TC22004, capping development phases at 50 acres, triggering tiered tree preservation at 35 acres (20% preservation for 35-acre suburban developments and 30% for larger sites), adding five-foot and ten-foot grading setbacks near buffers, and requiring 0.6 opacity boundary buffers across all tiers. Commissioners pressed staff on clear-cutting enforcement, monitoring loopholes on small lots, and why the affordable housing density/preservation incentive stops at 80% AMI rather than targeting deeper 30%-50% AMI need. Staff confirmed the Planning Commission and JCCPC reviewed the measure ahead of the September 11 public hearing.

agenda_items.title: 23-0638: Durham Open Space and Trails Commission (DOST) Interlocal Agreement Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff planner Karl Kaszmarek outlined proposed updates to the Durham Open Space and Trails Commission interlocal agreement to adopt gender-neutral language, substitute 'resident' for 'citizen,' reduce maximum membership from 30 to 17 by removing self-appointed and Planning Commission seats, convert Council and BOCC liaisons to non-voting ex-officio status, and authorize $50 stipend eligibility. Commissioners raised brief clarifying questions on term alignment and city-county coordination.

agenda_items.title: 23-0652: DSS Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) and Emergency Rental Assistance (ERAP) Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DSS staff reported that LIHR received 353 applications after reopening (with ~200 still pending) and recommended shifting to a year-round application window and covering 100% of tax bills for seniors 60+ at or below 30% AMI. Staff also warned that remaining NC PRO 2.0 emergency rental assistance funds ($1.6M-$1.8M of $7.1M total, spending ~$240,000/month) would be exhausted around March 2024 amid roughly 7,295 annual eviction filings. Commissioners Heidi Carter, Wendy Jacobs, and Nimasheena Burns urged immediate City-County coordination on sustainable eviction diversion funding and courtroom social worker capacity.

agenda_items.title: 23-0660: ACEs, Resilience, and Opioid Crisis / Harm Reduction Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, Jess Baskett, Dr. Jeff Jenks, Lindsay Bickers-Bock, and Dennis Hamlet reviewed Durham County's trauma-informed Community Resiliency Model (CRM) training expansion, juvenile/youth policy priorities, and $400,000 in FY24 opioid settlement funding for Community Linkages to Care. Presenters detailed overdose trends, peer support outreach, naloxone distribution and vending machines, and the addition of xylazine test strips to harm reduction kits, while commissioners asked about school-based resilience coordination and detention center linkage outcomes.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Forward 2029 Strategic Planning Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Office of Strategy and Performance staff presented the roadmap for the FY2025-2029 'Durham County Forward 2029' strategic plan in partnership with consultant Dr. Monica Allen (Insight Performance Management Group). Staff outlined seven focus areas, community and employee engagement schedules, and plans to present a draft strategic framework in February 2024.

agenda_items.title: 23-0663: Naming Committee Request for Carl D. Hodges Conference Room (Ag Building)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Naming Committee representatives presented options to name the Agriculture Building conference room (Rooms 129A/B) in honor of Cooperative Extension leader Carl D. Hodges, noting Option 2 plaque placement as the preferred design ahead of the September 11 public hearing.

agenda_items.title: 23-0669: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Status and Realignment Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Claudia Hager and staff reported that roughly 40% ($24 million across 39 projects) of Durham County's $62.4 million ARPA award had been encumbered and proposed realigning approximately $15.8 million—largely from unallocated broadband/state-matched funds—into $3.5 million for joint City-County affordable housing (including $700,000 for McKissick Square/Geer Street and $2 million for Southside Phases 3-4), $2 million for Homeless Services Center planning, senior home repair, land trust support, $6 million in water/sewer infrastructure, and DSS Medicaid-expansion ERP upgrades. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Heidi Carter pressed staff to address eviction diversion gaps and capital housing needs for re-entering mothers and children.

agenda_items.title: 23-0674: Board Discussion and Vote on Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following up on the August 28 deferral, County Attorney Al Andrews advised that modifying the appointment ballot required suspending board rules. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns moved to suspend the rules and then moved to convert the open Durham Tech Board of Trustees seat from a four-year to a two-year term to preserve board continuity amid state legislative changes, both passing 4-0; Attorney Andrews then announced the board's ballot selection appointing Dr. Tara Fikes to the two-year term.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (Suspend Rules; Two-Year Term; Ballot Appointment of Dr. Tara Fikes)

agenda_items.discussion_summary: At 06:13:08, the board recessed into closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) and (a)(6) to instruct staff regarding real property acquisition terms and employment contract compensation. Reconvening at 06:26:50, Chair Howerton reported that direction was given to staff with no action taken, and the board adjourned by voice vote at 06:27:00.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Voice vote to enter closed session and adjourn)

meetings.title: Special Joint City Council & Board of County Commissioners Comprehensive Plan Public Hearing
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Mayor Elaine O'Neal co-presided over the August 31, 2023 Special Joint City Council and Board of County Commissioners Public Hearing to take community testimony on the draft Durham Comprehensive Plan ahead of formal October adoption votes. City-County Planning Department staff (Lisa Miller and Sara Young) outlined the growth management strategy, proposed reducing the existing 2005 Suburban Tier by approximately 10.8 square miles to establish the Urban Growth Boundary (UGB) while accommodating a projected 143,000 additional housing units, and introduced edits to Policies 164 and 165 along with six contested fringe areas. Roughly sixty-five in-person and remote speakers debated keeping Arrowhead, Patterson Road, Cheek/Redwood Road, and Farrington Mill Road inside versus outside the UGB and Southeast Future Growth Area, weighing affordable housing supply and landowner equity against watershed protection, septic/infrastructure capacity, and rural preservation; no board votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Joint Public Hearing Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Elaine O'Neal and Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the joint meeting and conducted roll calls confirming all five County Commissioners (Howerton, Jacobs, Burns, Allam, Carter) and City Council members were present. Chair Howerton read the public charge and confirmed that over 50 in-person speakers and 15+ virtual speakers had registered, clarifying that elected officials would listen without back-and-forth debate and deliberate separately in subsequent meetings.

agenda_items.title: Staff Presentation: Draft Durham Comprehensive Plan, UGB Reduction, and Policies 164-165
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Planning Assistant Director Lisa Miller and Director Sara Young summarized the three-year Comprehensive Plan process, emphasizing smart infill growth, housing supply estimates (143,000 potential units versus 60,000 needed by 2050), and the proposed 10.8-square-mile reduction from the 2005 Suburban Tier to form the Urban Growth Boundary. Staff highlighted Planning Commission-recommended edits to Policy 165 requiring case-by-case map amendments to demonstrate affordable housing, environmental, and equity benefits, and Policy 164 mandating biennial UGB assessments. Staff also reviewed six disputed areas—Stagville/Old Oxford, Farrington Mill, Patterson Road, Cheek/Redwood, Hamlin Road, and the northwest corner of the Southeast Future Growth Area.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Testimony on Comprehensive Plan, Urban Growth Boundary, and Rural Preservation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Across nearly three hours of in-person and remote testimony, Arrowhead landowner Adam Abram, attorney Patrick Byker, homebuilders representatives (John Hasbrouck, Holly Fraccaro), engineers (Tim Sivers), and landowners on Patterson, Cheek, and Farrington Mill Roads urged retaining existing Suburban Tier parcels in the UGB to support housing affordability, prevent low-density two-acre sprawl, and protect property values. Conversely, numerous Arrowhead and Southeast Durham residents, Care for Durham conservation advocates, coalition speakers (Coalition for Affordable Housing and Transit), and environmental voices cited Policy 166 watershed rules, Voluntary Agricultural District pledges, Forest View Elementary overcrowding (104% capacity), Lick Creek stormwater degradation, and transit/infrastructure costs in supporting the staff/Planning Commission map keeping Arrowhead and rural fringe tracts outside the UGB. Chair Howerton closed the public hearing at 03:13:42 without board action.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (Public hearing closed for future board deliberation)

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Aug. 28, 2023
disagreements.issue: Procedural Rules and Term-Length Precedent for Deferring the Durham Tech Board of Trustees Appointment
disagreements.summary: During agenda adjustments, Commissioner Nida Allam moved to pull and defer the Durham Technical Community College Board of Trustees appointment from August 28 to the September 5 work session to address whether reappointing a term-limited incumbent to an expired slot yields a full term or shortened term, sparking pushback from Chair Brenda A. Howerton over past board precedent.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pull the Durham Tech appointment until September 5 so the board can examine bylaws and deliberate whether the expired/term-limited seat should be filled for a full or partial term.
side_a_arguments: No other applicants were considered for the expired term-limited seat, so the full board needs time to discuss the term-length implication before voting.
Under the current board's tenure since Commissioners Allam and Burns joined, a reappointment structured this way had not previously occurred.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain awareness that prior Boards of Commissioners have filled similar expired/term-limited appointments under existing bylaws and require staff to document historical precedent if delaying the vote.
side_b_arguments: While not done since the two newest commissioners took office, the board had handled similar appointments under its bylaws in earlier years.
Directed staff to pull historical records of prior appointments to inform the discussion.
disagreements.resolution: The board approved pulling the Durham Tech Board of Trustees vote to the September 5, 2023 work session, where it subsequently voted 4-0 to suspend the rules, set a two-year term, and appoint Dr. Tara Fikes.

meetings.title: Joint Board of County Commissioners and Durham Public Schools Board of Education Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Board of Education Chair Bettina Umstead co-convened the August 15, 2023 Joint BOCC/BOE Meeting (with Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs presiding for the final 15 minutes after Chair Howerton departed at 01:56:50). Durham Public Schools officials presented a multi-year Operational Services Life Safety Plan identifying a $2.6 million shortfall and ~$500,000 in annual maintenance needs across aging schools, followed by an in-depth Growing Together Initiative briefing outlining five new elementary regions, 50/50 neighborhood walk-zone and lottery application seats, K-12 Arts/Global Languages/STEM pathways, and $18 million in MacKenzie Scott philanthropy. Board members from both bodies engaged in candid discussion regarding racial and socioeconomic integration, retaining white and middle-class families, and an estimated $6.4 million annual DPS revenue loss from North Carolina Opportunity Scholarship expansion by 2026, before receiving back-to-school hiring updates showing 5.8% teacher vacancies, 68 bus driver openings, and the $90 million new Northern High School opening; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Welcome and DPS Operational Services Life Safety Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda A. Howerton and BOE Chair Bettina Umstead opened the joint meeting, turning the floor to DPS COO Larry Johnson, Facilities Executive Director Frederick Davis, and Durham County Fire Marshal Chief Chris Shepard to present the Life Safety Plan. Officials reported that fire and life-safety inspections across aging facilities required a three-to-five-year remediation plan covering fire barriers, rated doors, dampers, and egress signage, estimating $4.3 million in identified projects plus ~$2.5 million TBD (leaving a $2.6 million gap after $1.7 million in ESSER funds) alongside roughly $500,000 in recurring annual upkeep. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Heidi Carter praised the collaborative preventive safety inventory.

agenda_items.title: DPS Growing Together Initiative Update (Elementary Regions, Magnets, and Equity Strategy)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS Deputy Superintendent Dr. Debbie Pittman, Executive Director Matthew Palmer, and Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga presented implementation of the 'Growing Together' student assignment plan launching in 2024-25 (with secondary updates in 2025-26), establishing five geographic elementary regions, K-12 Arts/Global Languages/STEM theme alignment, transitioning School for Creative Studies to grades 6-8, and splitting application school access into 50% neighborhood walk-zone and 50% lottery seats backed by $18 million from MacKenzie Scott's gift. Commissioners and school board members engaged in extensive dialogue over building community buy-in across all demographics, reducing transportation bottlenecks, and combating an estimated $6.4 million annual loss to expanded state Opportunity Scholarship vouchers by 2026-27.

agenda_items.title: Back-to-School Readiness, Educator Recruitment/Retention, and Northern High School Opening
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS officials Dr. Stacey Stewart, Dr. Alverez Lassiter, and Frederick Davis briefed both boards on back-to-school projections (31,044 expected traditional-calendar and year-round students), workforce metrics showing instructional vacancies down to 5.8% (4.9% overall) alongside 68 ongoing bus driver vacancies, and educator housing collaborations including Self-Help Credit Union's South Square townhomes and Duke TeachHouse. Chair Howerton departed at 01:56:50, passing the gavel to Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs, as Davis showcased the opening of the $90 million new Northern High School (ahead of a September 14 ribbon cutting); members accepted the Durham Pre-K update as written and adjourned without public comments at 02:11:53.

disagreements.meeting_title: Joint Board of County Commissioners and Durham Public Schools Board of Education Meeting
disagreements.issue: Racial/Socioeconomic Integration Strategy and State Voucher Threats Under DPS Growing Together
disagreements.summary: During the Growing Together briefing, commissioners and school board members debated how aggressively the new five-region elementary model should balance neighborhood walk zones against socioeconomic diversity and retaining affluent/white families amid North Carolina's expansion of universal Opportunity Scholarship vouchers.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prioritize equitable neighborhood walk-zone access and targeted investments in historically underserved schools while countering family flight and voucher losses through visible program quality across all five regions.
side_a_arguments: Neighborhood schools must be strengthened with Arts, Global Languages, and STEM programming so families remain in public schools rather than exiting to charters or private vouchers.
State budget projections estimate $6.4 million in annual DPS losses by 2026-27 as voucher uptake grows from 945 to over 2,600 students.
disagreements.side_b_position: Scrutinize whether the 50% walk-zone / 50% lottery balance and geographic boundaries will inadvertently deepen racial and socioeconomic segregation as new schools open.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners questioned whether walk-zone concentrations could re-segregate certain campuses without active diversity monitoring and accessible magnet transportation.
Requested longitudinal demographic tracking to evaluate whether student assignment shifts preserve county-wide integration goals.
disagreements.resolution: Informational joint discussion concluded without formal action; DPS staff committed to monitoring enrollment demographics, launching magnet/application lotteries in January 2024, and returning with implementation updates.

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Jul. 10, 2023
disagreements.issue: Whether to Proceed With or Defer the ABC Board Appointment Pending Investigation of Website Posting Complaint
disagreements.summary: Following Jacqueline Wagstaff's citizen complaint that Durham County's website listed 'no vacancies' for the ABC Board throughout June, commissioners debated whether to hold the appointment and whether holding without immediately reopening applications accomplished fairness.
disagreements.side_a_position: Hold off on voting on the ABC Board appointment until staff investigates and verifies that the public application process was free of technical irregularities.
side_a_arguments: Deferring a single non-regulatory advisory/board appointment by one cycle preserves public trust without operational harm.
Staff needs time to verify website audit logs before finalizing an appointment rather than deciding whether to re-advertise prematurely.
disagreements.side_b_position: Questioned the utility of delaying the vote for a month unless new applications would also be accepted if warranted, while willing to defer if verification is the goal.
side_b_arguments: If applications are not reopened, holding a vote on the same applicant pool for one month may not change the substance of the complaint unless irregularities trigger re-advertising.
disagreements.resolution: Resolved by board consensus to hold the ABC Board appointment until the late August meeting pending County Attorney and Clerk verification of the online application posting, with re-advertising triggered only if irregularities were found.

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Jun. 26, 2023
disagreements.issue: Equity Guarantees, HBCU/School Access, and MWBE Benchmarks for Proposed Regional Multi-Sport Complex
disagreements.summary: Following Discover Durham and the Durham Sports Commission's presentation on a major 250,000-sq-ft indoor and 37-acre outdoor sports complex, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged staff to replace broad promises with binding equity, local access, and MWBE commitments before seeking county funds.
disagreements.side_a_position: Do not advance county support without written details on MWBE inclusion, affordable local resident/youth access, hotel coordination, and consultation with HBCU (NCCU) and high school athletic leadership.
side_a_arguments: Local programs such as NCCU basketball lack adequate practice courts and local youth are often priced out of tourism-driven facilities.
The board's equity standards require concrete written access, minority/women-owned contracting plans, and community stakeholder outreach—not general assurances.
disagreements.side_b_position: Continue feasibility scoping toward a fall funding and site recommendation centered on sports tourism economic impact and the 2029 World University Games.
side_b_arguments: Durham lacks competitive indoor/outdoor tournament capacity compared with peer communities, missing out on youth access and sports-tourism revenue.
Staff welcomed the feedback and pledged to return in the fall with expanded equity, access, and facility-sharing details.
disagreements.resolution: Informational update concluded with no vote; presenters committed to incorporating Burns's MWBE, HBCU, and local access benchmarks into the fall recommendation.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners - Regular Session for Jun. 12, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 12, 2023 regular session with all five commissioners present, highlighted by the unanimous 5-0 adoption of Durham County's FY 2023-24 $844,940,496 Annual Budget Ordinance featuring a 3-cent property tax increase, a $19.22/hour county living wage floor, $187.95 million for Durham Public Schools (+$10.8M / $4,650 per pupil), $7.9 million for Durham Pre-K, $2.4 million for Durham Tech scholarships, and new Familiar Faces and opioid MAT investments. To comply with Session Law 2021-191 conflict-of-interest rules, the board separately passed 4-0-1 three nonprofit budget amendments for Downtown Durham Inc. ($200,000), Museum of Durham History ($76,000), and the NC Museum of Life and Science ($2,358,124). Commissioners also passed 5-0 a landmark Chapter 4 Animal Control ordinance amendment establishing a Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Release (TNVR) program for community cats, approved initial findings and public-hearing resolutions 5-0 for $60 million in GO Refunding Bonds Series 2023, executed two pulled ARPA youth and maternal-health contracts 5-0, and granted Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs an excused absence for June 26.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, Minutes (May 1 & May 8), and Ceremonial Resolutions (Conan Morgan & Pride Month)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the regular session, led approval of the May 1 work session and May 8 regular session minutes 5-0, and joined commissioners in reading resolution 23-0415 mourning political strategist and 2022 bond consultant Conan Traval Morgan. Howerton then issued Pride Month proclamation 23-0422, accepted by LGBTQ Center of Durham interim director Natalie who noted a $25,000 matching challenge and LGBTQ training with Wake County, alongside comments from Commissioners Burns, Allam, Jacobs, and Howerton lifting up Juneteenth and anti-discrimination protections; staff also acknowledged CIO Greg Marrow's PTI and GovTech awards (23-0385/0386).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 23-0296 through 23-0435, Excluding 23-0425, 23-0433, 23-0434)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and commissioners pulled item 23-0425 (GO Refunding Bonds) and items 23-0433 and 23-0434 (ARPA community grant contracts) for separate discussion. The remaining consent agenda items were moved, seconded, and passed 5-0 by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: 23-0414: Adoption of FY 2023-24 Annual Budget Ordinance ($844,940,496)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public comment by Dewan Langley (requesting $250,000 for Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation and $210,330 for JCPC while thanking County Manager Kimberly Sowell for $105,300 added to JCPC), the board voted 5-0 to adopt the FY 2023-24 Annual Budget Ordinance totaling $844,940,496. Commissioners highlighted the $19.22/hour minimum wage floor, +$10.8M for DPS ($187,951,627 total / $4,650 per pupil plus classified/certified raises), $7.9M for Pre-K, $2.4M for Durham Tech Promise, Familiar Faces data integration, detention center MAT medical leadership, 17 net new positions (incl. Elections, Veterans, Stormwater outreach) alongside $2.5M in position reductions, and concern over projected $6.4M annual DPS losses to state Opportunity Scholarship vouchers.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Budget Work Session #4 on June 5, 2023, as commissioners worked with County Manager Kimberly Sowell, Budget Director Keith Lane, and staff to finalize consensus items ahead of the June 12 FY 2023-24 budget adoption vote. Three major policy clashes emerged during the session: Commissioners scrutinized the Animal Protection Society (APS) of Durham's $201,958 (23%) shelter funding increase and sole-source contract longevity before reaching a 3-commissioner consensus to fund the request pending operational follow-up; Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs clashed with Commissioner Heidi Carter over threatening to withhold future school capital funding until Durham Public Schools presents reuse plans for the former Northern High School and Durham School of the Arts campuses; and Commissioners Carter, Allam, and Jacobs pushed back against Chair Howerton's push to add $80,000 for two Boys and Girls Club vans directly onto the add/delete list outside departmental nonprofit vetting. Commissioners also discussed $100,000 for advisory board stipends ($50 in-person / $25 virtual), $1.9 billion in 10-year Capital Improvement Plan cost escalations, Museum of Durham History expansion timing, RTP's 3.5-cent special tax district request, and Session Law 2021-191 recusal compliance; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: 23-0406: Animal Protection Society (APS) of Durham FY24 Budget Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: APS Director Shafonda Allen and staff presented a $201,958 (23%) contract increase to $1,080,333 for running the county animal shelter, alongside Manager Sowell's proposed flat/10% alternatives. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned the 30-year sole-source relationship, capacity/intake hours, reserve balances, and audit transparency, while Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs praised APS's 33-year partnership, volunteer leverage, and modest 3% wage ask, requesting benchmarking data against peer counties. Near the end of the session (03:13:00), three commissioners gave an informal thumbs-up to incorporate the full $201,958 increase subject to follow-up reporting on shelter hours and benchmarks.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Informal consensus (3 commissioners thumbs-up for $201,958 increase)

agenda_items.title: 23-0407: Boards and Commissions Stipend Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Shannon Trapp and Clerk Monica Wallace outlined the $100,000 FY24 stipend program paying appointed volunteers $50 per in-person meeting and $25 per virtual meeting to offset participation barriers, leaving implementation details such as joint City-County boards to board guidance. Commissioner Heidi Carter urged matching the City of Durham's flat $50 rate regardless of format on joint boards so county appointees are not treated inequitably.

agenda_items.title: Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Update and Surplus School Site Reuse Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane and Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager reviewed the $1.9 billion 10-year Capital Improvement Plan, highlighting severe construction escalations (Animal Shelter rising from $30M to $45M-$50M; new Durham School of the Arts nearing $200M) and plans for a 2026 GO bond referendum. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs sparked a sharp debate by warning she would vote against future school capital projects unless DPS delivers concrete reuse plans for vacated Northern High School and DSA campuses, while Commissioner Heidi Carter urged respecting the elected Board of Education's authority.

agenda_items.title: Museum of Durham History Supplemental Funding Request ($568k Design & $108k Operations)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Museum Executive Director Patrick Mucklow requested $568,000 toward design costs at 500 West Main Street and $108,000 in annual operating/salary support as the museum outgrows the 1938 Hubbs/Admin Annex site. County Manager Kimberly Sowell and staff recommended deferring capital design commitments outside the FY24 operating budget until the Joint City-County Facilities/Capital committee evaluates space needs alongside the Main Street renovation project.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Deferred outside FY24 operating budget

agenda_items.title: Add/Delete Budget List, Boys & Girls Club Van Request Debate, RTP Special Tax, and SL 2021-191 Recusals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reviewing the Add/Delete reconciliation sheet with David Ades and Keith Lane, commissioners discussed Boys & Girls Club's late $80,000 request for two student transport vans: Chair Howerton urged immediate funding for DPS youth transport, while Commissioners Carter, Allam, and Jacobs objected to bypassing staff/departmental nonprofit vetting via the add/delete list (ultimately directing staff to explore surplus vehicles or ARPA funding while adopting a formal nonprofit vetting policy). Commissioners also reviewed Research Triangle Park's 3.5-cent special tax district request (noting property-tax mechanics) and County Attorney guidance on Session Law 2021-191 separate voting for boards where commissioners serve as directors.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Direction to staff (No formal votes)

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
disagreements.issue: Magnitude and Oversight of APS Shelter Funding Increase (23% / $201,958 vs. Flat / 10%)
disagreements.summary: Commissioners split over whether to fully grant the Animal Protection Society of Durham's 23% ($201,958) funding increase given its 30-year non-competitive sole-source contract and capacity pauses, or honor its full operating/wage request.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support full $201,958 funding in light of APS's 33-year partnership, heavy private fundraising, 650+ volunteers, and overdue staff wage increases.
side_a_arguments: The County covers only ~34% ($841,000) of the shelter budget while APS fundraises nearly three-quarters of total costs and provides immense volunteer labor value.
APS's requested 3% wage adjustment is modest given county employees are moving to a $19.22/hr living wage floor.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question an immediate 23% increase without recent competitive RFPs, clearer reserve/profit-and-loss separation, and operational review of intake capacity pauses.
side_b_arguments: Holding a sole-source shelter contract for roughly 30 years without competitive RFPs warrants stronger financial audit review and performance transparency.
At points when the shelter hit capacity, intake stalled; requested clearer operational reporting before committing permanent increases.
disagreements.resolution: Resolved via informal work-session poll at 03:13:00 with three commissioners giving thumbs-up to add the $201,958 APS increase to the FY24 budget subject to follow-up data on shelter hours and peer benchmarks; subsequently enacted in the June 12 budget.

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
disagreements.issue: Conditioning Future School Capital Funding on DPS Reuse Plans for Surplus Campuses
disagreements.summary: During the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan briefing, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Heidi Carter disagreed over whether the board should leverage county bond/capital approvals to force DPS reuse plans for vacated Northern High School and Durham School of the Arts sites.
disagreements.side_a_position: Withhold support for new school capital allocations unless DPS produces concrete reuse plans for vacated public school facilities.
side_a_arguments: Escalating bond costs (such as DSA rising toward $200 million) require joint city-county-school discipline so aging campuses are not left vacant or underutilized.
Commissioners control capital funding and must demand coordinated multi-agency planning.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer to the elected Board of Education's statutory governance over school facility disposition and reuse decisions rather than imposing capital vetoes.
side_b_arguments: School board members are separately elected officials accountable to voters for managing DPS property decisions.
Capital funding decisions should support joint student needs without undermining school board autonomy.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken during the CIP briefing; County staff noted ongoing multi-agency coordination ahead of the 2026 bond cycle.

disagreements.meeting_title: Board of County Commissioners - Budget Work Session #4 (June 5, 2023)
disagreements.issue: Boys & Girls Club $80,000 Van Request and Nonprofit Vetting Integrity in the Add/Delete Process
disagreements.summary: A sharp disagreement broke out over Chair Brenda A. Howerton's push to insert $80,000 for two Boys and Girls Club transport vans into the budget add/delete list, with three commissioners warning the request bypassed departmental nonprofit vetting.
disagreements.side_a_position: Do not insert unvetted mid-budget nonprofit requests onto the add/delete list outside established departmental and subject-matter-expert review.
side_a_arguments: Bypassing competitive grants and staff vetting sets a precedent that politicizes the add/delete process and creates inequities among worthy local nonprofits.
Requests from outside organizations must run through consistent formal policy criteria and ARPA/surplus channels rather than last-minute commissioner add-ons.
disagreements.side_b_position: Act urgently to fund two vans for the Boys and Girls Club so vulnerable Durham Public Schools students have safe transportation to after-school programming.
side_b_arguments: The Boys and Girls Club's existing vans are deteriorating and urgent youth transportation needs cannot wait until another budget cycle.
With only weeks left before adoption, commissioners must find an immediate way to support children already served by DPS.
disagreements.resolution: Although Commissioner Carter briefly offered collegial compromise, commissioners reached consensus not to insert the $80,000 into the general operating add/delete list, instead directing County Manager Sowell to explore surplus county vans or ARPA options and establish a clear nonprofit budget-request policy.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session - June 5, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 5, 2023 BOCC Work Session, which opened with virtual public comment urging commissioners to consider Durham Police Department gun violence data affecting Black boys and young men when finalizing budget allocations. The board unanimously approved an agenda adjustment adding a resolution honoring the late Conan Morgan to the June 12 regular session consent agenda and reviewed 17 consent items covering wastewater infrastructure, Youth Home security equipment, staffing contracts, and volunteer fire department agreements. Commissioners also heard presentations on the county's refined facility naming policy, the Durham County Transit Plan work program and GoTriangle microtransit budget adjustments, and upcoming affordable housing and ARPA RFP projects before adjourning to transition to the courthouse for afternoon budget deliberations.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Gun Violence Data and Budget Priorities
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Warren Langley of the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation spoke virtually during the public comment period, referencing Durham Police Department data showing that Black boys and young men are overwhelmingly affected by gun violence. He urged the Board of County Commissioners to weigh those data calls as they allocate funding in the upcoming FY23-24 budget. No other speakers signed up in person or virtually.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Adjustment: Resolution Honoring the Late Conan Morgan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A commissioner moved to suspend the rules and add a resolution honoring the late Conan Morgan to the consent agenda so that it could be approved, sent to the family, and read in its entirety at the upcoming Monday regular session. After brief procedural clarification with the chair, the motion was seconded and approved unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (17 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell walked the board through 17 consent agenda items for the upcoming regular session, including a $900,000 sewer utility fund balance appropriation and $817,993 sole-source exemption for Triangle Wastewater Treatment Plant rotors and gearboxes (23-0296), a millimeter-wave scanner for the new Durham County Youth Home (23-0325), a charter resolution renaming Triangle J Council of Governments to Central Pines Regional Council (23-0348), and multiple staffing and aeration basin service contracts. Regarding item 23-0370 on fire protection contracts with Bahama, Lebanon, and Redwood VFDs and extensions with Eno and New Hope VFDs, a commissioner asked to receive the planned July service-change presentation earlier given budget implications, and staff also committed to emailing a requested model report before Monday.

agenda_items.title: County Facility Naming Policy and Naming Committee Recommendation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented the naming committee's work—including County Attorney Allen Andrews, Deborah Craig-Ray, and Julio Delgado—on refining Durham County's facility naming policy, review workflow, and placement options (including Option 3 on the left side upon entry). The next steps outlined were a public hearing and final approval vote on June 26, 2023, followed by an unveiling event on July 14, with commissioners thanking staff and noting comparisons to school district naming rules.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Transit Plan Work Program and GoTriangle Microtransit Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DCHC MPO Executive Director Doug Plachinski and transit staff presented the annual Transit Plan work program, project implementation staffing, equity and MWBE participation metrics, and accountability framework. Discussion addressed GoTriangle's ~$670,000 microtransit pilot exceeding its current-year budget because trips duplicated fixed-route bus corridors, requiring rule adjustments for phase two, as well as a $1.4 million funding reduction after GoTriangle removed 50% of the vehicle rental tax allocation effective July 2023. The work program was scheduled for Monday's consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: Affordable Housing Projects and ARPA/RFP Funding Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff member Claudia presented affordable housing pipeline items and upcoming RFP funding recommendations, including Reinvestment Partners' Harriet's Place (15 studio units at or below 30% AMI), McCormack Baron Salazar's maintenance and green-building standards, and Habitat for Humanity home repair and minor/substantial rehabilitation programs for seniors and households with disabilities. A commissioner raised cost concerns over Harriet's Place carrying a $5 million budget (~$400,000 per studio unit), while staff noted recommended funding amounts for all RFP categories—including a day center—would return to the board.
