meetings.title: Joint BOCC-Board of Education Meeting for January 31, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners and the Durham Public Schools (DPS) Board of Education held a joint meeting on January 31, 2023, opening with approval of the November 29, 2022 joint meeting minutes. DPS Chief Financial Officer Paul LeSieur presented a detailed accounting of approximately $158 million in federal COVID relief (ESSER I, II, and III) funding used for summer learning, temporary school support staff, IT cybersecurity, nutrition, transportation, and 13 workstation technicians, while warning of the upcoming fiscal cliff and noting five completed federal/state audits. Officials then reviewed DPS's early draft FY2024 baseline budget—discussing local funding for bus driver pay above $18 per hour, implementation of the classified staff salary study, teacher supplement increases ($833), ~$5 million in lapsed salaries, state Leandro underfunding, and tax pressures from the recently passed school bond. A DPS parent closed public comments with a five-point advocacy primer citing North Carolina's low national rankings in teacher pay and per-pupil funding, and commissioners praised the School Board for completing redistricting and adopting a new LGBTQI student policy.

agenda_items.title: Opening Quorum Check and Approval of November 29, 2022 Joint Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Board members waited briefly to confirm quorum, with Chair Brenda A. Howerton noting she would have to depart early and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs would cover. Once convened, a motion to approve the November 29, 2022 joint meeting minutes was moved, seconded, and approved.

agenda_items.title: DPS Federal COVID-19 / ESSER Funding Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS CFO Paul LeSieur walked through the district's CARES/ESSER I, CRRSA/ESSER II, and ARP/ESSER III funds (including $104.57 million in ESSER III and ~$158 million across major pots) deployed for summer learning, temporary school positions, student support services, IT cybersecurity, nutrition, transportation, and 13 workstation technicians supporting 1:1 devices. Officials discussed which recurring needs—such as the 13 technicians—would require local budget absorption once ESSER expires, and LeSieur noted DPS had already undergone five audits and monitoring visits through Q2 of FY23.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY24 DPS Budget, Classified/Teacher Pay, and Leandro Advocacy Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Officials discussed DPS's early draft FY24 baseline budget, highlighting local funds supporting bus driver pay above $18 per hour, classified salary study implementation (contingent on both County and State funding), an $833 teacher supplement increase, and ~$5 million in lapsed salaries used to cover gaps. Participants discussed North Carolina's failure to fund Leandro obligations and how joint county-school advocacy could educate parents on state underfunding. Commissioners requested staff vacancy figures, charter/homeschool enrollment data, and reminded members of potential tax impacts from the recently approved school bond alongside over $10 million in county ARPA investments supporting families and the DPS Foundation.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments and Closing Remarks on Redistricting and LGBTQI Student Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS parent Karthik Sundaramurthy shared a five-point advocacy primer covering competitive compensation, teacher pipeline, student mental health, readiness, and remedial plans, citing statistics that North Carolina ranks 38th in teacher pay, 48th in per-pupil spending, and 50th in funding effort. In closing remarks before adjournment, a commissioner congratulated the School Board on completing difficult school redistricting decisions and praised DPS's new LGBTQI student policy.

votes.item_title: Approval of November 29, 2022 Joint BOCC-Board of Education Meeting Minutes
votes.notes: Joint meeting of BOCC and DPS Board of Education; individual roll-call votes were not read.
votes.discussion_detail: A member moved and seconded approval of the November 29, 2022 joint meeting minutes, and the motion was approved.

meetings.title: BOCC - January 23, 2023 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham Board of County Commissioners reconvened from closed session with no action taken, approved the January 9, 2023 regular session minutes (5-0), and issued ceremonial proclamations honoring the North Carolina Central University 2022 Cricket Celebration Bowl championship football team and recognizing January 2023 as National Mentoring Month. Following a COVID-19 public health update noting 31% bivalent booster uptake locally, the Board unanimously approved (5-0) Item 23-0060, an interlocal agreement with the City of Durham and Budget Amendment 23BCC0057 appropriating $2,000,000 in General Fund fund balance for the Partnership for Equitable and Resilient Communities grant match after discussing the City-County funding split. The Board also received an informational presentation on the FY 2022 Annual Financial Audit and Annual Comprehensive Financial Report with no audit disagreements noted, and voted 5-0 to grant excused absences to Commissioners Nida Allam and Nimasheena Burns for the February 6 work session.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session Report, Public Charge, Pledge of Allegiance, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton reconvened the meeting from closed session, reporting that the Board provided direction to staff with no action taken, and read the public charge while Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs led the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Wallace read announcements covering COVID-19 vaccination clinic hours, the January 31 deadline for the $11.6 million National Opioid Settlement funding survey, the Durham Low Income Home Owner Relief Program, and Sheriff Clarence Birkhead's 'State of Urgency' youth gun violence play series with Durham Public Schools.

agenda_items.title: Approval of January 9, 2023 Regular Session Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton presented the January 9, 2023 regular session minutes for review and asked for any edits or a motion to approve. A motion and second were made with no revisions requested.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation Honoring North Carolina Central University 2022 Football Champions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board presented a resolution honoring the North Carolina Central University football team, Coach Trei Oliver, coaching and support staff, and student-athletes for winning the December 17, 2022 Cricket Celebration Bowl (41-34 in overtime over Jackson State University) and the 2022 HBCU national championship. University and team representatives thanked the Board for the recognition.

agenda_items.title: Proclamation Declaring January 2023 as National Mentoring Month
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs read a proclamation declaring January 2023 as National Mentoring Month in Durham County, highlighting the role of mentoring in academic engagement and youth development. Community mentoring leaders, including representatives from Sidekicks Academy and the Thomas Mentor Leadership Academy, spoke about supporting Durham Public Schools students and addressing youth violence.

agenda_items.title: COVID-19 and Public Health Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health staff reported on COVID-19 metrics, noting 645,354 total vaccine doses administered in Durham County but only 31% updated bivalent booster uptake among eligible residents (compared to 20% statewide) ahead of emerging variants such as XBB.1.5. Discussion also addressed ongoing wastewater screening and cumulative county case counts exceeding 100,000.

agenda_items.title: Item 23-0060: Interlocal Agreement and Budget Amendment 23BCC0057 for Partnership for Equitable and Resilient Communities Grant Match
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Sowell and Hayti Reborn Justice Movement Co-Executive Directors LA Jones and Steve Chalmers presented an interlocal agreement with the City of Durham and Budget Amendment 23BCC0057 appropriating $2,000,000 from General Fund fund balance for the Partnership for Equitable and Resilient Communities grant match. During discussion, a commissioner questioned why the County was contributing $2,000,000 compared to the City's $500,000 rather than splitting the $2.5 million match evenly at $1.25 million each, as well as plans to sustain the initiative after three years.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0027: FY 2022 Annual Financial Audit and Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: External auditors presented the results of the FY 2022 financial audit for the year ended June 30, 2022, including the Single Audit of federal and state major programs and internal controls review. Auditors reported no disagreements with management, no fraud or illegal acts identified, and no going-concern issues; staff confirmed no Board motion was required.

agenda_items.title: Board and Commission Selections and Excused Absences for February 6 Work Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Clerk reported having the board and commission selection tallies ready for distribution. Commissioners Nimasheena Burns and Nida Allam both requested excused absences for the February 6, 2023 work session because they will be attending UNC School of Government training, and the Board approved both absences in a single motion.

votes.item_title: Approval of January 9, 2023 Regular Session Minutes
votes.notes: Mover and seconder were not identified by name in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Routine approval of the January 9, 2023 regular session minutes without edits.

votes.item_title: Item 23-0060: Interlocal Agreement with City of Durham and Budget Amendment 23BCC0057 ($2,000,000 PERC Grant Match)
votes.notes: Chair Howerton announced the motion passed unanimously; 5 commissioners present.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the interlocal agreement between Durham County and the City of Durham supporting the Partnership for Equitable and Resilient Communities grant match and Budget Amendment 23BCC0057 appropriating $2,000,000 in General Fund fund balance, following discussion on the $2M/$500K County-City match ratio and post-three-year sustainability.

votes.item_title: Excused Absences for Commissioners Nimasheena Burns and Nida Allam for February 6, 2023 Work Session
votes.notes: Explicitly announced as passing 5-0.
votes.discussion_detail: Granted excused absences for Commissioners Nimasheena Burns and Nida Allam for the February 6, 2023 work session to attend UNC School of Government training.

meetings.title: BOCC - January 9, 2023 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: With Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs absent on county business with excused absences, Acting Chair Heidi Carter presided over a three-member quorum alongside Commissioners Nida Allam and Nimasheena Burns. The Board unanimously approved (3-0) the December 12, 2022 regular session minutes and the consent agenda. Following a presentation from General Manager Jay Gibson and Duke State Relations Assistant Director Katie Light, as well as a public hearing with no speakers and recorded supportive remarks from Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs, the Board voted 3-0 to adopt a resolution requesting that NCDOT honorarily designate a portion of NC Highway 751 and Cameron Boulevard from Kerley Road to Duke University Road as Coach K Highway.

agenda_items.title: Opening Remarks, Quorum Note, Public Charge, and Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting Chair Heidi Carter opened the meeting, noted that Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs were out of town on county business with excused absences, and confirmed a three-commissioner quorum with Manager Sowell and new County Attorney Alan Andrews present. Clerk Monica Wallace read announcements including COVID-19 vaccination clinic hours, the National Opioid Settlement survey, and a Thursday Lunch and Learn series.

agenda_items.title: Approval of December 12, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting Chair Carter presented the December 12, 2022 regular session minutes for comments or revisions. With none offered, Commissioner Nida Allam moved approval and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting Chair Carter opened the consent agenda, noting the items had been thoroughly reviewed at the prior work session. Commissioner Burns raised brief comments and questions, after which she moved approval and Commissioner Allam seconded.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Resolution Requesting NCDOT Honorarily Designate NC Highway 751 / Cameron Boulevard as Coach K Highway
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Jay Gibson and Duke University Assistant Director for State Relations Katie Light presented a resolution under N.C.G.S. 136-18(8) requesting NCDOT designate NC Highway 751 and Cameron Boulevard from Kerley Road to Duke University Road in honor of former Duke men's basketball coach Michael William Krzyzewski ('Coach K'). Commissioner Allam read the resolution, and a friendly amendment was discussed subject to NCDOT's 400-word limit. After a public hearing with no speakers, recorded remarks in support from Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs were played before the Board unanimously adopted the resolution.

votes.item_title: Approval of December 12, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
votes.notes: Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs were absent on excused county business.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved the December 12, 2022 regular session minutes without revision.

votes.item_title: Resolution Requesting NCDOT Designate NC Highway 751 and Cameron Boulevard (Kerley Road to Duke University Road) as Coach K Highway
votes.notes: Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs were absent on excused county business and submitted recorded statements in support.
votes.discussion_detail: Adopted the resolution requesting NCDOT honorarily designate the specified segment of NC Highway 751 and Cameron Boulevard as Coach K Highway, allowing an additional whereas clause if accommodated within NCDOT's 400-word limit.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners Work Session for January 3, 2023
meetings.executive_summary: At its January 3, 2023 work session, the Board swore in new County Attorney Alan Andrews, heard Chair Brenda A. Howerton's remarks expressing concern over community gun violence, and reviewed nine consent agenda items including $5,693,238 in General Fund balance for the Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP 2.0), a $349,810 Hub RTP sewer/water project amendment, a $225,000 Neal Middle School bioretention grant, and a Transit Plan Governance Study interlocal agreement amendment. The Board also received Made in Durham's annual report covering BULLS Academy and a new Durham Tech MOA, discussed a proposed $150,000 Boys and Girls Club after-school pilot, and reviewed commissioner conference updates and board directives. At the close of the session under Item 23-0021, the Board took four unanimous 5-0 roll-call votes to suspend the rules, appoint Commissioner Heidi Carter as temporary chair for the January 9 meeting, suspend rules for absences, and grant excused absences for Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs on January 9.

agenda_items.title: Opening, Remarks on Gun Violence, Swearing-In of County Attorney Alan Andrews, and Citizen Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the first meeting of 2023, led the public charge and Pledge of Allegiance (with Commissioner Nida Allam), and spoke out against recent community shootings and gun violence. The Board held the swearing-in ceremony for new County Attorney Alan Andrews, followed by citizen comments where no speakers signed up in person, online, or by email.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (9 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The County Manager walked the Board through nine upcoming consent agenda items: 22-0688 ($12,500 tobacco prevention grant), 22-0735 ($42,000 Durham Congregations in Action food security micro-grants), 22-0737 ($349,810 Hub RTP sanitary sewer and reclaimed water project SE058 amendment and change order), 23-000x ($5,693,238 General Fund balance appropriation for DSS Emergency Rental Assistance Program ERAP 2.0), 23-0005 ($225,000 Neal Middle School bioretention grant), 23-0006 (Transit Plan Governance Study cost-sharing interlocal amendment with Durham and Orange County), 23-0007 (restaurant lease amendment), 23-0008 (2022 Edward Byrne Justice Assistance Grant interlocal agreement), and a Utilities Division contract amendment with Gans/Gaines Oil Company. Commissioners asked clarifying questions on the Hub RTP infrastructure pipeline and ERAP 2.0 rental assistance.

agenda_items.title: Made in Durham Annual Report and Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Made in Durham presenters delivered their annual report covering the BULLS Academy life sciences pathway, the Opportunity Youth Collaborative, and NCIP. Presenters highlighted efforts to connect young Durham residents to 4,500 regional life science careers and noted a newly executed MOA with Durham Technical Community College to share real-time data tracking student progression.

agenda_items.title: Boys and Girls Club After-School Pilot Partnership Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners discussed a pilot expansion partnership with the Boys and Girls Club (where Durham Public Schools already drops off buses) requesting $150,000 for expanded staffing and services, alongside library ARPA programming funds and student meal support. Speakers emphasized removing financial barriers for families and expanding trained after-school capacity.

agenda_items.title: Commissioner Comments and Board Directives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners shared updates on recognizing Coach K, local museum exhibits, coordinating services for individuals cycling between jail, emergency departments, and homelessness, the Triangle's 2027 World University Games bid, and takeaways from the NACo conference in Chicago (including Bull City United parallels and $50,000 in LATCF funding eligibility). Staff also briefly reviewed the status of pending Board directives.

agenda_items.title: Item 23-0021: Temporary Chair Appointment and Excused Absences for January 9, 2023 Regular Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Because Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs would both be out of town January 9–11, 2023, County Attorney Alan Andrews advised that a three-member quorum could meet on January 9 if rules were suspended to appoint a temporary chair, though items requiring a supermajority would need to be rescheduled. The Board took four unanimous 5-0 roll-call votes to suspend rules, appoint Commissioner Heidi Carter as temporary chair for January 9, suspend rules for absences, and approve excused absences for Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs.

votes.notes: Roll call vote announced as approved unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended the Board's rules of procedure to allow appointment of a temporary chair for the January 9, 2023 regular session while both the Chair and Vice Chair are away.

votes.item_title: Item 23-0021 (Motion 2): Appoint Commissioner Heidi Carter as Temporary Chair for January 9, 2023
votes.notes: Roll call vote announced as approved unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Appointed Commissioner Heidi Carter to serve as Temporary Chair for the January 9, 2023 regular session.

votes.item_title: Item 23-0021 (Motion 3): Suspend Rules for Absences for January 9, 2023
votes.notes: Roll call vote announced as approved unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended rules to consider and approve excused absences for Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs for the January 9, 2023 meeting.

votes.item_title: Item 23-0021 (Motion 4): Approve Excused Absences for Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs for January 9, 2023
votes.notes: Roll call vote announced as approved unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved excused absences for Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs for the January 9, 2023 regular session.

meetings.title: BOCC - December 12, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the December 12, 2022 regular session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners, with all five seated commissioners participating. The board unanimously approved prior meeting minutes, 23 consent agenda items, and pulled item 22-0726 accepting an Emergency Services grant with Duke Energy. Following a public hearing, the board voted 5-0 to adopt a final assessment resolution and $200,000 budget amendment for Little Acres Drive road repairs. Commissioners also unanimously approved $10,383,139 in American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) community grant awards before adjourning into closed session for economic development incentive negotiations.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Commissioner Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order and read the public charge, followed by the Pledge of Allegiance led by Commissioner Nimasheena Burns. The clerk read public health and community announcements including COVID-19 and flu vaccination hours, the NC Homeowner Assistance Fund, Durham Food Security Network openings, Solarize the Triangle, and Low Income Energy Assistance Program (LIEAP) dates. Commissioners also offered holiday remarks and discussed honoring retiring County Attorney Lowell Siler/Darby in the new year.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (November 7, November 28, and December 5, 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board considered minutes from the November 7 and December 5 work sessions and the November 28 regular session. No edits or corrections were offered by commissioners.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 22-0635 through 22-0734, excluding 22-0726)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton pulled item 22-0726 for separate presentation at the end of the consent agenda and highlighted support for Durham Tech early childhood initiatives, suggesting a future board update. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted two items of importance without pulling them. The remaining consent items were approved together.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0726: Emergency Services Grant with Duke Energy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Emergency Services Director Jim Groves introduced Chief Emergency Manager Elizabeth Schroeder to present the grant item involving Duke Energy. Commissioners welcomed the grant funding without objection and approved the item unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0701: Little Acres Drive Repairs Final Assessment Resolution and Budget Ordinance Amendment No. 23BCC00052
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and Jay Gibson presented the final assessment resolution and general fund appropriation for repairs to Little Acres Drive. Resident Laura Wheeler spoke in support of the neighborhood petition, explaining that the original developer had passed away and neighbors had faced prohibitive private estimates for years. Commissioners praised staff for working through statutory and procedural hurdles to create a model for future private road repair petitions and approved the combined resolution and $200,000 budget amendment.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0718: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Update and Community Grant Awards ($10,383,139)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Manager Claudia Hager and staff presented an update on the county's ARPA portfolio, noting broadband RFP activity, infrastructure investments, and community grant recommendations totaling $10,383,139 across early childhood, maternal health, youth enrichment, and crime intervention initiatives. Commissioners asked clarifying questions about applicant eligibility for organizations with regional footprints and commended staff and review committees for an equitable evaluation process.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Economic Development Incentives)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted to enter closed session pursuant to G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4) to discuss the location or expansion of industries or businesses and tentative economic development incentives. Upon returning to open session at 02:58:37, the chair reported direction was given to staff with no formal decisions made.

votes.item_title: Approval of Minutes (November 7 and December 5 Work Sessions; November 28 Regular Session)
votes.notes: Mover and seconder not explicitly identified by name in transcript audio.
votes.discussion_detail: No edits or corrections were requested by board members prior to the roll-call vote.

votes.item_title: Item 22-0701: Little Acres Drive Final Assessment Resolution and Budget Ordinance Amendment No. 23BCC00052 ($200,000)
votes.notes: Vice Chair Jacobs clarified whether the resolution and budget amendment were one motion or two; Chair Howerton confirmed both were combined in one motion.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the public hearing with Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and resident Laura Wheeler, the board voted on a single combined motion covering both the final assessment resolution and the $200,000 general fund balance appropriation for Little Acres Drive repairs.

votes.item_title: Item 22-0718: Approval of ARPA Community Grant Proposals ($10,383,139)
votes.notes: Approved proposals totaling $10,383,139.
votes.discussion_detail: Manager Claudia Hager walked through the ARPA update and community grant recommendations, followed by commissioner praise for staff and nonprofit partners before unanimous approval.

votes.item_title: Motion to Enter Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4))
votes.notes: Returned at 02:58:37 with no formal action taken.
votes.discussion_detail: The board adjourned into closed session to discuss industrial/business location or expansion and tentative economic development incentives.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for December 5, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: During the December 5, 2022 work session, Senior Assistant County Attorney Larissa Williamson initially presided to conduct the annual board leadership elections, resulting in the unanimous re-election of Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs. The board suspended the rules and unanimously approved public official bonds (item 22-0690) and the 2023 BOCC meeting calendar. Commissioners then previewed 16 consent agenda items—including a $1.5 million Pay-Go addition for the 300 East Main Street affordable housing redevelopment and a Greater Triangle Commuter Rail MOU extension—heard from the Sheriff and staff on gun violence prevention and the new Community Intervention and Support Services department, and reviewed $10.38 million in ARPA community grant recommendations ahead of the December 12 vote.

agenda_items.title: Annual Election of Chair and Vice Chair
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Assistant County Attorney Larissa Williamson opened the work session, read the public charge, and presided over the election of the board chair. Brenda A. Howerton was nominated and re-elected chair, after which she took the gavel and read a statement highlighting the county's $794 million budget with no property tax increase, school and pre-K investments, maternal health nurses, and ARPA deployment. Wendy Jacobs was then nominated and unanimously re-elected vice chair.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0690: Approval of Public Official Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board was requested to suspend its rules and approve official bonds for Sheriff Clarence Birkhead, Register of Deeds Sharon Davis, Tax Administrator Dwayne Bronson, and Chief Financial Officer Susan Tezai. Commissioners unanimously voted to suspend the rules and then unanimously approved the bonds.

agenda_items.title: Approval of 2023 BOCC Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners considered the 2023 Board of County Commissioners meeting calendar. The board voted unanimously to suspend the rules and subsequently voted unanimously to adopt the 2023 meeting schedule.

agenda_items.title: Review of Consent Agenda Items (Including 300 E. Main St. Affordable Housing and Commuter Rail MOU)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy Manager Claudia Hager walked commissioners through 16 consent items, including the McKee family cemetery relocation (22-0635), AV support (22-0656), a Westaff IT staffing amendment (22-0660), a $1.3 million three-year Microsoft enterprise agreement (22-0661), a Greater Triangle Commuter Rail study MOU extension (22-0674), a $2,422 TB screening amendment (22-0675), an Innovative Interfaces amendment (22-0678), and item 22-0697 adding $1.5 million in Pay-Go funding and Loan No. 3 for the 300 East Main Street affordable housing redevelopment. Commissioners commended the board and developer partner for covering construction and supply-chain cost gaps to keep the affordable housing project moving forward.

agenda_items.title: Gun Safety, Sheriff Permit Administration, and Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead and staff discussed firearm safety, background checks, pistol permits, and guns stolen from unlocked vehicles, noting local registration would be a board policy decision while expressing support for responsible gun legislation. Commissioners highlighted the county's new Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) department—consolidating My Brother's Keeper, Project BUILD, and Bull City United—alongside Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) and an upcoming February Public Health presentation by Donna Rosser treating gun violence as a public health issue.

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Community Grants Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Manager Claudia Hager and staff presented recommended ARPA nonprofit allocations across early childhood capacity building ($1.6M), affordable childcare scholarships ($12M), child and youth social-emotional enrichment ($1.5M), culturally affirming maternal health support, and four Crime Intervention Initiative recipients (Durham Crisis Response Center, Communities In Partnership, Triangle Literacy Council, and Durham County Teen Court and Restitution). Staff noted local funds were planned for the Hayti project and that remaining housing, food security, and library/Cooperative Extension allocations would be refined ahead of the December 31, 2024 federal obligation deadline, with a formal vote scheduled for December 12.

votes.item_title: Election of Brenda A. Howerton as Chair
votes.notes: Nominee Brenda A. Howerton did not cast a roll-call vote on her own nomination.
votes.discussion_detail: Presiding County Attorney Larissa Williamson called for nominations for Chair; Brenda A. Howerton was nominated with no other nominations offered and approved by roll call.

votes.item_title: Election of Wendy Jacobs as Vice Chair
votes.notes: Nominee Wendy Jacobs was not called in the four-name roll call.
votes.discussion_detail: Chair Howerton called for Vice Chair nominations; Wendy Jacobs was nominated with no competing nominations and approved unanimously by the four voting members.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules for Item 22-0690 (Public Official Bonds)
votes.discussion_detail: Board voted to suspend rules at the work session to take formal action on public official bonds.

votes.item_title: Item 22-0690: Approval of Public Official Bonds
votes.discussion_detail: Approved bonds for Sheriff Clarence Birkhead, Register of Deeds Sharon Davis, Tax Administrator Dwayne Bronson, and CFO Susan Tezai.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules for 2023 BOCC Meeting Schedule
votes.discussion_detail: Board suspended work session rules to act on the 2023 BOCC meeting calendar.

votes.item_title: Approval of 2023 BOCC Meeting Calendar
votes.discussion_detail: Following a clerk reminder that the prior vote only suspended the rules, the board took a second motion and roll-call vote to adopt the 2023 meeting calendar.

meetings.title: BOCC - November 28, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: At its November 28, 2022 regular session, the Durham Board of County Commissioners opened by unanimously approving a contract hiring Allen A. Andrews as Durham County Attorney effective January 3, 2023. The board approved the November 14 minutes, the full consent agenda (items 22-0673 through 22-0705), and item 22-0715 certifying the voter-approved 2022 General Obligation Bond referendum results alongside presentations from Durham Public Schools, Durham Tech, and the Museum of Life and Science. After a presentation on the 2022 White House Conference on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health, commissioners concluded a lengthy quasi-judicial hearing for the Mason Farms conservation subdivision, voting 4-0 to approve both Major Special Use Permit M2200001 (community wastewater system) and Major Site Plan B2100325.

agenda_items.title: Contract Approval Hiring Allen A. Andrews as Durham County Attorney
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a pre-meeting closed session, Chair Howerton called the regular meeting to order and sought a motion to hire Allen A. Andrews as Durham County Attorney starting January 3, 2023. Commissioners unanimously authorized signing the contract, and Andrews briefly addressed the board expressing enthusiasm for serving Durham County.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0707: Approval of November 14, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After the public charge, Pledge of Allegiance, and clerk announcements (including delinquent tax advertising and LIEAP dates), the board considered the November 14 regular session minutes with no edits requested.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 22-0673 through 22-0705)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: No commissioners requested to pull any consent items from 22-0673 through 22-0705, and the package was approved unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0715: Certification of 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Results
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The county manager and commissioners recognized county staff (Claudia Hager, Deborah Craig-Ray, David Ades, and Susan Tezai), Durham Public Schools, Durham Technical Community College (highlighting a 35,000-square-foot life sciences training facility), the Museum of Life and Science, and Blue Ribbon Committee volunteers for the successful bond campaign. Commissioners praised voters for overwhelmingly passing the historic referendum and unanimously certified the statement of results for publication.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0644: Learnings from the 2022 White House Conference on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Food Security Coordinator Mary Oxendine presented takeaways from attending the September 27 White House Conference on Hunger, Nutrition, and Health, beginning with a Durham land acknowledgment.

agenda_items.title: Quasi-Judicial Hearing: Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit (M2200001) and Major Site Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: During the continued quasi-judicial hearing, the board heard technical testimony from Gary McConnell of McConnell and Associates regarding community wells, drawdown tests, and groundwater impacts, as well as an evidentiary objection regarding witness standing at 05:02:26. At 05:04:13, the board voted 5-0 to extend the meeting until 11:30 PM. Commissioner Heidi Carter questioned planning staff on UDO conservation subdivision purpose statements, the 80% primary conservation open-space requirement, and resident appeal rights to the Board of Adjustment, while County Attorney Massey clarified the substantial, material, and competent evidence standard before the board voted 4-0 to approve both the special use permit and the major site plan.

votes.item_title: Authorization of Employment Contract with Allen A. Andrews as Durham County Attorney
votes.notes: Chair stated 2022 by slip of tongue; Andrews confirmed 2023 start.
votes.discussion_detail: Following closed session, the board voted unanimously to authorize signing the contract hiring Allen A. Andrews as County Attorney effective January 3, 2023.

votes.item_title: Item 22-0707: Approval of November 14, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
votes.discussion_detail: Approved without edits.

votes.item_title: Item 22-0715: Certification and Publication of 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Results
votes.discussion_detail: Board adopted the resolution accepting and certifying the 2022 general obligation bond referendum results and authorizing publication of the statement of results.

votes.item_title: Extend Meeting Past 11:00 PM Until 11:30 PM
votes.discussion_detail: At 10:40 PM during the Mason Farms quasi-judicial hearing, Chair Howerton requested a motion to extend the session past 11:00 PM to 11:30 PM.

votes.item_title: Case M2200001: Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit (Community Wastewater System)
votes.notes: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns was not called / did not vote during the roll call on this item.
votes.discussion_detail: Following testimony on community wells and runoff, legal guidance on quasi-judicial standards, and staff's approval recommendation, the board approved Major Special Use Permit M2200001 consistent with the submitted plans and staff conditions.

votes.item_title: Major Site Plan Approval: Mason Farms Conservation Subdivision

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for November 7, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: At the November 7, 2022 work session, the Board of County Commissioners heard public comments calling for a 'Family First County' DSS child welfare resolution and urgent mass grading, clear-cutting, and blasting protections in Southeast Durham. Commissioners reviewed upcoming consent agenda items, including grants for EMS community paramedicine and MAT partnership with Lincoln Community Health Center ($73,660), Youth Home nutrition ($5,239), Social Services Duke Energy rate settlement funds ($38,000), Public Health ($8,000), State Library assistance ($153,182), Detention Center fan replacements, and an $18,000 Burt's Bees Foundation grant to update the county's 35-year-old rare plant inventory. Planning and environmental staff also briefed the board on state-reviewed sedimentation and erosion control amendments—including flocculant mandates and stop-work order authority—as well as Triassic Basin well vulnerability and legal limits on local blasting regulation. No formal votes were recorded in the work session digest.

agenda_items.title: Citizens' Comments: DSS Family First Reform and Southeast Durham Grading/Blasting
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A public speaker urged commissioners to adopt a 'Family First County' resolution incorporating Emancipate NC's recommendations during DSS leadership transition to keep children safely with their families and prioritize prompt reunification. Resident Pam Andrews thanked Vice Chair Jacobs and Chair Howerton for visiting Bahama, thanked Fire Marshals for responsiveness on blasting loopholes, and urged immediate completion of mass grading and clear-cutting amendments as annexations impact Southeast Durham creeks.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review: Budget Amendments, Detention Center HVAC, and Rare Plant Inventory
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff walked through consent budget ordinance amendments including item 22-0568 ($73,660 NCDHHS grant to EMS for MAT coordination with Lincoln Community Health Center), item 22-0594 ($5,239 NCDPI Youth Home nutrition grant), item 22-0595 ($38,000 Duke Energy settlement funds for DSS), item 22-0605 ($8,000 Public Health outdoor learning grant), item 22-0616 ($153,182 State Library operating grant), item 22-0627 (Detention Center roof exhaust and axial fan replacement), and item 22-0628 ($18,000 Burt's Bees Foundation grant for a rare plant community biological inventory). Vice Chair Jacobs praised the Burt's Bees grant—updating data last collected 35 years ago—and asked how planning staff would integrate it into rezoning and site plan open-space reviews.

agenda_items.title: Sedimentation, Erosion Control, Mass Grading, Blasting, and Groundwater Well Protection Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff briefed commissioners on proposed sedimentation and erosion control ordinance amendments scheduled for the November 15 NC Sedimentation Control Commission meeting, including making Durham the first NC jurisdiction to require flocculants, adding stop-work order authority, and closing agricultural dumping loopholes alongside separate fast-tracked mass grading/tree preservation amendments. Onsite Water Protection Supervisor Patrick Eaton explained that Triassic Basin wells are typically deep and low-yield, making borehole collapse or sedimentation difficult to repair. Commissioner Heidi Carter asked whether the Comprehensive Plan over-concentrated development in Southeast Durham and pressed staff to explore rezoning proffers for affordable housing and a developer-funded well testing and repair fund for blasting impacts.

meetings.title: Board of County Commissioners - Special Session (Opioid Discussion with AG Josh Stein) - 10.14.22
meetings.executive_summary: All five county commissioners convened in a special session on October 14, 2022 with North Carolina Attorney General Josh Stein, Sheriff Clarence Birkhead, County Manager Kim Sowell, and public health and criminal justice leadership to strategize on deploying opioid settlement funds. Attorney General Stein reviewed fatal overdose trends—citing 108,000 U.S. deaths in 2021, over 3,500 in North Carolina, and 71 in Durham County in 2020—and explained that 85% of North Carolina's $750 million share of the $26 billion national settlement flows directly to local governments. County staff and commissioners outlined an upcoming community-wide survey and town hall, emphasized intensive case management and supportive housing, and discussed building a local peer support specialist pipeline and advocating to repeal the federal Medicaid Inmate Exclusion Policy. As an informational special session, no votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Welcome, Introductions, and Remarks by NC Attorney General Josh Stein on Opioid Settlements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton welcomed Attorney General Josh Stein, acknowledging a quorum of all five commissioners alongside Sheriff Birkhead, County Manager Sowell, General Manager Joanne Pierce, CJRC Director Gudrun Parmer, and Public Health leadership. Attorney General Stein expressed condolences following the prior night's shooting in Raleigh, detailed rising fentanyl-driven overdose deaths nationally and locally, and explained why North Carolina structured its settlement agreement to direct 85% of the state's $750 million share to counties and municipalities.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Strategic Planning, Peer Support Workforce, Supportive Housing, and Medicaid Advocacy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County staff explained plans to launch a community survey and host a town hall to identify treatment and recovery service gaps before investing settlement dollars. Commissioners and staff discussed expanding outpatient treatment, supportive housing, case management, and peer support specialist pipelines—including justice-involved training, preventing provider burnout, and potentially using ARPA funds or hosting a statewide peer support conference in Durham—as well as joint advocacy with the Attorney General to end the federal Medicaid Inmate Exclusion Policy for individuals leaving jail.

meetings.title: BOCC - September 12, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 12, 2022 Durham Board of County Commissioners Regular Session with all five commissioners present following Commissioner Nida Allam's return from maternity leave. The Board unanimously approved meeting minutes, the consent agenda (excluding pulled item 22-0508), and ceremonial proclamations for National Recovery Month, Operation Green Light for Veterans, and World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day. Following a lengthy quasi-judicial hearing and board debate over whether to continue the case for neighbor expert review after a notice URL error, the Board voted 5-0 to approve Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit M220001 and Major Site Plan D2100325 for a 141-lot conservation subdivision served by private community wells and drip-irrigation wastewater systems. The Board also referred item 22-0540 back to staff due to a notification defect, unanimously approved renaming Park Drive to Sankar Way (SN22001), and voted 5-0 to approve the City-County Interlocal Agreement for DSS administration of the Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program (22-0508) after contentious public comment over CPS practices led to a speaker's removal.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance, Public Charge, and Community Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs led the Pledge of Allegiance, and Chair Howerton read the public charge. Clerk announcements highlighted COVID-19 and pediatric vaccination clinics, Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) outreach, the Food Security Network meeting, a Women's Health Conference, Vietnam Veterans memorial activities, and the Safe School Summit, alongside a moment of silence for 9/11 and the passing of former County Attorney Lowell Siler. Commissioner Nida Allam joined the dais at 00:35:53.

agenda_items.title: Approval of August 2022 Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presented the minutes from the August 11 work session and the August 8 and August 22, 2022 regular sessions. No corrections or edits were requested by the commissioners.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations: National Recovery Month (22-0515), Operation Green Light (22-0516), and World Alzheimer's Day (22-0561)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter read proclamation 22-0515 recognizing September as National Recovery Month, joined by Recovery Community of Durham leader Michelle McKinney and Board Chair Larry McGill. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs read proclamation 22-0516 endorsing Operation Green Light for Veterans (November 7-13), and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns read proclamation 22-0561 designating September 21 as World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day, with remarks from Susan Sewell of Dementia Inclusive Inc.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0508)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board pulled item 22-0508 for public comment and voted unanimously to approve the remainder of the consent agenda, which included the FY22-23 Bull City Community Schools contract with the DPS Foundation (22-0440), Whispering Pines stormwater ARPA grant resolution (22-0479), $20,000 NC DHHS tobacco-free grant (22-0492), Justice Assistance Grant review (22-0493), a $158,866 InTelecom Detention Center AV/telecom contract (22-0509), and Board of Elections temporary staffing (22-0510). Following the vote, Commissioner Burns highlighted the approval of $5.2 million in 2016 bond funds for the newly named Murray-Massenburg Elementary School.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0539: Mason Farms Major Special Use Permit (M220001) and Major Site Plan (D2100325)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Cole Renninger and Planning Director Sara Young presented Triple I Capital Management's quasi-judicial applications for a 287.723-acre conservation subdivision (141 single-family lots, >50% open space, <=6% impervious surface) off Preston Andrews Road served by private community wells and a subsurface drip-irrigation wastewater treatment system. Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and four expert witnesses testified that all Unified Development Ordinance review factors were met, while neighboring residents Catherine Ross, Thomas Freeman, and Pamela Andrews urged postponement because of a wrong City URL on the hearing notice and unfamiliarity with quasi-judicial expert rules. After closing the hearing and debating a 30-to-60-day continuance versus deciding on the completed record, the Board approved both M220001 and D2100325 unanimously.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (Hearing opened 5-0; M220001 approved 5-0; D2100325 approved 5-0)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0540: Partial Closing of Akron Boulevard
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented item 22-0540 concerning the proposed closing of a 970-linear-foot portion of Akron Boulevard removed from the NCDOT secondary road maintenance system. Staff recommended pulling the item from the agenda and referring it back to staff due to a public notification defect.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Pulled / Referred back to staff (No vote)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0541: Street Renaming Case SN22001 (Park Drive to Sankar Way)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the Research Triangle Foundation's request under G.S. 153A-239.1 to rename Park Drive, a private business park street affecting three constructed buildings, to Sankar Way. The Board voted 5-0 to open the public hearing, heard no speakers, and voted 5-0 to approve SN22001.

agenda_items.title: Other Business 22-0543 (Removed) and Pulled Consent Item 22-0508: Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program Interlocal Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton announced item 22-0543 was removed for a future agenda, then took up pulled consent item 22-0508 establishing a City-County Interlocal Agreement for DSS to administer the Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) Program. Speakers Amanda Wallace and Lee Smith opposed DSS administering the program over Child Protective Services grievances, and Chair Howerton had a deputy escort Smith out for speaking off-topic after refusing to stop. Commissioner Burns and staff clarified that the updated LIHR program lowered residency requirements from 10 to 5 years and provides grants up to 50% of property taxes ($1,000 to $1,500 by AMI tier) before the Board approved the ILA 5-0.

votes.item_title: Approval of August 11 Work Session and August 8 & August 22, 2022 Regular Session Minutes
votes.notes: Unanimous roll-call approval following Nida Allam's return to the Board.
votes.discussion_detail: No additions or corrections were proposed for the August 11 work session and August 8 and 22 regular session minutes, and the motion passed unanimously by roll call.

votes.item_title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0508)
votes.notes: Item 22-0508 (City-County LIHR Interlocal Agreement) was pulled for public comment and voted on separately at the end of the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: Upon request to pull item 22-0508 for citizen speakers, the Board moved, seconded, and unanimously approved all remaining consent items, including grant recognitions, school capital funding transfers, Detention Center telecom/AV contracts, and Board of Elections temporary staffing.

votes.item_title: Open Quasi-Judicial Public Hearing for Item 22-0539 (Mason Farms M220001 and D2100325)
votes.notes: Followed staff presentation and pre-hearing clarifying questions from commissioners; witnesses were then sworn in.
votes.discussion_detail: Before taking sworn testimony from applicant experts and neighboring property owners on the Mason Farms community wastewater system and site plan, the Board voted unanimously by roll call to open the quasi-judicial public hearing.

votes.item_title: Approve Major Special Use Permit M220001 (Mason Farms Community Wastewater System, Item 22-0539)
votes.notes: Nimasheena Burns noted while voting aye that staff must address communication/notice issues going forward ('y'all got to tighten up').
votes.discussion_detail: After extensive testimony from four applicant expert witnesses and three neighboring residents requesting a postponement due to a broken URL on the mailed notice, the Board debated whether a continuance was legally justified. Concluding that competent, material, and substantial expert evidence established compliance with all 13 UDO review factors and general findings, Commissioner Heidi Carter moved to approve M220001, which passed 5-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Approve Major Site Plan D2100325 (Mason Farms Conservation Subdivision, Item 22-0539)
votes.notes: Associated by-right conservation subdivision major site plan contingent on MSUP M220001 approval.
votes.discussion_detail: Following approval of Major Special Use Permit M220001, a commissioner moved approval of Major Site Plan D2100325 as a by-right development meeting all Unified Development Ordinance requirements, which passed 5-0 by roll call.

votes.item_title: Open Public Hearing for Item 22-0541 (Street Renaming SN22001: Park Drive to Sankar Way)
votes.notes: Private street renaming requested by Research Triangle Foundation.
votes.discussion_detail: Following staff's brief summary confirming statutory compliance under G.S. 153A-239.1 and zero agency objections, the Board unanimously opened the public hearing on street renaming case SN22001.

votes.item_title: Approve Street Renaming Case SN22001 (Park Drive to Sankar Way, Item 22-0541)
votes.notes: No speakers appeared during the public hearing.
votes.discussion_detail: With no members of the public signed up to speak, Chair Howerton closed the hearing and the Board voted 5-0 by roll call to rename Park Drive to Sankar Way.

votes.item_title: Approve Pulled Consent Item 22-0508 (City-County ILA for DSS Administration of Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program)
votes.notes: Pulled for public speakers criticizing DSS/CPS; Commissioner Burns and DSS staff clarified updated 5-year residency and tiered grant rules prior to the vote.
votes.discussion_detail: After public comments criticizing DSS over child welfare cases—including the removal of speaker Lee Smith for off-topic remarks—Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and DSS staff outlined the expanded Low-Income Homeowners Relief program tiers ($1,000 to $1,500 up to 50% of property taxes, reduced 5-year residency requirement). The Board then approved the City-County interlocal agreement 5-0 by roll call.

disagreements.issue: Continuance vs. Immediate Quasi-Judicial Decision on Mason Farms Community Wastewater Permit (M220001)
disagreements.summary: Following neighbor testimony protesting a broken City website link on the mailed public notice and unfamiliarity with quasi-judicial expert-witness rules, Chair Brenda A. Howerton read an attorney-prepared draft continuance to November 14, 2022, triggering board debate over whether continuing the hearing was legally appropriate or fair to all parties.
disagreements.side_a_position: Continue the quasi-judicial hearing (for 30 to 60 days) to allow neighboring residents time to review documents and retain experts given notice confusion.
side_a_arguments: The mailed notice letter directed residents to an incorrect City URL, creating barriers to accessing staff materials prior to the hearing.
Neighbors unfamiliar with quasi-judicial evidentiary rules requested additional time to consult wastewater and hydrology experts.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed to vote immediately on the closed evidentiary record because all legal notice requirements and UDO review factors were satisfied.
side_b_arguments: Planning Director Sara Young confirmed the broken URL was not a statutory or UDO notice defect, and the applicant already held an extended hearing with sworn experts.
Under quasi-judicial law, if competent, substantial evidence meets every UDO standard and no rebuttal expert evidence exists, the Board cannot deny or delay merely out of neighborhood opposition.
disagreements.resolution: After legal counsel advised putting a motion on the floor to vote up or down, Commissioner Carter moved approval of M220001, Commissioner Jacobs came around to the UDO standard, and the Board voted 5-0 to approve both M220001 and D2100325 without a continuance.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for September 6, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs opened the September 6, 2022 BOCC Work Session before Chair Brenda A. Howerton assumed the chair, with Commissioner Nida Allam absent on maternity leave (four commissioners present). Commissioners reviewed September 12 consent agenda items, heard comprehensive policy briefings on the 18-year North Carolina Opioid Litigation Settlement framework (22-0524) and the Management Advisory Group classification and compensation study (13 public-sector peers plus O*NET data), and engaged in pointed debate over GoTriangle's draft Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study showing costs rising 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B and questioning phased corridors and federal New Starts viability. The Board also received updates on $62.4 million in ARPA spending and Phase 1 community grants (22-0390/ARPA) and Durham's $1.7 million FY22 Food Security Initiative, unanimously suspended the rules (4-0) to adopt Durham's 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals (22-0529), and held the first required public hearing on a $950,000 CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant application.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs called the work session to order at 9:10 AM with no citizen commenters present, and County Manager Kimberly Sowell walked commissioners through 22 consent items for September 12, including Whispering Pines ARPA stormwater planning (22-0478, $500,000), LIHR ILA (22-0508), Governor's Highway Safety Program grant (22-0514), Master Aging Plan ILA (22-0518), Stanford L. Warren Library interior design amendment (22-0519, $105,240), sanitary sewer extensions (22-0523), Murray-Massenburg Elementary bond transfer (22-0528, $5.20M), Kirstie Fontaine LLC equity contract (22-0530, $101,400), Westaff and Cure Violence Global contracts for Bull City United (22-0531, 22-0532), and Cates' Corner student learning center (22-0534). Commissioners pressed staff on sewer capacity under the 1972 City-County agreement, adding gender identity/expression clauses to contracts, and Bull City United temporary-to-permanent hiring.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0524: Proposed Framework for Acceptance and Distribution of Opioid Litigation Settlement Proceeds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NCACC Director Nidhi Shashtaveda and Interim General Manager Gudrun Palmer outlined North Carolina's $750M+ 18-year opioid settlement framework—including Durham County's front-loaded payments (~$450,000 initial balance settling to ~$511,000 annually through 2038)—comparing Option A's 12 vetted high-impact strategies with Option B. Staff inventoried local efforts such as Detention Center Phase 2 MOUD induction, Community Paramedics, Lincoln Community Health Center, and Durham Joins Together. Board consensus directed staff to deploy a community survey prior to public town halls, build a public webpage inventorying existing resources, eliminate co-pay barriers at Lincoln, prioritize equity, and require funded housing/employment providers to allow low-barrier MOUD access.

agenda_items.title: Classification and Compensation Study Update (Management Advisory Group International)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: MAG Senior Vice President Dr. Russell Campbell detailed the countywide classification and compensation study methodology, including 14 job evaluation factors, online employee questionnaires (Sept 20-Oct 3), supervisor reviews (Oct 4-11), O*NET private-sector data, addressing salary compression, and targeting three separate pay plans with a draft report before Thanksgiving. Commissioners endorsed expanding the survey peer list from 10 to 13 jurisdictions by adding Wake, Guilford, and Charlotte-Mecklenburg counties, and Commissioner Heidi Carter urged structuring the forthcoming compensation philosophy to ensure a living wage even where market rates fall short.

agenda_items.title: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Feasibility Study Update (GoTriangle)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman, GoTriangle CEO Chuck Lattuca, and Chief Development Officer Katharine Eggleston presented draft Phase 2 findings showing projected West Durham-to-Garner/Clayton capital costs surged 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B ($42M/year O&M, 12,000-18,000 daily riders by 2040, opening 2033-2035), putting the 50% federal New Starts rating at risk. GoTriangle outlined three possible starter phases—West Durham to RTP ($1.6B), Raleigh to RTP/Ellis Road ($1.0B), and Southeast Wake ($600M)—alongside urgent October IIJA Rail Crossing Elimination grant applications for Plum Street, Driver Street, and Ellis Road. Commissioners sharply challenged any Phase 1 excluding Durham County, raised small Black business impacts on Driver Street, and questioned whether Bus Rapid Transit or local micro-transit alternatives merit comparison alongside the $300M Durham Transit Plan update.

agenda_items.title: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager reported on the $62.4 million ARPA allocation ($5.1M budgeted / $1.9M expended in FY22; $6.8M budgeted in FY23), Frontier's >$2M State GREAT Grant and the county's broadband RFP for 100% northern Durham coverage, and over $230 million in city/county requests competing for roughly $10 million in Phase 1 community grants closed August 15. Staff previewed October policy sessions on Phase 2 grants, joint City-County affordable housing/mental health/youth ILAs, and fund balance capacity building for smaller nonprofits. Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, and Carter debated revising the ARPA framework so Phase 2 targets larger transformative investments—especially permanent affordable housing—rather than small fragmented awards.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0529: Proposed Items for 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray and Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey reviewed updated 2023 NCACC legislative goals ahead of the September 12 submission deadline, adding Commissioner Burns' proposal to raise the NC high school dropout age from 16 to 18, separating Chair Howerton's childcare funding item (300% FPL), incorporating Vice Chair Jacobs' physical/behavioral health data-sharing edit, consolidating protection for public officials/employees/election workers, adding Commissioner Carter's Extreme Risk Protection Order ('red flag') gun safety language, and proposing G.S. 166A-19.24 remote-meeting authority for public bodies. The Board voted 4-0 to suspend the rules and 4-0 to approve the legislative goals package.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0390: County Food Security Initiative Update and Upcoming Plans
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt and Food Security Coordinator Mary Oxendine reported that ~10% of Durham residents experience very low food security (1 in 4 Latinx residents and 1 in 6 Black residents) and summarized FY22's $1.7 million County investment (69% to BIPOC-led organizations, >29,000 households served, 3,500 produce boxes, $400,000 to 26 nonprofits). They outlined FY23 priorities including $475,000 in community grants, a $150,000 comprehensive food system assessment, a cross-departmental City-County-DPS team, and a $167,000 USDA grant to study an incubator Farm Campus, while warning Blue Cross funding for Double Bucks expires at year-end. Commissioners urged addressing senior/immigrant transportation barriers, food waste, and farmworker wages.

agenda_items.title: Follow-Up on Commissioner Directives and First Public Hearing on CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Drew Cummings updated commissioners on pending directives, and Commissioner Carter asked that the single-use plastic bag fee return to the October work session before going to the Joint City-County Committee. Cummings then presented the first of two required public hearings for a $950,000 state CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant (backed by a $100,000 local match) to fund home and septic repairs outside Durham city limits through the Durham Home Repair Collaborative ahead of a September 28 second hearing. After opening and closing the public hearing with no speakers, the Board voted 4-0 to suspend the rules for holding a public hearing during a work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-0 (Rules suspended to hold hearing; Grant resolution deferred to Sept. 28)

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules to Vote on 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals During Work Session (Item 22-0529)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Rules suspension required to take binding action at a work session ahead of NCACC's September 12 deadline.
votes.discussion_detail: Because September 12 was the NCACC deadline for submitting 2023 legislative goal proposals and fell before the next regular voting meeting, the Board voted 4-0 by roll call to suspend its rules to adopt the package.

votes.item_title: Approve Proposed Items for 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals Process (Item 22-0529)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Included Leandro funding, high school dropout age 16-to-18 pilot/mandate, standalone childcare funding, remote meeting statutory authority, gun safety/red flag ERPOs, transit, and courts funding.
votes.discussion_detail: Following review of revisions requested at the August 22 meeting—plus new items on the dropout age (16 to 18) and remote public-body meeting clarity—the Board unanimously approved the final 2023 NCACC legislative goals list by a 4-0 roll call.

votes.item_title: Motion to Suspend the Rules to Hold CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization Grant Public Hearing During Work Session
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. No grant resolution action was taken; second public hearing and formal resolution scheduled for September 28, 2022.
votes.discussion_detail: After Chief of Staff Drew Cummings presented the first required public hearing for a $950,000 state CDBG Neighborhood Revitalization grant (with $100,000 county match) for unincorporated home/septic repairs and no speakers came forward, the Board voted 4-0 by roll call to suspend the rules authorizing the public hearing during a work session.

disagreements.issue: Durham Inclusion in Phase 1 vs. Alternative Investments for the Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Study
disagreements.summary: Following GoTriangle's report that full West Durham-to-Garner/Clayton commuter rail costs jumped 50% to $2.8B-$3.2B, commissioners clashed over GoTriangle's proposed starter-phase options, private-sector/business displacement concerns, and whether commuter rail remains viable compared with Bus Rapid Transit and local micro-transit.
disagreements.side_a_position: Durham County must be included in any Phase 1 corridor with Wake County (not Johnston County first), with aggressive federal IIJA/FRA grant pursuit and private-sector/RTP funding participation.
side_a_arguments: Durham taxpayers passed the half-cent transit sales tax long ago while Johnston County has no dedicated transit tax.
With 2050 traffic maps turning solid red and regional job growth concentrating east of Durham, leaving Durham residents out of Phase 1 would cut them off from economic mobility.
Staff and GoTriangle must pursue 80/20 federal Rail Crossing Elimination grants immediately and bring RTP/business leaders into early co-funding talks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question high Durham-segment costs ($1.6B), Driver Street small Black business displacement, lack of complete federal funding plans, and whether $3.2B-scale spending would be better directed to BRT and localized rapid transit.
side_b_arguments: Commissioners need a full menu of feasible federal funding pots before committing, as current revenue appears insufficient for a $2.8B-$3.2B build.
East Durham's Driver Street corridor contains roughly seven small Black-owned businesses that could be harmed by host-railroad crossing closures.
Localized micro-transit or Bus Rapid Transit along corridors like 15-501 and West Durham-Ellis Road may serve Durham's near-term needs better than relying on long commuter lines.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion concluded without a vote; GoTriangle committed to bring back a federal grant matrix and conduct a 45-day public engagement period, while County staff scheduled a Durham Transit Plan update for October.

meetings.title: BOCC - August 22, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 22, 2022 Regular Session with four commissioners present (Commissioner Nida Allam absent on maternity leave). The Board heard an update on the Solarize the Triangle/Durham solar subsidy program, recognized outgoing 20-year System of Care staffer and commissioners' NACo leadership appointments, and jointly read a Resolution in Support of Reproductive Justice and Freedom responding to the Dobbs Supreme Court ruling and reinstatement of North Carolina's 20-week abortion ban. After citizen Antoinette Haas commented on workforce development, Greater Durham Black Chamber funding (22-0464), and Engineering due diligence funds (22-0489), the Board voted 4-0 to approve the consent agenda excluding pulled items 22-0485 and 22-0487, which passed 4-0 separately after a Kids Voting / 4-H Cooperative Extension presentation. Commissioners also received Public Health Director Rod Jenkins' COVID-19 and monkeypox briefing (flagging vaccine disparities among Black residents), reviewed draft 2023 NCACC legislative goals (22-0494) while deferring formal adoption to September, and announced appointments to seven boards and commissions.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Solarize Durham Update, Staff Tribute, and NACo Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the meeting and Sustainability Manager Tobin Freed reported on the Solarize the Triangle campaign, noting Durham City and County each contributed $50,000 toward low-income solar installations boosted by the 30% federal Inflation Reduction Act tax credit. The Board also recognized retiring 20-year Family Partner Coordinator Tika for System of Care leadership and acknowledged NACo committee vice-chair and network appointments for Commissioners Burns and Jacobs.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Resolution in Support of Reproductive Justice and Freedom
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners Heidi Carter, Nimasheena Burns, Wendy Jacobs, and Chair Brenda A. Howerton jointly read a ceremonial resolution affirming bodily autonomy, expanding Durham County Public Health reproductive/family planning access, and directing staff to identify local actions protecting abortion and reproductive care access following the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision and federal court reinstatement of North Carolina's 20-week ban. Burns also credited absent Commissioner Nida Allam for background work and delivered prepared remarks linking reproductive rights to maternal health investments.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Ceremonial reading / No formal roll-call vote

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Approval and Pulled Kids Voting Items (22-0485, 22-0487) & Tax Settlement Review (22-0491)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Citizen Antoinette Haas spoke on workforce development item 22-0461 ($250,000), argued $50,000 for the Greater Durham Black Chamber of Commerce (22-0464) was too small, and criticized $150,000 for Engineering legal/due diligence costs (22-0489). After pulling items 22-0485 and 22-0487 for Cooperative Extension briefing, the Board passed the remainder of the consent agenda 4-0. Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt and Kids Voting Coordinator Carolyn Krueger highlighted statewide 4-H and Orange County partnerships before the Board approved 22-0485 and 22-0487 by 4-0 vote, followed by Tax Administrator Dwayne Brenson explaining North Carolina's 10-year tax collection statute of limitations on item 22-0491.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Public Health Focus Update (COVID-19 and Monkeypox)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 702 new COVID-19 cases over seven days, four additional deaths, 88.9% BA.5 variant prevalence, ~200 daily at-home test distributions, and 1,500 pre-ordered Moderna/Pfizer autumn boosters. Jenkins also highlighted 19 confirmed monkeypox cases in Durham County—100% male and 78.58% Black/African American—urging Black residents to utilize free, discreet JYNNEOS vaccinations as the department transitioned to intradermal dosing.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0494: Review of Proposed 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray led the Board through updated draft NCACC legislative goals ahead of the September 12 submission deadline, covering Leandro school funding, community college support (Allam), standalone childcare/women-and-children funding and nursing home oversight (Howerton), Familiar Faces data sharing and homestead circuit-breaker/transit goals (Jacobs), economic development and workforce housing (Burns), an $18.50 living wage and youth gun safety laws (Carter), broadband preemption (Allam), and protections for election workers/public officials alongside increased NC courts funding. Commissioners agreed to defer formal voting until the September 6 work session to allow final edits.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby announced the Board's ballot appointments across seven bodies: Demetrius Smith (Boxing and Wrestling Commission), Miran (Criminal Justice Advisory Committee), Andrew Nurkin (Durham Cultural Advisory Board), Brandon Davis (Planning Commission), Nisha Williams (Durham Racial Equity Commission), Russell Pierce (Homeless Services Advisory Committee), and Milan McMillan, Ida Stringer-Standback, Miguel Jackson, and Willis Richard (Library Board). Commissioner Burns flagged potential dual City/County appointments for Clerk coordination.

votes.item_title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 22-0485 and 22-0487)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Included citizen-commented items 22-0461 ($250k workforce development), 22-0464 ($50k Greater Durham Black Chamber), 22-0489 ($150k Engineering due diligence), and 22-0491 (annual tax settlement).
votes.discussion_detail: After citizen Antoinette Haas commented on items 22-0461, 22-0464, and 22-0489 and Vice Chair Jacobs requested staff presentations on Kids Voting items 22-0485 and 22-0487 and an explanation of 22-0491, the Board clarified the pull list and approved all consent items except 22-0485 and 22-0487 by a 4-0 roll call.

votes.item_title: Approval of Pulled Consent Items 22-0485 and 22-0487 (Kids Voting Durham / 4-H and Orange County Partnerships)
votes.notes: Nida Allam absent on maternity leave. Approved after remarks by Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt and Kids Voting Coordinator Carolyn Krueger.
votes.discussion_detail: Following Donna Rewalt and Carolyn Krueger's overview of how Kids Voting Durham's 16-year civic education model is expanding through 4-H and Orange County partnerships to strengthen local school and after-school curricula, the Board voted 4-0 by roll call to approve both items.
