meetings.title: Joint BOCC-Board of Education Meeting for August 16, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda A. Howerton and DPS Board of Education Chair Bettina Umstead co-presided over the August 16, 2022 Joint BOCC-Board of Education Meeting, with all five County Commissioners present including Nida Allam. The joint body deferred a scheduled teacher housing update to the next meeting, corrected a typo and unanimously approved the May 10, 2022 joint minutes, and heard staff briefings on the November 8 $550.2 million General Obligation Bond Referendum timeline ($423.5M for DPS, $112.7M for Durham Tech, and $13.9M+ for the Museum of Life and Science at a projected 2.5-cent tax increase). DPS capital leadership reviewed active construction—including Lyons Farm Elementary's August 29 opening with October solar installation, the new Northern High School, and Murray-Massenburg Elementary—while debating the reuse of surplus school sites like old Northern High School and downtown DSA for affordable teacher housing. Child Care Services Association also reported Durham Pre-K had grown to 24 sites, 40 classrooms, and 607 locally funded seats, sparking discussion on South Durham expansion and DPS kindergarten-readiness data sharing.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Agenda Amendment (Teacher Housing Deferral), and Approval of May 10, 2022 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda A. Howerton and BOE Chair Bettina Umstead opened the meeting and removed the DPS teacher housing item from the agenda because staff was not yet ready for a full update. Commissioners and BOE members then noted a minor typographical correction in the May 10, 2022 joint meeting minutes and approved them unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Timeline and Blue Ribbon Committee Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager and Chief Communications Officer Deborah Craig-Ray outlined the $550+ million November 8 bond package ($423.5M DPS, $112.7M Durham Tech, $13.9M Museum of Life and Science; projected 2.5-cent tax rate impact), noting Local Government Commission approval in September, early voting starting October 20, and non-partisan factual voter education led by the Blue Ribbon Committee. Board members asked about LGC timing, property tax communication, and aligning DPS and County informational materials.

agenda_items.title: DPS Capital Projects Update and Surplus Site Planning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DPS Chief Operating Officer Dr. Julius Monk, Construction Director Frederick Davis II, and Director Matthew Palmer updated both boards on Lyons Farm Elementary (opening August 29 with $3M solar installation slated for October), new Northern High School (topping-out ceremony held July 27 for 2023 opening), Murray-Massenburg Elementary (850 seats opening 2024), six elementary renovations adding Pre-K wings, and Durham School of the Arts planning. Officials discussed Safe Routes to School coordination, the 3-tier bus bell schedule, and repurposing soon-to-be-vacated campuses (old Northern High, 17-acre downtown DSA site, and Lowes Grove's ~73-unit teacher housing concept).

agenda_items.title: Durham Pre-K Enrollment, Funding, and Kindergarten Readiness Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Child Care Services Association leaders Katie Linder and Linda Chappelle reported that Durham Pre-K expanded from 16 sites/28 classrooms to 24 sites/40 classrooms and 607 locally funded seats backed by over $5 million in County investment, drawing 1,600+ applications and 778 acceptances while piloting ~40 wrap-care slots and $1,300/month BK-licensed classroom reimbursement rates. Commissioners and BOE members questioned South Durham site equity, dual-language programs, and executing a data-sharing agreement with DPS to track kindergarten outcomes.

votes.item_title: Approval of May 10, 2022 Joint BOCC-Board of Education Meeting Minutes (as Corrected)
votes.notes: Joint voice vote with Durham Public Schools Board of Education; all five BOCC members present during the meeting.
votes.discussion_detail: After deferring the teacher housing agenda item by consensus and flagging a typographical error in the May 10, 2022 joint minutes, the two boards approved the corrected minutes unanimously by voice vote.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Committee Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: BOCC Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided remotely over the August 10, 2022 Joint City-County Committee Meeting alongside County Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns (Commissioners Nida Allam and Heidi Carter absent) and City Council members Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton, and Councilwoman DeDreana Freeman. After waiting for Mayor Pro Tem Middleton to establish a City quorum, the committee voted 6-0 on a motion by Jacobs seconded by Burns to approve the February 11, 2022 minutes. The committee then held an extended policy discussion with Museum of Durham History leaders Patrick Mucklow, Lou Myers, and Bob Ashley regarding the museum's ~$11-$15 million expansion vision, City lease terms, alternative City-owned sites such as 505 W. Chapel Hill St. and Fayetteville Street, and unresolved City-County governance and funding roles, agreeing to convene a staff-and-leadership working group before October.

agenda_items.title: Quorum Wait and Approval of February 11, 2022 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton delayed opening formal business until Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton joined to establish a Durham City Council quorum. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs moved and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded approval of the February 11, 2022 minutes, which passed 6-0 on roll call.

agenda_items.title: Museum of Durham History Future Space, Site Options, and Governance Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Museum of Durham History Executive Director Patrick Mucklow, founding board member Lou Myers, and Board Chair Bob Ashley presented plans to expand their current City-leased Hub site along the planned Rail Trail—originally estimated at $11M in a 2020 Vines Architecture study and now ~$15M—while asking both governments to clarify long-term governance and ownership ('who is the daddy'). Councilwoman DeDreana Freeman and Mayor Elaine O'Neal urged evaluating City-owned alternatives such as 505 W. Chapel Hill Street and Hayti/Fayetteville Street, City Manager Wanda Page clarified no land-donation talks had occurred, and the committee agreed to convene a joint working group of managers, attorneys, and museum leaders prior to October.

votes.notes: Joint City-County vote passed 6-0: BOCC members Burns, Jacobs, Howerton voted Aye (Allam and Carter absent); City Council members Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Councilwoman DeDreana Freeman, and Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton also voted Aye.
votes.discussion_detail: Once Mayor Pro Tem Mark-Anthony Middleton arrived to satisfy the City Council quorum, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs moved and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded approval of the February 11, 2022 Joint City-County Committee minutes, passing unanimously 6-0 on a combined roll call.

meetings.title: BOCC - August 8, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 8, 2022 Regular Session with all five commissioners present—Commissioner Nida Allam's final meeting before maternity leave. The Board approved June 27 and July 11 minutes 5-0, honored retiring Duke Regional Hospital President Katie Galbraith, proclaimed Child Support Awareness Month ($15.95M collected in FY21-22), and read a statement on Durham County's new Non-Discrimination Ordinance effective July 1. Commissioners approved the main consent agenda 5-0 and then addressed five pulled items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477), hearing sharp public criticism of DSS/CPS child welfare funding alongside strong support for three major County real estate acquisitions: $6 million to buy the former John Avery Boys & Girls Club for Bull City United/CISS, $12.15 million net to acquire the 17-acre Shops at Hope Valley (including a former Kroger) for a consolidated 54,000-square-foot Board of Elections facility, and an adjacent 3+ acre Bram Office Supply parcel for Durham Tech expansion; all five pulled items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Pledge, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes (June 27 and July 11, 2022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns led the Pledge of Allegiance, and clerk announcements highlighted COVID-19 testing/vaccines, Sheriff Speaks on eviction prevention, Pre-K, the Transit Plan survey, August 15 ARPA deadlines, LIHR applications, and the 'I Voted' sticker contest. The Board then approved the June 27 and July 11, 2022 meeting minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognitions and Non-Discrimination Ordinance Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners presented a Resolution of Appreciation honoring retiring Duke Regional Hospital President & CEO Katie B. Galbraith for her partnership during the pandemic. Commissioner Heidi Carter read the Child Support Awareness Month 2022 proclamation with DSS Director Ben Rose ($15,946,090.39 collected in FY21-22 for 8,373 children), and Chair Howerton read a statement marking the July 1 effective date of Durham County's Non-Discrimination Ordinance in unincorporated areas.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Batch 1 (Excluding Five Pulled Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Five items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477) were pulled for public comment and staff presentations, and the Board approved all remaining consent items 5-0 by roll call. Following the vote, Commissioner Burns announced the third Stanford L. Warren Library community input session set for August 17.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items (22-0439, 22-0447, 22-0470, 22-0476, and 22-0477): DSS Grants and Strategic County Real Estate Purchases
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers Kiki Woods, Alexis Nguyen, Kelly Smith, and Antoinette Haas opposed DSS receiving $33,000 in Chafee/LINKS foster-youth funds (22-0439) and $878,457 in aging Home & Community Care Block Grant funds (22-0447) over CPS removal allegations, while Commissioner Burns clarified the latter is federal aging daycare funding. Staff and agency leaders (Joanne Pierce, Perry Manns, Nancy Mitchell, Elections Director Derek Bowens, and Durham Tech President J.B. Buxton) then detailed three strategic acquisitions: $6M LOBs financing to buy the former John Avery Boys & Girls Club for Bull City United/CISS (22-0470), $12,146,717 net ($14M minus repair credits) for the 17-acre Shops at Hope Valley to house a consolidated 54,000-sq-ft Board of Elections center and early voting site while honoring 24 existing tenant leases pending public engagement (22-0476), and the 3+ acre Bram warehouse adjacent to Durham Tech (22-0477); all five items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Closing Commissioner Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Nida Allam announced that Durham County Public Health was scheduling monkeypox vaccinations for high-risk residents and noted this was her final meeting before departing on maternity leave, after which the Board adjourned 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for August 1, 2022, Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 1, 2022 Part 2 Work Session, beginning mid-briefing on Durham's draft Comprehensive Plan before turning to the City-County HEART pilot interlocal agreement, 2023 NCACC legislative goal proposals, NCACC voting delegate selection, commissioner directives, and a closed session. Staff outlined the HEART pilot's deployment of three City-funded County EMT-Basics alongside Crisis Call Diversion, 3-person Community Response Teams, and Care Navigation with zero safety backup incidents in its first month. Commissioners voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and appoint Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs as NCACC voting delegate and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as alternate. Following a closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) (with four commissioners present, Nida Allam absent), the Board voted 4-0 to authorize staff to submit a $100,000 opening bid for a county real property purchase and respond to any upset bids.

agenda_items.title: Draft New Comprehensive Plan Briefing and Feedback
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff continued presenting the draft Durham Comprehensive Plan (incorporating an Urban Growth Boundary retracted by 13 square miles relative to 2005 tiers, Future Growth Areas, 20 place types, and 227 policies to accommodate 130,000 new residents and 60,000 housing units by 2050). Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, Carter, and Howerton pushed for expanded rural outreach (including Bahama), large printed maps, clearer Urban Growth Boundary enforceability, public-land priorities, and equitable 15-minute neighborhood infrastructure before breaking for lunch at 00:46:31.

agenda_items.title: City-County Interlocal Agreement for EMT Support of Community Safety Department's HEART Pilot
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Durham Community Safety Director Ryan Smith, Deputy City Manager Bo Ferguson, Clinical Manager Abena Bediako, Assistant Director Aniese Vance, and EMS Chief Mark Lockhart presented the one-year HEART pilot (Crisis Call Diversion in 911, 3-person unarmed Community Response Teams pairing clinicians, peers, and City-funded County EMT-Basics, Care Navigation follow-up, and Co-Response), reporting zero safety or law enforcement backup incidents during its first month of operation. All five commissioners questioned dispatch scripts, clinician retention, shared clinical data platforms, co-responder de-escalation, and scaling non-police response countywide.

agenda_items.title: Initial Solicitation of 2023 NCACC Legislative Goals
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deborah Craig-Ray and department heads Jim Groves (Emergency Management), Ben Rose (DSS), Curtis Massey (County Attorney's Office), and Rod Jenkins (Public Health) presented staff proposals—including emergency-management insurance-fee funding, Medicaid expansion/50% state child-welfare cost share, remote-meeting authority under locally declared emergencies, lower lead-hazard thresholds, prenatal care access, and a flagged conflict over social-worker title protection—alongside commissioner priorities on Leandro funding, transit, workforce housing, living wage, gun safety, community colleges, broadband preemption, and election-worker safety. Commissioners deferred formal adoption to a later session.

agenda_items.title: NCACC 115th Annual Conference Voting Delegates and Commissioner Comments/Directives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board voted 5-0 to suspend its rules and 5-0 to appoint Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs as voting delegate and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns as alternate for the NCACC 115th Annual Conference. Chair Howerton announced her appointment to the NACo Board of Directors, Vice Chair Jacobs highlighted 988 behavioral-health call data and Familiar Faces data-sharing models from Johnson County, Kansas, Commissioner Carter flagged the pending plastic bag fee and teacher-housing legal work, and Commissioner Burns directed staff via Register of Deeds records to compile an inventory of unutilized school-board-owned real estate.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5)) and $100,000 Property Opening Bid Authorization
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With four commissioners present (Burns, Carter, Jacobs, Howerton; Allam not recorded on roll call), the Board voted 4-0 to enter closed session to instruct staff on property acquisition and employment contract negotiations under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5). Returning to open session at 03:29:21, the Board voted 4-0 to authorize staff to submit an opening bid of $100,000 to acquire the discussed real property parcel and respond to upset bids as needed.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 1

The Board heard citizen comments urging ARPA funding for permanent re-entry housing and protesting DSS Child Protective Services actions in the Wynn/Nguyen case, prompting Chair Howerton to remind the audience that commissioners cannot intervene in active legal proceedings. County Manager Kimberly Sowell then led a review of upcoming August consent agenda items—sparking extended commissioner questions on Adult Drug Treatment Court funding and Lincoln Community Health Center's $10 MAT co-pays (22-0432), Wellpath Detention Center medical staffing increases (22-0446), and Durham Pre-K's planned 86-student childcare center at 300/500 East Main Street (22-0450). Finally, Research Triangle Foundation leadership presented the annual Hub RTP and Boxyard update highlighting $4.7 billion in announced RTP private investment, 42.5% MWBE participation, and $15.3 million spent of Durham County's $20 million infrastructure commitment.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order and read the public charge. Leticia Soria requested ARPA funds for permanent re-entry housing, while Operation Stop CPS advocates Amanda Wallace, Samantha Nguyen/Wynn, and Kiki Woods protested DSS child removals in the Wynn/Nguyen case; Chair Howerton clarified for the audience that elected commissioners cannot legally intervene in ongoing custody proceedings.

agenda_items.title: August Consent Agenda Review

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Note: Although archived under the date and title 'BOCC Work Session August 1, 2022 Part 2', the recording and transcript capture Durham County's April 4, 2022 Work Session presided over by Chair Brenda A. Howerton with all five commissioners present. After reading two emailed citizen comments on My Brother's Keeper Durham and Holton Career & Resource Center transit access and reviewing 13 consent items (22-0156 through 22-0209)—including Stanford L. Warren Library waterproofing (22-0189) and seven ambulances (22-0202)—the Board held extended work-session briefings on youth and community mental health (22-018), black maternal health disparities (22-0215), a revised $550.2M 2022 General Obligation Bond / FY22-31 CIP proposal lowering projected tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents (22-0217), and Triangle J COG's Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Opportunity Analysis (22-0206). Commissioners pressed for actionable commitments for community doulas and teen-mom nonprofits, scrutinized DPS green-bond audits and surplus property reuse, and debated whether commuter rail justifies its regional cost before adjourning cleanly without taking substantive policy votes.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, MLK Remembrance, Public Charge, Citizen Comments, and Consent Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened with a moment of silence marking the 54th anniversary of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination (April 4) and read emailed comments from Dwaren Langley on My Brother's Keeper Durham and Chris Tiffany on transit access to evening meetings. County Manager Kimberly Sowell then reviewed 13 consent items (22-0156 to 22-0209), including NCDHHS school health nursing funds ($262,706), Bioquell EMS ambulance sanitizers (22-0185), $1.58M Stanford L. Warren Library waterproofing and Muter Construction contract (22-0189, eight-to-ten-month timeline), utility contracts, seven ambulances without currently available anti-idling units (22-0202), Bull City Community Schools impact data (22-0204), Immigrant & Refugee Affairs ILA (22-0207), and a Library Foundation grant.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-018: Youth Trauma and Community Mental Health Crisis Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dr. Ernestine Briggs-King (Duke / Center for Child & Family Health), Tara Bohley (UNC School of Social Work), and Ann Oshel (Alliance Health) presented data on pandemic trauma, youth suicide surges (citing a 57% jump from 2007-2018 and Black children under 13 dying by suicide at over twice the rate of white peers), insurance/navigation pathways, and Medicaid Transformation toward Tailored Plans and a statewide foster-care carve-out RFP. Commissioners demanded county-level service gap mapping, telehealth/broadband parity, County 911 behavioral health integration, and action to deploy a previously budgeted $1 million in uncommitted mental health funds.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0215: Black Maternal Health Update and Community Doula Partnership
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, Nursing Director Hattie Wood, Deputy Director Liz Stevens, Duke MFM specialist Dr. Maria Small, and community leaders Joy Lampkin Foster, Joy Spencer, Maya Jackson (MAAME Inc.), and Tamika Brown (HEARTS) detailed severe racial disparities—noting Black women face 3-4x higher pregnancy-related mortality, 48% higher preterm birth risk in NC, and worsening preterm trends locally—alongside requests for a full-time maternal nurse educator, County/Detention Center doula MOUs, home blood pressure cuffs, an on-site ultrasonographer, and direct equitable funding for Black-led CBOs. Tension emerged as Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and community presenters criticized a year of meetings without firm financial commitments, while Chair Howerton directed General Manager Joanne Pierce to schedule a focused follow-up ahead of budget adoption.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0217: FY22-31 Capital Improvement Program and Proposed November 2022 $550.2M GO Bond Referendum
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane and General Manager Claudia Hager presented a revised 10-year CIP trimming projected FY24 property-tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents ($88/year on a $350,000 home) by deferring DSS Main and select IS&T/renewable items while fully funding the $550.2M November 2022 GO Bond request: $423.5M for DPS, $112.7M for Durham Tech (life sciences, health sciences, and campus boundary land acquisition), and ~$14M for the Museum of Life and Science. Museum CEO Carrie Heinonen, Durham Tech President J.B. Buxton, and DPS Construction Director Frederick Davis II detailed project readiness, while commissioners probed Low-Income Homeowners Relief adjustments, Board of Elections space costs, $40M green-bond email advocacy versus completed energy audits, and surplus school parcel reuse.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0206: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Opportunity Analysis (TJCOG) and Commissioner Directives/Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Triangle J COG Director John Hodges-Coppel and GoTriangle's Jay Heikes presented land-use, affordable-housing (2,700 legally restricted and NOAH corridor units; 15% with expiring covenants), and travel-market analyses showing 4% of four-county land holds 30% of primary jobs and 96,000 daily Wake-Durham inter-county commuters. Commissioner Burns questioned the commuter rail rationale for low-wage bus riders while Jacobs, Carter, and Howerton debated first-mile/last-mile links and South Florida rail lessons; afterward, Chief of Staff Drew Cummings reviewed directives and Burns criticized inaccurate public claims by a school board member regarding teacher pay and affordable-housing advocacy while requesting a farewell proclamation for retiring Duke basketball coach Mike Krzyzewski.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No substantive votes (adjourned by roll call)

disagreements.issue: Urgency of Direct County Funding Commitments for Community-Based Black Maternal Health Organizations
disagreements.summary: After community-based doula and teen-parent organizations described nearly a year of meetings without firm county commitments while Black maternal and infant outcomes worsened, commissioners differed on how quickly and concretely to respond during the work session.
disagreements.side_a_position: Defer formal funding commitments until General Manager Joanne Pierce meets with staff and CBOs to prepare concrete budget proposals.
side_a_arguments: Work sessions are designed for listening and information gathering rather than making immediate budget appropriations on the dais.
Staff and CBOs should meet offline to distill clear, succinct dollar asks ahead of the upcoming budget cycle.
disagreements.side_b_position: The Board must act urgently now rather than continuing endless meetings after already leaving a $1M mental-health commitment and last year's Hear Her recommendations unimplemented.
side_b_arguments: Babies and mothers are still dying nearly a year after the June 3, 2021 presentation without dedicated action steps.
Silos between hospital systems, Public Health, and Black-led grassroots providers cannot persist without direct funding and written County commitments.
disagreements.resolution: Chair Howerton directed General Manager Joanne Pierce to convene the CBOs and return concrete funding proposals for the upcoming FY23 budget cycle.

disagreements.issue: Adding a $40 Million DPS Green Energy Bond Request Before Energy Audits Are Completed
disagreements.summary: Commissioner Wendy Jacobs pressed for clarity on whether DPS's $423.5M bond package adequately funded its renewable energy goals and green-bond line items, while Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and DPS Director Frederick Davis II cautioned against adding an unvetted $40M figure prior to energy audits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Wait for DPS's funded internal energy audits before adding another $40M onto taxpayers beyond the hard-won reduction to a 2.5-cent bond tax rate.
side_a_arguments: No board or school-board advocate could explain what the $40M green-bond email campaign specifically covered, and installing solar before upgrading windows and insulation is inefficient.
Staff worked hard to bring the CIP bond tax impact down from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents for residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Ensure DPS's modernization and energy-efficiency/generation commitments are explicitly tracked and adequately funded through clear CIP or audit-backed line items.
side_b_arguments: County staff created a transparent dedicated renewable-energy line item, and DPS should confirm its 2030/2050 carbon-reduction goals are similarly resourced.
Once DPS completes its energy audit, future two-year CIP updates can incorporate vetted renewable energy projects.
disagreements.resolution: Budget staff and DPS clarified that $3M in 2016 bonds was already allocated for Lyons Farm solar and a districtwide energy audit, leaving future green-energy allocations for the subsequent CIP update once the audit concludes.

disagreements.issue: Rationale and Equity of Commuter Rail Investments vs. Local Bus and Micro-Transit Priorities
disagreements.summary: Following Triangle J COG's Opportunity Analysis briefing, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the equity rationale for prioritizing expensive commuter rail over local bus service, while Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Chair Brenda A. Howerton emphasized regional job connectivity and public-private transit-oriented development.
disagreements.side_a_position: Pursue a regional multimodal rail spine paired with public-private TOD partnerships and dedicated first-mile/last-mile connectors so Durham residents can reach Triangle job centers.
side_a_arguments: Eight of the region's top ten job hubs, major universities, and 37% of Durham's legally restricted affordable housing lie within the corridor.
South Florida's Tri-Rail and Brightline demonstrate that electric shuttles, joint development value capture, and multi-county alignment can serve both riders and regional growth.
disagreements.side_b_position: Question whether commuter rail serves low-income bus riders earning under $40,000 or leaves behind local bus rapid transit and neighborhood bus connections.
side_b_arguments: Few of the 9,000 downtown apartments or corridor jobs serve very-low-income residents without guaranteed affordable fares and simultaneous BRT/feeder investments.
Commissioners remain skeptical that four separate governments will build feeder bus rapid transit in tandem with rail, risking low-income neighborhoods being left behind.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion ended without a vote; staff noted the Durham County Transit Plan update later in 2022 would weigh both bus and commuter rail allocations.

meetings.title: BOCC - July 11, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the July 11, 2022 Regular Session with all five commissioners present. The Board unanimously approved June 13 minutes (5-0), celebrated seven 2022 NACo Achievement Awards (22-0420), approved the consent agenda 5-0, and received a COVID-19 and monkeypox briefing (22-0405). In item 22-0421, following statutory public hearings, the Board adopted three General Obligation bond orders totaling $550,240,000—$423,505,000 for Durham Public Schools (5-0), $112,740,000 for Durham Technical Community College (5-0), and $13,995,000 for the Museum of Life and Science (4-0-1, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns recusing due to Museum board membership)—and called the November 8 special bond referendum. Following a sharply divided public hearing on Community Cats/TNVR (22-0394) pitting animal welfare groups against Audubon conservationists and Sheriff's Animal Services, Commissioners Carter, Burns, and Jacobs resolved a board disagreement by voting 5-0 to adopt the AWAC ordinance framework as a model while directing staff, the Sheriff's Office, APS, and nonprofits to return operational procedures within roughly six months rather than lifting trap permits immediately.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners announced the BULLS BioWork Academy, NACo committee participation, and August 15 ARPA grant deadlines. Citizen speakers included AWAC chair Jan Paul clarifying Community Cat/TNVR ordinance terms and Operation Stop CPS advocates Amanda Wallace and Samantha Nguyen regarding the Wynn children, after which the Board approved the June 13 work session and regular session minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton recognized Durham County departments for winning seven 2022 NACo Achievement Awards: Durham County Transit Plan, Tax Administration Chatbot, Board of Elections Ballot Tracking, DSS LIHR, DSS ERAP, Durham County Library Innovation League, and EMS Mobile Integrated Healthcare/Community Paramedicine. Commissioners thanked IS&T, DSS, Tax, Elections, Library, and EMS staff before voting 5-0 to approve Consent Agenda items 22-0321 through 22-0428.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0405: COVID-19 and Monkeypox Public Health Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 776 weekly COVID-19 cases (241.41 per 100,000), 343 cumulative deaths, 53.6% BA.5 variant dominance, newly started 0-5 pediatric vaccinations, and Durham's selection among North Carolina's first seven counties to receive monkeypox vaccine doses.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing 22-0421: 2022 General Obligation Bond Orders ($550,240,000 Total) and Referendum Resolutions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy County Manager Claudia Hager presented the $550,240,000 General Obligation Bond package (projected 2.5-cent property tax impact; 2.3535% net debt ratio). After public hearings—where three residents supported and Ryan Calloway opposed the school bond over past accountability, while Duke Health, Novo Nordisk, Made in Durham, and Chamber leaders backed the Durham Tech bond—the Board adopted the $423,505,000 School Bond Order (5-0), the $112,740,000 Community College Bond Order (5-0), and the $13,995,000 Museum Bond Order (4-0-1, Nimasheena Burns abstaining), and passed corresponding November 8 special bond referendum resolutions.

Commissioners resolved an internal disagreement over immediate permit repeal versus operational planning by voting 5-0 to adopt the AWAC draft as a model while directing stakeholders to establish TNVR procedures within roughly six months.

disagreements.issue: Immediate Permit Repeal vs. Structured Six-Month Operational Rollout for Community Cat (TNVR) Ordinance Amendment (22-0394)
disagreements.summary: Following divided public testimony from animal welfare advocates (supporting immediate TNVR), Audubon conservationists (opposing feral colonies), and Sheriff's Animal Services (warning of staffing and nuisance constraints), Commissioners Heidi Carter, Nimasheena Burns, and Wendy Jacobs debated whether to lift trapping permit restrictions immediately or establish Sheriff-agency procedures first.
disagreements.side_a_position: Immediately adopt the AWAC ordinance language lifting Sheriff trapping permit restrictions so volunteer nonprofits can begin TNVR right away while final implementation rules are refined.
side_a_arguments: APS is at full capacity and still forced to euthanize healthy cats because existing ordinance rules restrict nonprofits from conducting TNVR.
Independent nonprofits and volunteer veterinarians are ready to begin trapping, spay/neutering, and vaccinating cats immediately at no immediate County cost.
disagreements.side_b_position: Do not immediately remove trapping permits or assign open-ended responsibilities before Sheriff's Office buy-in, funding, holding space, nuisance remedies, and a firm ~6-month timeline are established.
side_b_arguments: The Sheriff's Office has already stopped trapping due to overcrowding and lacks staff/equipment; shifting work immediately to outside groups without contracts, funding, or enforceable rules creates accountability and citizen-nuisance gaps.
Open-ended 'later date' ordinance language lacks urgency—staff must set a clear ~6-month deadline (targeting early 2023) with all stakeholders at the table.
disagreements.resolution: Commissioner Carter agreed to withdraw immediate implementation in favor of a compromise motion—adopted 5-0 at 03:44:52—adopting the AWAC ordinance draft as a model and directing staff to work with the Sheriff's Office, AWAC, APS, and nonprofits to finalize procedures within roughly six months.

meetings.title: BOCC Regular Session for July 11, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the July 11, 2022 regular session of the Durham County Board of Commissioners, with all five commissioners present. The Board celebrated seven National Association of Counties (NACo) Achievement Awards and approved the consent agenda, including capital project closeouts for completed Durham Public Schools and Durham Tech projects. Following three statutory public hearings, commissioners adopted bond orders and special referendum resolutions placing $550.24 million in general obligation bonds on the November 8, 2022 ballot—$423.505 million for Durham Public Schools (5-0), $112.74 million for Durham Technical Community College (5-0), and $13.995 million for the Museum of Life and Science (4-0, with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns abstaining). After an emotional public hearing and sharp board debate over immediate permit-removal versus structured implementation, the Board voted 5-0 to adopt a Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Release (TNVR) community cat program in principle using the Animal Welfare Advisory Committee's amendments as a model, directing staff, the Sheriff's Office, APS, and nonprofits to finalize operational regulations within six months.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Public Charge, and Citizen Comments on Child Welfare
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, read the public charge, and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns led the Pledge of Allegiance. During citizen comments, speakers including Samantha Nguyen raised urgent concerns regarding Child Protective Services and custody placements involving her grandchildren. Chair Howerton noted that the Board heard her concerns but could not intervene in judicial custody matters.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (Work Session and June 13, 2022 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton presented the minutes from the recent work session and the June 13, 2022 regular session. No corrections or edits were requested by commissioners.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item: Recognition of 2022 NACo Achievement Awards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton recognized Durham County departments for winning seven 2022 National Association of Counties (NACo) Achievement Awards: the Durham County Transit Plan, Tax Administration chatbot, Board of Elections ballot tracking application, DSS Low-Income Homeowners Relief Program, DSS Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP), Durham County Library Innovation League, and EMS Mobile Integrated Healthcare Community Paramedic Program. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns commended IS&T Director Greg Marrow and County staff for innovating during the COVID-19 pandemic and recovery from the County's cyberattack.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Including Item 22-0415 Capital Project Closeouts)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: No items were pulled from the consent agenda for separate discussion. Commissioners later highlighted Item 22-0415, which closed completed capital projects including Jordan High School renovations, Hub Farm improvements, Lowe's Grove, Eno Valley, Glenn Elementary roof work, and several Durham Tech projects.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0405: Durham County Public Health Focus COVID-19 Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 776 COVID-19 cases in the past seven days (a seven-day moving average of 111, down 8.27%), 343 total deaths, and 85,612 cumulative cases since the pandemic began. He noted that vaccines for children aged 0–5 and Pfizer boosters for ages 5–11 were now available, and highlighted free at-home COVID-19 test distribution through Community Access Points.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0421: 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Overview, Public Hearings, Bond Orders, and Special Referendum Resolutions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager presented the $550.24 million 2022 General Obligation Bond package—$423.505 million for Durham Public Schools (school renovations, HVAC, safety/security, high school replacement, and a new elementary school), $112.74 million for Durham Technical Community College (86,000 sq ft Allied Health building and 36,000 sq ft Life Sciences facility), and $13.995 million for the Museum of Life and Science—noting an estimated 2.5-cent property tax rate impact and a November 8, 2022 election date. During the School Bond hearing, Rachel Owens, Karen Purvis, and DAE President Michelle Burton urged support for aging 50-year-old school buildings and climate-resilient facilities, while Brian Callaway opposed the bond's magnitude and cited past DPS accountability concerns; during the Durham Tech hearing, Duke Health's Deborah Clark Jones, Novo Nordisk's Shayla Nunn Jones, Made in Durham's Casey Steinbacher, and Chamber representative Brian Fox endorsed the workforce training investments. Commissioners adopted all three bond orders and the two special referendum resolutions, with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns abstaining on all Museum of Life and Science votes due to her service on its board.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0394: Public Hearing and Adoption of Proposed Amendment to Durham County Animal Control Ordinance (Community Cat TNVR Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Willie Darby summarized the Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (AWAC) draft ordinance removing legal barriers to a Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Release (TNVR) program—redefining community cats, exempting them from stray/nuisance/rabies-tag provisions, shortening shelter hold times from five days to 72 hours, and leaving trapping operator selection (Sheriff vs. nonprofit) to be finalized. Twelve speakers split sharply during the public hearing: Humane Society, Best Friends Animal Society, Independent Animal Rescue, and APS Executive Director Shafonda Allen urged adopting the AWAC draft to relieve an over-capacity shelter, while Sheriff's Animal Services Lt. Wendy Penner and Audubon Society leaders Andrew Hudson and Barbara Driscoll opposed TNVR over nuisance calls, lack of Sheriff staffing, public health risks, and bird/wildlife predation. After Commissioner Heidi Carter's push to immediately lift trapping permit requirements met resistance from Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, and Chair Howerton over unfunded mandates and undefined governance, Carter revised her motion to adopt the TNVR program using AWAC's draft as a model while directing stakeholders to finalize regulations and procedures within a six-month target.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Darby announced the Board's appointments: Daniel Edwards and Rachelle Scott to the ABC Board, Nicole Thompson to the Durham Convention Center Authority, Vanessa Safai and Kate Safari to the Durham County Women's Commission, and Alec Hurdle to the Juvenile Crime Prevention Council.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board voted to enter closed session pursuant to NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5) regarding real property acquisition or employment contract terms and NCGS 143-318.11(a)(3) to consult with counsel regarding Case No. 20 CVS 3058 (McGrit v. Durham County Government). Upon reconvening at 03:54:00, Chair Howerton reported that the Board gave directions to staff and adjourned.

disagreements.issue: Immediate Permit-Removal Implementation vs. Phased Stakeholder Regulation of Community Cat TNVR Ordinance (Item 22-0394)
disagreements.summary: Following a divided public hearing over feral/community cat management, commissioners disagreed over whether to immediately remove Sheriff's Office trapping permit requirements so independent nonprofits could begin TNVR work immediately, versus waiting to adopt full operational rules, funding, and agency responsibilities with a firm deadline.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the AWAC draft ordinance immediately or immediately lift the trapping permit barrier so volunteer and nonprofit partners can begin TNVR while detailed regulations are finalized later.
side_a_arguments: The Animal Protection Society shelter is completely over capacity, and current trap-and-euthanize practices cost ~$70,000/year for ~350 cats without controlling the estimated 60,000 community cats.

Removing the Sheriff's trapping permit requirement immediately would allow qualified community partners like Best Friends Animal Society and Independent Animal Rescue to begin trapping, spaying, neutering, and vaccinating right away.
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject immediate unilateral trapping by unassigned nonprofits and avoid leaving next steps vague ('at a later date'); require formal collaboration with the Sheriff's Office, APS, AWAC, and nonprofits under a defined timeline to address staffing, holding space, veterinary capacity, and nuisance enforcement.
side_b_arguments: Allowing unassigned nonprofits to trap and release immediately creates an unfunded mandate without established holding capacity, veterinary staffing, oversight, or budget clarity (Burns).
It is premature to finalize operational assignments without the Sheriff's Office and County staff in the room to work through nuisance-call impacts (Howerton).
Leaving implementation to an unspecified 'later date' is unacceptable; the Board must name all required stakeholders and set a concrete target deadline to return with regulations (Jacobs).
disagreements.resolution: Commissioner Carter stepped back from immediate permit-removal and revised her motion to adopt a TNVR program using the AWAC ordinance amendments as a model while directing the County, Sheriff's Office, AWAC, APS, and nonprofits to develop regulations and procedures within a six-month target (around February 2023). The compromise motion passed 5-0.

meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 27, 2022 regular session with Commissioners Nida Allam, Nimasheena Burns, and Heidi Carter present (Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs had an excused absence). meetings.title: BOCC - June 13, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the June 13, 2022 regular session with all five commissioners present. Commissioners then unanimously adopted (5-0) the historic >$750 million FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance (Item 22-0327) with no property tax increase, funding $11.8 million in County employee compensation increases, $177 million+ for Durham Public Schools (an ~$11 million increase), $12 million+ for Durham Tech, and $6.4 million for Durham Pre-K. The Board also approved 2022 GO bond pre-application resolutions ($550.24 million total across DPS, DTCC, and the Museum of Life and Science) and four nonprofit fund-balance appropriations (with required board-service abstentions) before unanimously passing the Triangle Bikeway resolution (Item 22-0296) despite sharp commissioner concerns over public engagement and transit equity.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 22-0296)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs asked about an interlocal agreement with Emergency Management supporting the City's Community Safety Department, and staff confirmed that item had been pulled from the agenda for a future date. Chair Howerton pulled Item 22-0296 (Triangle Bikeway resolution) to discussion, and the remaining consent items passed 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0342: Public Hearing and Adoption of UDO Text Amendment Omnibus Changes 17 (TC2100006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staffer Michael Stock presented UDO Omnibus Changes 17 (recommended 11-2 by the Planning Commission), noting that three small-lot amendments were removed after Preservation Durham raised concerns over potential demolitions of older homes and that staff revised sight-distance triangle and accessory structure provisions per Planning Commissioner comments. Commissioners Carter, Jacobs, and Burns asked about affordable housing compliance reporting, Expanding Housing Choice metrics, plain-language graphics for residents, and legislative advocacy against preemptive state laws; with no public speakers signed up, the Board adopted the ordinance and consistency statement 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0327: Adoption of FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board unanimously adopted (5-0) the FY 2022–23 Annual Budget Ordinance exceeding $750 million—the largest in County history—without raising the property tax rate. agenda_items.title: Items 22-0379, 22-0383, 22-0384, & 22-0385: Budget Ordinance Amendments for External Organizations (NCGS 14-234.3 Compliance)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: In separate special votes complying with Session Law 2021-191 / NCGS 14-234.3, the Board approved four unassigned general fund balance appropriations: $1,953,341 for the NC Museum of Life and Science (4-0, Burns abstaining), $160,000 for Downtown Durham Inc. votes.item_title: Resolution Supporting Regional Implementation of the Triangle Bikeway (Item 22-0296)
votes.discussion_detail: Following questions from Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns about community outreach, youth ATV needs, and bus-integration equity, Vice Chair Jacobs moved the resolution supporting the regional vision for the Triangle Bikeway (committing no County funds), which passed 5-0.

disagreements.issue: Triangle Bikeway Resolution: Community Engagement, Transit Equity, and Recreational Priorities (Item 22-0296)
disagreements.summary: Although the Board ultimately adopted the non-binding Triangle Bikeway resolution 5-0, Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns challenged the sufficiency of community outreach and questioned prioritizing bike corridors over bus integration and youth ATV recreation, while Vice Chair Jacobs urged approval as a necessary first planning step.
disagreements.side_a_position: Questioned rushing forward with bike-lane resolutions without documented community-organization feedback, bus-system integration, or safe facilities for youth riding ATVs.
side_a_arguments: The packet lacked responses from most contacted community organizations aside from the Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People (Howerton).
Bikeways do not address youth racing ATVs on highways who need safe recreational spaces (Howerton).

Roughly 80% of bus riders are not commuting 20–30 miles on dark bike trails; the Board 'rams things through' on bike lanes and must ensure intentional outreach and bus integration going forward (Burns).
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve the resolution as an essential initial regional planning step that commits zero County funding.
side_b_arguments: The resolution only endorses the regional vision so partners like Wake County, RTP Foundation, and NCDOT can explore future phased funding for the ~$63 million Durham/Orange segments.
Approving the plan is procedurally required before any future implementation or grant applications can occur.
disagreements.resolution: Staff confirmed the resolution committed no County funding and pledged to send additional outreach responses and explore ATV recreation separately; the Board approved the resolution 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #4 - Monday, June 6, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the FY 2022–23 budget work session (titled on YouTube as June 6, 2022 Budget Work Session #4, though speakers referenced May 17, 2022 primary election day during the broadcast), with all five commissioners present. Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the manager's recommended budget featuring extraordinary revenue growth, a flat property tax rate, $6.4–$6.5 million in general fund ARPA support, 2.5%/3.5% employee COLAs, 3%–4% merit pay, and 36.7 new general fund FTEs, while cautioning that FY23 revenue spikes may not recur in FY24. CFO Susan Tezai presented fund-balance projections (39.08% total and 19.48% unassigned for FY22, maintaining the County's AAA management credit rating and 69.55 days of cash liquidity amid $8 million in pending FEMA reimbursements and $1.6 million in cyberattack recovery costs). Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson briefed the Board on the 2025 reappraisal kickoff, 1.25% holdbacks, and $719 million in partial exemptions, while HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry detailed rising turnover above 18% and proposed pay/benefit enhancements including paid family leave. Commissioners concluded by discussing the upcoming add/delete list, school funding flexibility, and Chair Howerton's request to see what cuts would be needed to add $2 million without raising taxes.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022–23 Recommended Budget Major Revenue and Expenditure Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane presented the FY 2022–23 manager's recommended budget, highlighting extraordinary revenue growth driven by FY21–22 collections while maintaining a flat property tax rate. Key priorities included $6.4–$6.5 million of ARPA funding in the general fund, 2.5% COLAs for employees above $75,000 and 3.5% below $75,000, 3%–4% merit pay, focused EMS/public safety compensation adjustments, and 36.7 new general fund FTEs.

agenda_items.title: Fund Balance, Cash Liquidity, and Reserve Policy Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CFO Susan Tezai reported that Durham County's 35% total / 16% unassigned fund-balance policy remains critical to maintaining its AAA rating, projecting FY22 fund balance at $269.6 million (39.08% total, 19.48% unassigned) and 69.55 days of operating cash on hand. She noted the County had filed nearly $8 million in FEMA COVID-19 claims with no reimbursement received yet and incurred ~$1.6 million in cyberattack recovery costs, and previewed future policy updates focusing on unassigned reserves and liquidity.

agenda_items.title: Tax Valuation, Holdbacks, Exemptions, and 2025 Reappraisal Preview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson reviewed property tax projections—including >3% real property growth, 8% personal property, and >15% motor vehicle growth—and explained the County's 1.25% holdback and $719 million in statutory partial exemptions (~$5.2 million in foregone revenue). Because current bills still rely on January 1, 2019 values ahead of the January 1, 2025 reappraisal, Commissioner Burns warned of severe sticker shock and displacement pressure on Black and lower-income homeowners, urging expansion of the Low-Income Homeowner Relief program.

agenda_items.title: Employee Compensation, Turnover, and New Benefits Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry reported that County turnover climbed 3.9% above the 18% governmental benchmark with 302 employees eligible to retire in FY23, and noted that 83% of employees (earning ≤$75,000) would be eligible for up to 7.5% combined COLA/merit increases while 17% above $75,000 could receive up to 6.5%. She also detailed the County's $15/hour living wage floor (with the lowest actual employee at ~$16.78/hour) and proposed FY23 benefits including four weeks of paid family leave, five days of funeral leave, wellness clinic family access, and pet insurance, laying groundwork for a formal compensation philosophy.

agenda_items.title: Board Budget Q&A, Add/Delete Process, and DPS Funding Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff outlined the upcoming email Q&A and add/delete list workflow, explaining how Durham Public Schools receives current-expense allocations rather than PRC-earmarked funds. Commissioners discussed comparing per-pupil funding across counties (noting Wake County mixes debt service into reported totals), Vice Chair Jacobs praised a new $500,000 Public Art Fund allocation, and Chair Howerton asked staff to identify what cuts would be needed to free up $2 million for community priorities without raising taxes.

meetings.title: BOCC - Work Session - Monday, June 6, 2022 (Part 1)
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 1 of the June 6, 2022 BOCC work session with all five commissioners present (no formal votes were taken). The Board heard citizen comments from Bike Durham urging faster capital transit delivery, reviewed consent agenda items for the upcoming regular session, and vetted Item 22-0323 to establish a two-phase independent, confidential County Ombuds Office with consultants from the Town of Chapel Hill. Commissioners also received an informational briefing on the Triangle Bikeway study ahead of the June 13 vote and engaged in an extended policy debate with City Transportation Director Sean Egan over the FY23 Transit Work Program, $10.8 million FTA-funded Durham Station upgrades ($2.7 million local match), City staffing requests, sidewalk cost-sharing, and how to deploy the ~$87–$100 million half-cent sales tax fund balance held for major regional transit projects.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comments (Bike Durham on FY23 Transit Work Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order and read the public charge. Bike Durham board member Eric Landfried urged commissioners to work collaboratively with the City Council to fund additional transit project-delivery positions—noting projects like the Village Transit Center had been delayed since 2013—oppose project-by-project sidewalk cost-sharing, and require clear project charters.

agenda_items.title: Review of Consent Agenda Items for Upcoming Regular Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Kimberly Sowell walked through draft consent items including Justice Center courtroom AV upgrades ($136,073.96, Item 22-0272), $364,074 in NC DHHS funding for public health communicable disease nurses (Item 22-0278), Hoopla digital library services ($200k range, Item 22-0307), $40,000 for IS&T (Item 22-0319), a new County Attorney FTE (Item 22-0325), and MWBE/HUB certification efforts (Item 22-0345). Commissioners asked clarifying questions on public health hiring, library reporting, and MWBE certification.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0323: Discussion of Establishing a Durham County Ombuds Office
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager and Chapel Hill mediator-consultants Tiffany Sneed and Matthew Sullivan presented a proposal to create an independent, impartial, confidential Ombuds Office—starting with County employees in Phase 1 before expanding to residents in Phase 2. Commissioners Carter, Allam, Howerton, and Burns questioned whether reporting lines to the County Manager could compromise perceived independence, how the non-investigative role interacts with HR grievance policies, and whether a single FTE could handle countywide employee and public caseloads.

agenda_items.title: Triangle Bikeway Study Informational Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO coordinator Dale McKeel presented findings from the two-year Triangle Bikeway study ahead of the June 13 action item to endorse the regional plan. Commissioners Allam and Carter asked about trail amenities, while Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns requested the full study report and raised questions about stakeholder participation.

agenda_items.title: City of Durham Transit Projects, Durham Station, and FY23 Transit Work Program Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Transportation Director Sean Egan presented schematic designs for Durham Station (15,000 daily riders; awarded $10.8 million federal FTA grant requiring a $2.7 million local match), the Better Bus Project covering 12 miles of sidewalk gaps and Fayetteville/Holloway corridor upgrades, Treyburn vanpools, and GoDurham Connect in East Durham. Commissioners engaged in an extensive debate with Egan and County Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman over whether half-cent transit sales tax revenues (~$30–$32 million/year with ~$87–$100 million accumulated fund balance) should cover City staffing and sidewalk work or require City cost-sharing to preserve funds for regional rail/BRT.

disagreements.issue: Durham County Transit Plan: City Staffing/Sidewalk Cost-Sharing vs. Utilizing $100M Transit Fund Balance
disagreements.summary: Commissioners and City/County transportation leaders disagreed over whether to require City of Durham cost-sharing for additional transit project-delivery staff and sidewalk improvements, and whether the accumulated ~$87–$100 million half-cent transit sales tax fund balance should be tapped to accelerate local bus/access projects or preserved for major regional transit investments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require City cost-sharing for City transit staff and sidewalk improvements, establish clear tri-board financial/governance policies with GoTriangle, and preserve the transit sales tax fund balance for regional commuter rail or Bus Rapid Transit (BRT).
side_a_arguments: Durham County generates only ~$30–$32 million/year in transit revenues (potentially losing ~$25 million over 20 years from rental-car tax changes), so sidewalk repairs and amenities—basic city functions—should not crowd out core transit service and regional BRT/rail (Jacobs, Carter).
The ~$87–$100 million fund balance exists specifically because voters approved the sales tax for major regional projects like commuter rail (Jacobs).
Cost-sharing ensures 'skin in the game' and clear governance policies among the County, City, and GoTriangle (Howerton, Jacobs, County Manager staff Ellen Beckman).
disagreements.side_b_position: Support funding requested City transit staff positions without punitive cost-share delays and leverage the ~$100 million transit fund balance to deliver overdue bus stop, sidewalk, and corridor improvements immediately.
side_b_arguments: Without additional staffing capacity, $25–$35 million in transit corridor projects face 8%–10% annual construction cost escalation (~$1 million/year lost per year of delay) while transit-dependent riders (80% people of color, two-thirds zero-car households) wait for basic shelters and sidewalks (City Director Sean Egan, Bike Durham).
Approving requested staffing positions is critical so historically excluded neighborhoods do not remain left behind on overdue transit and shelter repairs (Allam).
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton requested GoTriangle fund-balance documentation and staff continued developing formal cost-sharing and governance policies through the tri-board governance study.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #3 Part 1
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 1 of Budget Work Session #3 on June 3, 2022, with all five commissioners present for departmental FY 2022–23 budget reviews (no formal votes taken). Information Services & Technology (IS&T) reviewed four newly recommended FTEs and CIP technology replacements, while new ABC Board GM L. Sordell projected $61.43 million in revenue and a $2.5 million County distribution (with commissioners requesting an additional $100,000). Sheriff Clarence Birkhead outlined requests for an external Detention Center maintenance contract, a $735,000 (5%) pay adjustment to combat academy and officer attrition, and a 3% detention night-shift differential. Office of Emergency Services Director Jim Groves detailed ambulance fleet replacements, a proactive Fire Marshal commercial fee schedule (+$36,000 estimated revenue), increasing EMS billing from 157% to 200% of Medicare rates ($2.7–$3.8 million projected revenue), and detailing two County EMTs to the City's Community Safety crisis teams; General Manager Joanne Pierce also reviewed the newly created Community Intervention & Support Services (CISS) department and Soil & Water presented its Agricultural Economic Development Grant program.

agenda_items.title: Information Services & Technology (IS&T) Budget and CIP Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CIO Greg Marrow presented IS&T's 'Run, Grow, Transform' FY23 budget, highlighting four newly awarded positions (two business analysts, one project manager, and one service desk technician) and upcoming CIP technology replacement needs. He noted IS&T remained below local government benchmarks at 3.0% of the County budget and 2.5% of total staffing compared to 4.7% and 4.8% industry averages.

agenda_items.title: Durham County ABC Board Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: New ABC Board General Manager L. Sordell projected $61.43 million in gross revenue for FY23, reviewed store remodels, the new Highway 55 store and >$1.5 million upset bid on the old property, a Page Road/TW Alexander build, July 1 mixed-beverage delivery launch, and a 6% across-the-board staff raise. The ABC Board budgeted $2.5 million in County distributions (out of $3.78 million total local/law enforcement/rehab distributions), and commissioners discussed asking for an additional $100,000 distribution and potential County partnership on the vacated Fayetteville Street property.

agenda_items.title: Durham County Sheriff's Office Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead and command staff presented Priority #1—contracting with a third-party vendor to handle 24/7 Detention Center maintenance (HVAC, locks, elevators, plumbing) given General Services staffing shortages—and thanked the County Manager for recommending Priority #2 ($735,000 for a 5% law enforcement and detention pay adjustment) and Priority #3 (3% night-shift differential). Finance/HR staff showed that ongoing separations left the agency at a net 19-to-24-officer deficit even after graduating a 20-officer academy, while commissioners asked about SROs, mental health/opioid burdens in the jail, and state-mandated inmate housing.

agenda_items.title: Office of Emergency Services (EMS & Fire Marshal) Budget and Fee Schedule Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OES Director Jim Groves and Fire Marshal Jason Shepherd presented ambulance fleet replacement plans (adding Stealth Power anti-idling and box remounting saving ~$100,000/year), a restructured proactive commercial Fire Marshal inspection fee schedule (~$36,000 net revenue increase), and a proposal to raise EMS billing rates from 157% to 200% of the Medicare fee schedule (projected to generate $2.7–$3.8 million to offset general fund costs and pay raises). Groves also outlined Mobile Integrated Healthcare expansion and OES's commitment to detail two rotating County EMTs to the City's Community Safety crisis teams.

agenda_items.title: Community Intervention & Support Services (CISS) Department Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Joanne Pierce reviewed the newly formed CISS department uniting Bull City United (expanding from 17 to 25 staff across four additional census tracts via City ILA, with final six hires starting June 21), My Brother's Keeper, and Project BUILD gang prevention/intervention, requesting administrative support positions. Commissioners discussed developing community-based alternatives to youth detention and Chair Howerton urged clearer public communication so residents understand Bull City United's violence-mediation role.

agenda_items.title: Soil and Water Conservation District Agricultural Economic Development Grant Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Soil and Water staff and committee chair David Harris reviewed the Agricultural Economic Development Grant program ($75,000 budgeted in FY22 vs. consistently higher demand capped at $5,000 per farm/nonprofit and $1,000 per school). Commissioners Burns and Carter expressed support for increasing total grant funding, raising per-project caps, and considering non-food horticultural or organic soil incentives, while Vice Chair Jacobs questioned declining federal/state cost-share funding indicators on budget book page 110.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #3 Part 2
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over Part 2 of Budget Work Session #3 on June 3, 2022 (with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns departing at 00:29:27; no formal votes taken). Soil and Water Conservation District staff presented the BETC/CCAP student green-infrastructure training program—highlighting a 20% environmental literacy gain across two participating schools—and requested a $68,919 Outreach Coordinator FTE alongside a community coalition ask of $200,000 to expand to four schools. Budget Director Keith Lane then walked commissioners through the FY 2022–23 Add/Delete list, detailing administrative grant adjustments, ~$800,000–$900,000 in general fund items potentially shifted to ARPA, and proposed additions including +$1 million for Durham Public Schools, +$146,000 for Bull City Community Schools, $50,000 for TJCOG Solarize, $50,000 for MWBE support, $125,000 for the Ombuds FTE, two $140,000 attorney positions, and $69,000 for Soil & Water, leaving a net ~$300,000–$400,000 balance covered by general fund balance with no tax rate increase. Commissioners differed briefly over hiring a full-time transportation attorney versus using outside legal consultants and deferred that personnel discussion to closed session.

agenda_items.title: Soil and Water BETC/CCAP Program Presentation and Outreach Coordinator Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Soil and Water staff detailed the four-week summer BETC/CCAP program, where certified high school teachers and students design and install state-spec rain gardens (~$45,000 per school/year), achieving a 20% increase in environmental literacy and workforce pathways. Staff requested a $68,919 Outreach Coordinator FTE, while Commissioner Heidi Carter referenced a coalition request from Matt Kopac and nine environmental groups for $200,000 (expanding from two to four schools and adding $80,000 to CCAP); Commissioner Allam requested greater language-equity outreach to public housing families and Vice Chair Jacobs praised workforce outcomes and flood-mitigation targeting in Braggtown.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022–23 Budget Add/Delete List Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane presented the FY23 Add/Delete spreadsheet, noting net-zero administrative adjustments (+$450,000 maternal health grant, +$65,000 city-funded immigrant/refugee position, -$31,000 Pre-K adjustment, -$150,000 duplicate early childhood line) and removing a $625,000 Sheriff/Youth Home increase that County Manager Sowell clarified was a misunderstanding. Proposed additions included +$1 million for DPS (with DPS expected to tap its fund balance for the remainder of its $1.9 million request), +$146,000 for Bull City Community Schools, +$71,000 for Pre-K wraparound care, $50,000 for TJCOG Solarize, $50,000 for MWBE support, $125,000 for an Ombuds FTE, $140,000 for a general attorney, $140,000 for a transportation attorney, and $69,000 for Soil & Water, offset by shifting ~$800k–$900k to ARPA and potentially +$100,000 from the ABC Board—requiring ~$300,000–$400,000 from general fund balance while keeping the tax rate flat.

agenda_items.title: Discussion of Transportation Legal Counsel (In-House FTE vs. Consultants) and DPS Fund Balance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs questioned adding a dedicated $140,000 transportation attorney FTE, suggesting the County could instead hire consultants or recruit transportation expertise into the already-proposed attorney slot to control recurring staff costs. Chair Brenda A. Howerton countered that ongoing GoTriangle disputes require dedicated in-house transportation counsel because the County lacks internal expertise, and the Board agreed to hold that staffing conversation for closed session after confirming DPS's willingness to use fund balance toward its remaining $0.9 million request.

disagreements.issue: In-House Transportation Attorney FTE vs. Outside Legal Consultants
disagreements.summary: Commissioners differed during the Add/Delete list review on whether to fund a dedicated $140,000 in-house transportation attorney FTE or rely on outside consultants / an existing proposed attorney position.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prefer using outside consultants or recruiting transportation expertise within the already-planned new attorney position to minimize ongoing FTE costs.
side_a_arguments: Adding another permanent FTE increases recurring County personnel costs when specialized transportation advice might be procured more cost-effectively via consultants or combined into the general attorney hire.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hire a dedicated in-house transportation attorney FTE to advise the County on GoTriangle and complex transit matters.
side_b_arguments: Ongoing GoTriangle issues are creating problems because Durham County government currently has no internal legal counsel with transportation expertise to advise the Board (Howerton).
General Manager Claudia Hager noted that hiring part-time or contractual legal talent at that level can be difficult compared to a full-time role that could later be re-evaluated through attrition.
disagreements.resolution: No decision was made during the open work session; Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Jacobs agreed to defer the personnel discussion to closed session ahead of the June 6 work session and June 13 budget vote.

meetings.title: BOCC - May 23, 2022 - Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the May 23, 2022 regular session with all five commissioners present, opening with a moment of silence for victims of the Buffalo, New York shooting and a Memorial Day proclamation. The Board approved the consent agenda 5-0 (including a separate 5-0 approval of pulled items for a grant-funded mobile public health medical unit and a 10% construction materials testing contingency) and voted 5-0 to approve Zoning Map Change Z2100013 (Parmer Sector 3 on So-Hi Drive, rezoning ~4.3 acres from Rural Residential to Science Research Park). Commissioners held the public hearing on the FY 2022–23 County Manager's Recommended Budget (Item 22-0308)—extending speaker time from one to two minutes by a 5-0 vote—hearing pleas for Sheriff's Office/detention pay raises, living wages, and renewable energy investments. Following presentations on COVID-19 (CDC Yellow level) and Family Connects Durham, and heated public testimony on Item 22-0291 (Community Cat TNVR Animal Control Ordinance), the Board voted 5-0 to advance the TNVR draft ordinance to a public hearing (subsequently amended post-closed session to July 11, 2022).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, Announcements, and Approval of Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, read the public charge, asked Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs to lead the Pledge of Allegiance, and held a moment of silence for the victims of the Buffalo, New York shooting. Clerk Monica Wallace read community announcements, commissioners discussed pandemic business recovery grants ($21M Durham / $200M state) and rural broadband needs, and the Board approved prior May minutes 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items: Memorial Day 2022 Proclamation and DSS Eligibility Workers Month Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton read a Memorial Day 2022 proclamation honoring fallen military service members, accepted by Veteran Services representatives. Before the consent agenda, Vice Chair Jacobs also shared a DSS Board resolution proclaiming May 2022 as Eligibility Workers Month in recognition of income maintenance staff.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Consent Agenda (Including Pulled Items 22-0292 and 22-0286)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners pulled Item 22-0292 (grant-funded mobile public health medical unit) and Item 22-0286 (10% contingency for independent construction materials testing) for brief public explanations by Health Director Rod Jenkins and staff, and approved the remaining consent items 5-0. Immediately following the staff explanations, the Board voted 5-0 to approve Items 22-0292 and 22-0286.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing and Adoption of Zoning Map Change Z2100013 (Parmer Sector 3, 2102 & 2152 So-Hi Drive)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staffer Michael Stock and applicant attorney Worth Mills (Longleaf Law Partners) presented a general-use rezoning of ~4.3 acres from Rural Residential (RR) to Science Research Park (SRP) to resolve a 1989 split-zoning irregularity across the 51-acre parcel inside Research Triangle Park (recommended 10-0 by the Planning Commission). Commissioner Carter sought commitments on future So-Hi Drive bike facilities and stream/floodplain/tree protection during future site plan review, and the Board adopted the zoning ordinance and NCGS 160D-605 consistency statement 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0308: Public Hearing on FY 2022–23 County Manager's Recommended Budget
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board opened the public hearing on the FY 2022–23 recommended budget and voted 5-0 (on a motion by Commissioner Allam seconded by Commissioner Burns) to extend individual speaker time from one minute to two minutes. Speakers included detention and Sheriff's Office personnel (such as Annetta Page) urging competitive pay raises to address staffing crises, as well as advocates calling for renewable energy investments aligned with the County's 2018 clean energy resolution.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (speaker time extension); Public hearing informational

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0303: Public Health COVID-19 Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 1,083 current cases, a seven-day moving average of 154 (down 9.53% from the prior week), 15.5% PCR positivity, and Durham County's move into the CDC 'Yellow' community level along with the broader Triangle. He answered commissioner questions on wastewater surveillance, five-day isolation guidance, pediatric vaccines (ages 5–11), and Paxlovid antiviral access.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0290: Update on Family Connects Durham
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Center for Child and Family Health leaders Robert Murphy and Dr. Karen Appleyard Harmony, nurse Karen Halpin, and parent Vanessa Diaz presented outcomes for Family Connects Durham, which has served over 20,000 Durham families since 2008 (1,366 visits and 1,600 referrals in 2021 with an 86% one-month connection rate and >$3 in emergency medical savings per $1 spent). Staff noted pandemic adaptations to telehealth and efforts to hire a new Spanish-speaking nurse to restore Hispanic participation rates.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0291: Proposed Amendment to Animal Control Ordinance (Community Cat TNVR Program)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Willie Darby presented the draft Animal Control Ordinance amendment developed with AWAC and Best Friends Animal Society to enable a future TNVR program while deferring operational implementation until costs and staffing are resolved. Although not a formal public hearing, citizens and officials spoke on both sides: Sheriff's Animal Services Sgt. Wendy Penner (citing 2,368 trap requests since 2012 and severe nuisance complaints) and Capt. Mark Manning (warning of 20% higher call volume and >$535k–$700k+ in staffing/spay-neuter costs), wildlife rehabilitators, and Sharon Cadell urged caution or opposition, while APS Director Shafonda Allen urged ending trap-and-euthanize practices. The Board voted 5-0 to accept the draft subject to edits and schedule a public hearing, and amended the motion after closed session to set the public hearing for July 11, 2022.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments, Closed Session, and Excused Absence
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Attorney Darby announced appointments to the Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission (Monica Green), Women's Commission (Roberta Price), Durham Hospital Corporation Board of Trustees (Constanza Gomez-Jones, Hector Hidalgo, and Paul Moussa), and Racial Equity Commission (Jada Richardson). The Board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under NCGS 143-318.11(a)(5), reconvened with directions to staff, amended the TNVR public hearing date to July 11, 2022 (5-0), and approved an excused absence for Commissioner Heidi Carter on June 27, 2022 (5-0).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (Closed Session, TNVR date amendment, Excused Absence)
