meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #2 - May 19, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners held its second FY 2022-23 budget work session, reviewing the 10-year $1.8 billion Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), Durham Public Schools (DPS) operating request, and Durham Technical Community College (DTCC) budget. Budget staff presented debt-service projections showing the dedicated 8.61-cent property tax rate held flat in FY 2022-23 alongside a projected 2.5-cent tax increase in FY 2023-24 for a planned November 2022 general obligation bond, while commissioners debated a proposed $500,000 starter allocation for a 1% Public Art Fund. Tension emerged between commissioners and DPS leadership over a remaining $2 million gap between DPS's adjusted $11.875 million essential request and the Manager's $9.875 million recommendation, with commissioners criticizing School Board communication and questioning rising per-pupil spending amid a roughly 1,055-student enrollment drop. DTCC President J.B. Buxton outlined an $789,000 operating increase (+8.81%), expanded Article 46/Durham Promise workforce pathways, the BULLS life-sciences initiative, and bond-funded facility needs, followed by Board follow-up requests on behavioral health returned funds from Alliance Health, Community Paramedicine, CISS, and Soil and Water Conservation. No formal votes were taken during the work session.

agenda_items.title: CIP Financial Overview and 10-Year Capital Financing Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the FY 2022-31 CIP totaling $1.8 billion, including over $900 million for DPS and $106 million for IS&T infrastructure. Staff projected $76 million in FY 2022-23 debt service ($34 million for DPS), $16.9 million in PAYGO projects (including $4.1 million for 500 E. Main affordable housing and detention center window replacements), and holding the dedicated debt-service property tax flat at 8.61 cents with an estimated 2.5-cent increase in FY 2023-24 for a November 2022 GO bond. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns questioned allocating $500,000 to seed a 1% Public Art program while construction inflation strains capital reserves, and Heidi Carter asked whether $1 million in the $1.5 million Swap Fund could be reallocated.

agenda_items.title: Durham Public Schools (DPS) FY 2022-23 Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga, CFO Paul LeSieur, and Budget Director Alex Modesto presented DPS's $12.875 million local funding request—covering $5.3 million in fixed costs, raising minimum teacher supplements from $5,675 to $6,500 plus step increases ($1,135), Lyons Farm Elementary expansion, post-ESSER IT technicians, and $2.6 million in charter school pass-through—compared to the Manager's $9.875 million recommendation ($176 million total, $4,333 per pupil). DPS stated it could absorb ~$1 million for Lyons Farm and IT technicians using lapsed salaries and ESSER funds, narrowing its essential gap to $2 million ($11.875 million total). Commissioners criticized School Board members for failing to communicate directly while mischaracterizing BOCC support publicly, pressed DPS on an ~1,055-student enrollment decline to ~31,300, and discussed classified staff pay ($15.38 moving to $15.78/hour; $17/hour for bus drivers, with universal $17/hour estimated at $4.3-$4.4 million) and ESSER I/II/III spending.

agenda_items.title: Durham Technical Community College (DTCC) FY 2022-23 Budget Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DTCC President J.B. Buxton, CFO Andy Klich, and Chief Academic Officer Dr. Kara Battle presented a $789,000 operating increase (+8.81%) for utilities, facilities, campus security, and a shared apprenticeship coordinator, plus $380,000 in Article 46 Durham Promise growth (to $1.89 million) alongside requests to broaden Article 46 eligibility to non-credit Nurse Aide scholarships, Back to Work overflow, and adult basic skills losses (-$300,000 state FTE drop). Buxton also outlined scaling the BULLS life-sciences youth stipend program via ARPA funds (5 pilot students, 25 across Cohorts 1-2, targeting 60-100 annually plus construction and IT) and major capital plans ($1.1 million CIP HVAC retrofit and 2022 bond funding for Life Sciences, Allied Health, and Bacon/Cooper property acquisition alongside a $1.2 million RTP Bio federal earmark with Wake Tech). Commissioner Nimasheena Burns urged tying corporate economic incentives (JDIG/EDPNC) to private stipend sponsorships, and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs requested stronger microtransit/GoDurham Connect links to the Northern Durham campus and Treyburn.

agenda_items.title: Commissioner Follow-Up Requests and Behavioral Health Funding Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners requested follow-up briefings on Community Paramedicine, Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS)—with Burns emphasizing Black and Latino boys and My Brother's Keeper—and Soil and Water Conservation's BETC position and farmer grant staffing. Budget staff confirmed an agenda item for June 2 to amend the Alliance Health contract and return $5 million in unspent behavioral health funds ($2 million to offset county fund balance and $3 million reserved for behavioral health system discussions), while Heidi Carter asked for details on county vehicle replacement policies.

disagreements.issue: DPS Additional $2M Operating Request, Enrollment Decline, and Inter-Board Communication
disagreements.summary: Commissioners challenged DPS leadership over its request for $2-$3 million above the County Manager's $9.875 million increase recommendation amid declining enrollment and frustration with School Board members' public messaging and lack of direct outreach.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question additional ongoing funding above the Manager's $9.875M (+9% per-pupil) recommendation without clearer accountability on declining enrollment (~1,055 drop), classified/certified wage sustainability, and direct School Board communication.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns rebuked School Board members for never contacting commissioners directly while alleging BOCC lacked commitment to DPS teachers and staff.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted DPS enrollment fell from 32,596 in FY19-20 to ~31,300 projected while county per-pupil funding rose to $4,333.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stressed fiduciary duty to avoid unnecessary tax hikes amid inflation and warned against shifting narratives when BOCC asks accountability questions.
disagreements.side_b_position: Fund DPS's revised $11.875M essential local operating need (absorbing ~$1M in IT technicians and Lyons Farm expansion internally) to cover fixed costs, teacher salary supplements ($6,500 minimum), and post-pandemic student supports.
side_b_arguments: Superintendent Pascal Mubenga explained pre-pandemic growth reversed by ~1,300 students statewide due to COVID-19 and projected 20,000 more school-age children over five years, noting county dollars fund summer counselors and intensive behavioral COPE staffing (~6-7 adults per 18 students) uncovered by the state.
CFO Paul LeSieur noted charter pass-throughs (+$1.97M/+2.6M) consume substantial local increases and recurring fund balance use is unsustainable.

Commissioner Heidi Carter expressed support for meeting the $11.8M adjusted request while calling for a county-city-DPS community conversation on a sustainable living wage for over 1,000 low-paid school employees.
disagreements.resolution: Vice Chair Jacobs indicated consensus to examine funding DPS's revised $11.8M request while County Manager Kimberly Sowell asked DPS for eight-year enrollment trajectories and charter/fund-balance absorption options before budget adoption.

disagreements.issue: 1% for Public Art Starter Allocation ($500,000) in the Capital Improvement Plan
disagreements.summary: Commissioners questioned whether a proposed $500,000 allocation in the FY 2022-23 CIP to establish a 1% Public Art Fund was an appropriate priority given inflation-driven capital cost overruns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Oppose or scrutinize dedicating $500,000 to a new Public Art program during high inflation and tight debt-service fund balance reserves.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs expressed surprise at the $500,000 allocation when other urgent needs lack funding and projects like the 300 E. Main parking deck face $4M cost overruns.
Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned who requested the allocation and whether commissioners had aligned on spending half a million dollars on public art while human-service needs go unmet.
disagreements.side_b_position: Include the $500,000 starter placeholder based on prior CIP discussions for board review during budget markups.
side_b_arguments: County Manager Kimberly Sowell and GM Claudia Hager explained the line item reflected prior Board policy interest in a 1% art policy for capital projects and could be adjusted through the Ad/Delete budget process.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted the $500,000 CIP placeholder remained subject to Board removal or modification during upcoming budget work sessions.

meetings.title: BOCC Budget Work Session #1 - May 17, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners opened its FY 2022-23 budget work sessions with comprehensive briefings on revenue and expenditure drivers, fund balance policies, property tax valuation, and human resources compensation. Budget Director Keith Lane and County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell outlined a $794 million total budget ($550 million General Fund, +8.97%) holding the property tax rate flat by pairing $32 million in natural revenue growth—led by property taxes (+$13.9 million) and sales taxes (+$11.5 million total)—with $28 million in General Fund balance, while warning of $30 million in annual structural expenditure pressure going forward. CFO Susan Tezai reviewed the projected $269.6 million FY 2022 General Fund balance and OPEB reserve caps needed to protect Durham County's AAA bond rating, while Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson detailed the delayed 2025 countywide reappraisal, revenue-neutral tax math, and $719 million in exempt property. Human Resources Director Kathy Everett-Perry highlighted an 18% turnover threshold surpassed by +3.9%, 302 upcoming retirement eligibilities, proposed 5.5%–7.5% employee raises (reaching $18.10/hour minimum), free family care at the employee Wellness Clinic, and 4 weeks of Paid Family Leave. No formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and FY 2022-23 Budget Revenue and Expenditure Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the session to order, and Budget Director Keith Lane, County Manager Kimberly Sowell, and GM Claudia Hager walked through the $794 million recommended budget ($550 million General Fund). Natural revenue growth of $32 million (+$13.9 million GF property tax, +$6.8 million GF sales tax, +$5 million Medicaid Hold Harmless, +$2.7 million Register of Deeds fees, +$3.3 million EMS fees) plus $28 million in appropriated fund balance funds employee COLA/merit raises, +$9.88 million for DPS, +$4.3 million in health insurance, 36.7 new GF FTEs focused on internal support amid a 20% (~400-position) vacancy rate, and vehicle replacements. Commissioners pressed staff for a clearer cumulative tax-rate history chart for taxpayers and asked where an additional $2 million for DPS could be cut without raising taxes.

agenda_items.title: Finance Department Fund Balance Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief Financial Officer Susan Tezai presented the county's reserve position, projecting $269.6 million in total General Fund balance at FY 2022 year-end ($102.2 million unassigned at FY 2021 close) and explaining how state LGC minimums and county policies (including a 25% cap on OPEB committed reserves) preserve Durham's AAA credit rating. Staff and commissioners discussed revising the fund balance policy to balance rating-agency expectations against capital, inflation, and emergency reserve demands, with Nimasheena Burns underscoring that fund balance should support one-time rather than recurring obligations.

agenda_items.title: Tax Administration Valuation, Reappraisal, and Property Tax Relief Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson explained that county properties remain valued at January 1, 2019 assessments until the next countywide reappraisal in 2025, reviewed revenue-neutral calculations showing the 2016 and 2019 tax changes exceeded revenue-neutral, and noted $719 million in exempt property equates to roughly $5.2 million in foregone revenue. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns voiced deep concern about gentrification and tax-driven displacement in Black and brown neighborhoods ahead of 2025 and urged expanding the county's DSS Low-Income Homeowner Relief program—including reducing its 10-year residency requirement to 5–7.5 years—since state statute caps countywide exemptions.

agenda_items.title: Human Resources Employee Compensation, Retention, and Benefits Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry and benefits staff reported that employee turnover climbed 3.9 percentage points above the 18% county benchmark, with 246 non-retirement separations and 302 staff eligible for retirement in FY 2022-23, alongside 50 vacancies in Public Health and recent mid-year EMS, Youth Home, and Sheriff pay adjustments. Under the recommended budget, 83% of employees (1,529 earning up to $75,000) could receive up to 7.5% combined COLA (3.5%) and merit (up to 4%), lifting the lowest hourly pay from $16.98 to $18.10. New benefits include zero-copay primary care at the Wellness Clinic for employees and dependents, 5 days of funeral leave, pet insurance, and a 4-week Paid Family Leave policy covering serious family illness and COVID quarantine ahead of a broader MAG classification study.

agenda_items.title: Budget Work Session Follow-Up Process and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Kimberly Sowell and Chair Brenda A. Howerton reviewed the upcoming Ad/Delete list submission process, scheduled follow-up budget questions, and adjourned the work session informally at 03:14:29 without taking formal votes.

disagreements.issue: 2025 Tax Reappraisal Burden, Residential Displacement, and Homeowner Relief Eligibility
disagreements.summary: Commissioners debated how to mitigate rising tax burdens on longtime, lower-income residents ahead of the 2025 reappraisal and 2022/2026 bond referenda within statutory limits.
disagreements.side_a_position: Expand local Low-Income Homeowner Relief access (e.g., shortening the 10-year ownership rule to 5–7.5 years) and transparently present cumulative multi-year tax impacts to protect residents from gentrification and displacement.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns warned rapid gentrification in Black and brown neighborhoods plus stacked tax rate increases (2016, 2019, and upcoming bonds) threatens displacement once 2025 values reset after a six-year gap.
Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs pushed lowering the 10-year residency rule in the county's DSS grant program and tracking multi-year household bill impacts alongside legislative relief advocacy.
disagreements.side_b_position: Statutory uniformity rules prevent Durham County from unilaterally altering property exemptions or deferrals beyond existing state circuit-breaker laws without General Assembly action.
side_b_arguments: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson noted North Carolina General Statutes strictly govern property exemptions and homestead deferrals ($719M already exempt countywide), requiring grant-based local workarounds or Raleigh legislation.
disagreements.resolution: Staff noted pending DSS Board recommendations to revise the local homeowner grant tenure rule and agreed to provide clearer historical tax-impact graphics for taxpayers.

meetings.title: BOCC - MAY 9th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: At its May 9, 2022 Regular Session, the Board of County Commissioners heard public comment from DPS Instructional Assistant Association president Sunny Geraldo advocating for higher classified school staff pay before County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell formally presented the FY 2022-23 Recommended Budget ($794 million total / $550 million General Fund, holding the tax rate flat). The Board adopted proclamations honoring National EMS Week, Older Americans Month, Children's Mental Health Awareness Month, and National Foster Care Month, and unanimously approved the April 25 minutes (4-0 with Nida Allam absent from the early roll call) and the 15-item Consent Agenda (5-0), highlighted by a renewable energy interlocal agreement with DPS. Commissioners also unanimously adopted formal comments on the Draft FY 2023 Annual Transit Work Program (22-0249) deferring new GoTriangle (0.25 FTE) and City of Durham (3 FTE) staffing requests pending an updated governance ILA and cost-share agreement. Following a unanimous closed session for personnel matters, the Board voted 5-0 to approve a $40,800 consulting contract with Aligned Leadership LLC for Board leadership training.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Public Comment on DPS Classified Pay
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the meeting and Clerk Monica Wallace read announcements covering 500 E. Main construction impacts starting June 6, 2022 primary voting, Durham Pre-K enrollment, and the May 23 budget public hearing. Sunny Geraldo, president of the Durham Public Schools Instructional Assistant Association, urged commissioners to fund the Superintendent's requested classified staff pay increases so custodians, bus drivers, and instructional assistants earn a living wage above $15-$16/hour; Howerton clarified commissioners had not received a prior email requesting a meeting. Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns also highlighted the $1.2 million RTP Bio federal earmark at Durham Tech, Way to Go Durham vanpools/microtransit, and a May 13 health event.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (April 25, 2022 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton presented the minutes of the April 25, 2022 Regular Session for Board approval with no edits requested. Commissioner Heidi Carter moved approval and the Clerk called the roll, announcing unanimous approval (Burns, Carter, Jacobs, Howerton voting aye; Nida Allam was not recorded on this initial roll call).

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations (EMS Week, Older Americans, Children's Mental Health, Foster Care)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board issued four May proclamations: National EMS Week (May 15-21, 22-0236) accepted by EMS leaders highlighting behavioral health/crisis integration and retention; Older Americans Month (22-0237) accepted by Durham Center for Senior Life representatives emphasizing senior vaccination, social connection, and caregiver relief; Children's Mental Health Awareness Month (22-0245) read by Wendy Jacobs and accepted by Alliance Health and System of Care staff noting rising youth suicide and crisis demand; and National Foster Care Month (22-0247) read by Nida Allam and accepted by DSS Child Welfare Director Jovetta Whitfield and foster parents.

agenda_items.title: Manager's Recommended FY 2022-23 Budget Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell formally presented her recommended $794 million FY 2022-23 budget ($550 million General Fund, +8.97%), maintaining the current property tax rate while funding 5.5%–7.5% employee raises, +$9.88 million for DPS ($176 million total, $4,333 per pupil), +$789,000 for DTCC ($12.1 million operating), 3 additional school health nurses (toward 32 covering 44 schools), 2 maternal health positions, $625,000 in combined food security initiatives, 36 Sheriff vehicles (20 hybrids), 5 Youth Home counselors, ARPA-funded ADA/APD positions, $150,000 for cultural planning, $3.3 million in economic incentives, a renewable energy project manager, and a Mobile Library/Community Outreach unit. Commissioners commended Sowell's inaugural budget presentation ahead of the May 17 and May 19 work sessions and May 23 public hearing.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (15 Items: 22-0209 through 22-0268)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items pulled from the 15-item Consent Agenda, Commissioner Nida Allam moved approval and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs seconded while highlighting the Durham Public Schools interlocal agreement to join Duke Energy's Green Source Advantage renewable energy program. Passed 5-0 by roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: 22-0249: Draft FY 2023 Annual Transit Work Program Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and Staff Working Group Administrator Aaron Cain presented final recommended BOCC comments on the Draft FY 2023 Durham County Transit Work Program ($3.3 million paratransit facility, $1.8 million Durham Station upgrades, bus-shelter lighting/access). As discussed at the May 4 work session, the comments defer GoTriangle's 0.25 FTE request and the City of Durham's 3 FTE requests pending negotiation of an updated Transit Governance ILA and City-County cost-share policy, call for scope clarity on Fayetteville/Holloway corridor projects, and emphasize prioritizing bus speed, reliability, and BRT building blocks. Moved by Heidi Carter, seconded, and approved 5-0.

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for May 4, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: In a nearly seven-hour May 4, 2022 Work Session, the Board received briefings on North Carolina's national opioid settlement framework from NCACC, reviewed 12 consent agenda items—including expanding the 300 E. Main pre-K facility from 58 to 86 children and addressing staffing shortages forcing out-of-county placements at the Durham Youth Home—and devoted three hours to transit governance, the FY 2023 Transit Work Program, and GoTriangle's post-mortem expense report on the canceled $157 million Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit (DOLRT) project. Commissioners sharply questioned GoTriangle leaders on spending over $131 million on major engineering/management consultants and limited local Durham HUB participation, while strongly backing governance reforms that would give the BOCC formal approval authority over future annual transit budgets and deferring 3.25 requested City/GoTriangle FTEs pending a cost-share agreement. Following review of the City-County Youth Initiatives interlocal agreement and General Manager Claudia Hager's $62 million ARPA spending framework, the Board voted 5-0 to suspend its work-session rules and approved the ARPA spending framework before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Public Comment on Transit Work Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the session and Bike Durham member Eric Landfried urged adoption of the FY 2023 Transit Work Program's Route 9, crosstown, and Durham Station investments while advocating for the City's 3 requested transit FTEs and clearer public project maps.

agenda_items.title: NCACC Opioid Settlement Funds Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: NCACC Executive Director Kevin Leonard and General Counsel Amy Bason presented an overview of North Carolina's opioid litigation settlement Memorandum of Agreement, Option A/B funding flexibilities, expenditure restrictions, and lack of federal expiration deadlines compared to ARPA as Durham prepares strategic behavioral-health investments.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (12 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell walked through 12 upcoming consent items: 22-0229 (DPS Duke Energy Green Source Advantage ILA), 22-0234 (seven DSS hybrid Highlanders), 22-0242/0243/0257 (wastewater enterprise contracts), 22-0254 (300 E. Main pre-K expansion from 58 to 86 seats and $250,000 construction contingency), 22-0258/0259 (Administration Building refurbishment), and 22-0264 ($80,000 for out-of-county Youth Home placements). Youth Home Director Angela Nunn and Commissioner Burns highlighted severe juvenile detention staffing shortages (6 of 14 positions vacant) and 7–12 juveniles placed out of county with serious charges.

agenda_items.title: 22-0246: Transit Plan Governance Study Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and Atkins consultant Adam Howell presented recommendations from two joint Durham-Orange workshops to replace the 2013 transit ILA after DOLRT's cancellation: adding the City of Durham as a voting member of the Staff Working Group alongside County, DCHC MPO, and GoTriangle (plus five non-voting partners), establishing pre-draft county finance/management oversight, updating cost-increase caps for GoDurham and GoTriangle, and giving the BOCC primary approval/denial authority over the annual transit work program before GoTriangle's board votes. GoTriangle raised minority concerns regarding timeline delays under county-first approval and Town of Chapel Hill voting seats in Orange County; commissioners strongly backed county prior approval and better public dollar tracking.

agenda_items.title: 22-0248: Material Changes to 2017 Transit Plan and Draft FY 2023 Transit Work Program
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Aaron Cain and Ellen Beckman reviewed the Draft FY 2023 Transit Work Program and material changes requiring May 23 tripartite approval ($3.3 million paratransit facility, $1.8 million Durham Station repairs). Commissioners endorsed Beckman's recommendation to defer GoTriangle's 0.25 FTE and the City of Durham's 3 FTE requests while demanding a clear City-County cost-sharing policy and project-level financial accountability on Fayetteville/Holloway bus corridors.

agenda_items.title: GoTriangle Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit (DOLRT) Expense Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle CEO Charles Lattuca, CFO Saundra Freeman, and Chief Development Officer Katharine Eggleston broke down the $157 million spent on the canceled DOLRT project (80%/20% Durham-Orange average split): $131 million for management and design led by four national prime consultants (URS/AECOM $26.7M, HDR, HNTB, and Gannett Fleming/WSP $3.2M), $16 million administration/staff, $6 million real estate, and $3.8 million professional/operations costs. GoTriangle highlighted 8.8%–18.5% DBE subcontracting rates; Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the narrative, noting few firms were Durham County HUBs and pressing GoTriangle on $86M+ spent with major outside consultants before cancellation.

agenda_items.title: 22-0260: Renewal of ILA for Durham City-County Strategic Youth Initiatives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented updates to the Office on Youth Interlocal Agreement expanding Changed By Youth Ambassadors from 10 to 15 and launching round two of the Durham Youth Leadership Fund. Chair Howerton asked that future ILA amendments require consultation with both boards on staff/budget changes; Burns urged linking youth efforts to Carolina Across 100 and YouthWorks (1,500 applicants); and Jacobs noted an unfilled youth seat on the Racial Equity Commission.

agenda_items.title: ARPA Spending Framework Update, Rules Suspension, and Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GM Claudia Hager presented the refined $62 million ARPA spending framework aligned with Treasury's December 31, 2024 obligation and 2026 expenditure deadlines, covering Pre-K/learning enrichment ($8 million), workforce/BULLS, behavioral health, safe community/justice ($3 million), broadband RFP coordination with state GREAT grants, and an uncommitted placeholder. Following Q&A on RFP bundling and alignment with $13 million in strategic reserves, the Board voted 5-0 to suspend work-session rules and approved the ARPA spending framework before adjourning 5-0.

disagreements.issue: Transit Plan Governance Prior-Approval Authority and FY23 City/GoTriangle FTE Deferrals
disagreements.summary: GoTriangle registered minority opposition in joint workshops to giving BOCC prior approval/veto power over the annual transit budget, while Durham commissioners strongly backed increased oversight and supported deferring 3.25 requested City/GoTriangle FTEs.
disagreements.side_a_position: Grant the BOCC primary approval authority over the annual transit work program prior to GoTriangle board action, and defer City (3 FTE) and GoTriangle (0.25 FTE) requests until a formal ILA and cost-share agreement are adopted.
side_a_arguments: County staff (Ellen Beckman) and Commissioners Burns, Carter, and Howerton argued BOCC currently has zero formal budget vote despite levying the transit tax and faces unclear City/County/GoTriangle project responsibilities.
Staff noted deferring the 3.25 FTEs ensures clearer scope accountability on corridor projects (Fayetteville/Holloway) and establishes whether Durham or transit funds pay City staffing.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain GoTriangle/transit-operator-led timeline sequencing and approve requested City/GoTriangle staffing immediately.
side_b_arguments: GoTriangle expressed minority concern that sequential BOCC approval before GoTriangle board adoption could compress fiscal-year deadlines.
Public commenter Eric Landfried urged approving the City's 3 FTEs now to speed bus and station delivery.
disagreements.resolution: Commissioners endorsed staff's governance recommendations for ILA drafting and scheduled formal FY23 Work Program comments for adoption on May 9.

disagreements.issue: GoTriangle DOLRT $157M Consultant Expenditures and Local Durham HUB Inclusion
disagreements.summary: Commissioners pressed GoTriangle over $131 million spent on national prime consultants and sparse Durham-based HUB participation prior to DOLRT's 2019 cancellation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Criticize disproportionate consulting spending with large national engineering firms and inadequate participation by local Durham-based HUB businesses.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged GoTriangle's DBE summary, noting that the bulk of prime contracts went to national corporations and DBE subs were concentrated in Wake County or out-of-state rather than Durham's 347 registered HUBs.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton pressed GoTriangle on accountability and financial transparency to restore public trust.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defend federal FTA procurement compliance, DBE target attainment (8.8%–18.5%), and necessary 30%-to-final engineering work required before any federal grant award.
side_b_arguments: GoTriangle CFO Saundra Freeman and CDO Katharine Eggleston stated FTA rules prohibit federal reimbursement until a Full Funding Grant Agreement and mandate DBE (not local HUB) caps, while 2019 cancellation halted final subcontracting payouts.
disagreements.resolution: GoTriangle pledged continued detailed expense transparency and coordination on land-banked property disposition and future transit governance.

Siler (22-0244) upon his retirement effective April 30 after nearly 35 years of service to Durham County, including becoming Durham's first Black County Attorney in 2009. meetings.title: Durham Delegates Meeting with County Commissioners and Staff
meetings.executive_summary: In a virtual intergovernmental coordination meeting with Durham's General Assembly delegation (Sen. Mike Woodard, Sen. Natalie Murdock, Rep. Marcia Morey, Rep. Vernetta Alston, and Rep. Zack Hawkins), County Commissioners and senior staff reviewed state legislative prospects ahead of the May 18 short session and Durham County's 2022-23 legislative priorities. Delegation members briefed the Board on Medicaid expansion discussions, expungement bill corrections, Leandro and public education budget disputes, 988 behavioral-health crisis implementation, juvenile justice, and Durham Youth Home capital funding. Commissioners and General Manager Deborah Craig-Ray sought delegation support for expanding county Low-Income Homeowner Tax Relief (proposing a tenure reduction from 10 to 5 years and statewide circuit-breaker updates), Sedimentation Pollution Control enforcement, farmers market funding, capital bond vs. SCIF school grants ahead of November's >$500 million DPS and >$100 million DTCC bond plans, and emergency management remote-meeting authority (G.S. 166A-19.24). Sharp friction surfaced over stalled DPS educator affordable housing legislation (SB 203/HB 231), prompting staff to task County Attorney Willie Darby with confirming existing statutory conveyance authority, while legislators cautioned against reopening emergency-powers statutes during the short session. No formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: General Assembly Short Session Preview and Legislative Updates
agenda_items.discussion_summary: State lawmakers (Sen. Mike Woodard, Sen. Natalie Murdock, Rep. Marcia Morey, Rep. Vernetta Alston, and Rep. Zack Hawkins) outlined May 18 short-session dynamics alongside newly redrawn legislative maps, noting committee work on Medicaid expansion, expungement fixes, Leandro school funding, teacher pay, 988 crisis system rollout, CJRC/diversion grants, and Durham Youth Home funding.

agenda_items.title: County Legislative Priorities: Homeowner Tax Relief, Erosion Control, and Youth Home
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Deborah Craig-Ray, Budget Director Keith Lane, and Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Nimasheena Burns reviewed Durham County's priorities including SB 285 sedimentation enforcement, Youth Home construction funding, local farmers market grants, and property tax relief. Commissioners noted the county raised its Low-Income Homeowner Grant income cap from 30% to 80% AMI and DSS recommended trimming the residency threshold from 10 years to 5 years while seeking broader statewide circuit-breaker/senior/veteran relief in 2023.

agenda_items.title: DPS Educator Affordable Housing (SB 203/HB 231) and Nov. 2022 Capital Bonds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Participants debated stalled local bills for DPS teacher/staff affordable housing; legislative counsel and Sen. Woodard noted counties may already convey surplus property with affordability restrictions without new legislation, prompting the Board to direct Interim County Attorney Willie Darby to coordinate a UNC School of Government/DPS legal review. Staff and legislators also discussed state school SCIF vs. bond funding as Durham prepares >$500 million in DPS and >$100 million in DTCC bond proposals for November 2022, plus court IT and Assistant DA/PD funding shortages.

agenda_items.title: Emergency Management Statutory Amendments (G.S. 166A-19.24 & 19.31) and Closing Topics
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey requested legislation explicitly permitting remote open meetings during locally declared emergencies and clarifying civil/equitable ordinance enforcement, which legislators warned could trigger partisan backlash during a short session. Additional closing discussions addressed delaying state specialized foster-care transformation plans, hiring a dedicated Raleigh county lobbyist (urged by Sen. Woodard), plastic bag fee authority, clean transit/rail grants, Black maternal health, and protecting Durham's non-discrimination ordinance.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Delegates Meeting with County Commissioners and Staff
disagreements.issue: DPS Educator Affordable Housing Authority (SB 203/HB 231) and Inter-Board Advocacy
disagreements.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns clashed with characterizations of BOCC inaction on teacher affordable housing, while state lawmakers maintained the sole hurdle was Senate leadership despite existing statutory conveyance options.
disagreements.side_a_position: Reject claims that BOCC is blocking DPS affordable housing, question lack of active DPS lobbying in Raleigh, and pursue immediate legal verification of existing statutory authority.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns objected to Durham County commissioners being used as a 'political punching bag' and stated she was told the School Board had not consistently lobbied legislative leadership on the bill over the prior year.
Commissioner Heidi Carter and Chair Brenda A. Howerton welcomed clarification of existing county conveyance powers so project work could proceed without waiting on Raleigh.
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain that all local boards advocated and attribute the legislative stall solely to Senate leadership refusing local bills for teacher housing.
side_b_arguments: Sen. Mike Woodard pushed back, stating Durham County, DPS, and City officials all advocated for SB 203/HB 231 and that the Senate President Pro Tem's office simply blocked local bills while county staff already hold general-law authority to partner on restricted-use land.
disagreements.resolution: Interim County Attorney Willie Darby was directed to consult the UNC School of Government and DPS counsel to confirm whether existing statute enables restricted-use conveyance without special legislation.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Delegates Meeting with County Commissioners and Staff
disagreements.issue: Strategic Risk of Advancing Emergency Powers Amendments (G.S. 166A-19.24/19.31) in 2022 Short Session
disagreements.summary: County legal staff requested statutory fixes for remote emergency meetings and civil enforcement, whereas Durham lawmakers cautioned against opening Chapter 166A in a polarized General Assembly.
disagreements.side_a_position: Seek legislative clarity during the 2022 short session allowing local governing boards to meet remotely during local declarations of emergency and use civil/equitable remedies.
side_a_arguments: Senior Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey argued current statutes ambiguously limit remote meeting flexibility to gubernatorial emergency declarations rather than local crises like cyberattacks or local disasters.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer or avoid opening Chapter 166A emergency-powers bills during the May 2022 short session to prevent counter-amendments.
side_b_arguments: Rep. Vernetta Alston and Sen. Mike Woodard warned that pandemic-era hostility toward emergency powers among legislative majorities could lead to restrictive counter-measures rather than helpful local clarifications.
disagreements.resolution: Staff and delegation agreed to coordinate through NCACC and legislative counsel on whether to defer the proposals to the 2023 long session.

meetings.title: BOCC - April 11th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: The centerpiece of the April 11, 2022 Regular Session was Chair Brenda A. Howerton's annual State of the County Address, celebrating North Carolina's first all-women Board of Commissioners and the hiring of first female County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell while highlighting pandemic resilience, $62 million in ARPA allocations, $166 million+ in DPS funding, $5.62 million in Pre-K, the Long-Term Homeowner Grant program, the Racial Equity Commission, and major corporate expansions (Google Cloud, Eli Lilly, Beam Therapeutics, Smart Wires). agenda_items.title: Call to Order and 2022 State of the County Address
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order and Heidi Carter led the Pledge of Allegiance before Howerton delivered the 2022 State of the County Address. She recognized county employees for weathering both the 2020 cyberattack and COVID-19, welcomed new County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell, cited $62 million in ARPA funds, the $736 million FY 2022 budget ($166 million+ DPS, $5.62 million Pre-K, $942,000 Long-Term Homeowner Grant), creation of the Racial Equity Commission and Safety and Wellness Task Force, the LGBTQIA+ Non-Discrimination Ordinance, broadband outreach, the Transit Governance Study, and a revived Crime Cabinet.

agenda_items.title: Announcements and March 28, 2022 Minutes Approval

Heidi Carter moved and Nida Allam seconded approval of the March 28, 2022 Regular Session minutes, passing 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations: Fair Housing, Child Abuse Prevention, Durham Reentry Week
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The Board adopted three proclamations: Fair Housing Month (22-0203, read by Wendy Jacobs, highlighting appraisal bias and corporate iBuyers acquiring ~30% of starter homes); Child Abuse Prevention Month (highlighting 3,067 DSS reports, rising youth mental-health crises, and permanent first-responder classification for CPS investigators); and Durham Reentry Week (22-0220, April 25–29, read by Nimasheena Burns and received by CJRC Assistant Director Roshanna Parker and Religious Coalition for a Nonviolent Durham's Ben Haas).

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (15 Items: 22-0156 through 22-0207)

meetings.title: BOCC Work Session for April 4, 2022
meetings.executive_summary: During its April 4, 2022 Work Session—opened with a moment of silence on the 54th anniversary of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s assassination and written public comment urging investments in Black boys via My Brother's Keeper—the Board reviewed 13 consent agenda items, highlighting $262,706 in state school-health funding, $1.94 million for seven replacement ambulances, Bull City Community Schools outcome accountability, and a $1.58 million Stanford L. Warren Library waterproofing renovation. Mental health specialists from Duke, UNC, and Alliance Health briefed commissioners on a 57% surge in youth suicide and emergency crisis pressures, followed by a pointed Black Maternal Health discussion in which community-based organizations (MAAME, HEARTS, and Equity Before Birth) and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns pressed for binding financial commitments rather than repeated meetings. In the afternoon, staff and partners unveiled a revised FY 2022-31 Capital Improvement Plan cutting the projected FY 2023-24 bond tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents alongside bond requests from the Museum of Life and Science ($14 million), DTCC ($112.7 million), and DPS ($423.5 million), while TJCOG presented Greater Triangle Commuter Rail land-use and equity findings ahead of commissioners' closing pushback against public School Board criticism over teacher pay and housing. Only a routine adjournment vote occurred.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, MLK Remembrance, and Consent Agenda Review (13 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following a moment of silence for Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and a public comment from the Charles Hamilton Houston Foundation advocating support for Black boys, County Manager Dr. Kimberly Sowell reviewed 13 consent items: $262,706 for school nurses/mental health (22-0156), ABC drug-court grant (22-0169), two portable ambulance sanitizing systems (22-0185), $1.58 million Stanford L. Warren Library envelope/interior repairs (22-0189), utility/pump-station amendments (22-0194 through 22-0198), $1.94 million for seven ambulances pending Stealth Power retrofits (22-0202), Bull City Community Schools FY 2021-22 contract (22-0204), and a Library grant (22-0205). Commissioners requested fund-balance impact summaries on future agenda forms, a pump-station inventory, ambulance replacement schedules, and outcome metrics for Bull City Community Schools.

agenda_items.title: Community Mental Health Crisis and Youth Behavioral Health Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Joanne Pierce convened Dr. Ernestine Briggs-King (Duke Center for Child & Family Health), Tara Bohley (UNC School of Social Work), and Ann Oshel (Alliance Health) to brief the Board on trauma, adverse childhood experiences, a 57% youth suicide surge disproportionately hitting young Black children, emergency department boarding pressures, and Alliance Health's December Medicaid Tailored Plan rollout.

agenda_items.title: Black Maternal Health Equity Briefing and Community Organizations Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins, Nursing Director Hattie Wood, Deputy Director Liz Stevens, and Duke maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Maria Small reported that Black mothers face 3-4x higher mortality risk and requested a full-time lactation educator, doula expansion (including the detention center), home blood-pressure cuffs, and an ultrasonographer. Triangle Black Maternal Wellness Collaborative leaders Joy Lampkin Foster, Joy Spencer (Equity Before Birth), Maya Jackson (MAAME Inc.), and Tamika Brown (HEARTS) urged formal county funding and decision-making inclusion rather than siloed partnerships, sparking tension over the pace of county action.

agenda_items.title: 22-0217: FY 2022-31 Capital Improvement Plan Update and 2022 Bond Partners
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GM Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane outlined re-sequenced CIP schedules reducing estimated FY 2023-24 GO bond property-tax impact from 3.5 cents to 2.5 cents. Bond partner presentations followed from the North Carolina Museum of Life and Science ($14 million request), Durham Tech ($112.7 million for Life Sciences, Allied Health, and Bacon/Cooper land), and DPS Chief of Operations Frederick Davis II ($423.5 million GO bond within >$500 million total capital funding for Elementary F, six school expansions, and Durham School of the Arts replacement). Commissioners Burns and Jacobs praised Davis's MWBE outreach and joint public-land inventory efforts while Burns questioned an unvetted $40 million external 'green energy bond' email campaign.

agenda_items.title: 22-0206: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Opportunity Analysis and Closing Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: TJCOG Metro Planning Director John Hodges-Koppel and GoTriangle senior planner Jay Heikes presented corridor land-use, affordable housing, and travel-market analyses showing the rail corridor houses 30% of regional jobs (8 of the top 10 job hubs), 96,000 daily Wake-Durham commuters, 2,700 existing affordable units, and 70,000 residents in BIPOC/low-income/zero-car 'REINVEST' neighborhoods—stressing the necessity of first-mile/last-mile connectors. In closing comments, Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns pushed back sharply against public School Board criticism alleging BOCC stalled teacher affordable housing and $5,000 pay raises, Burns requested a Coach Krzyzewski proclamation, and Jacobs recapped an 80-leader South Florida transit tour before adjourning.

disagreements.issue: Action Timeline vs. Budget Process for Black Maternal Health Community Commitments
disagreements.summary: Black maternal health CBO leaders and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns demanded concrete funding commitments after nearly a year of meetings without action, while Chair Brenda A. Howerton and other commissioners insisted requests proceed through staff vetting and the FY 2022-23 budget cycle.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move beyond repeated presentations to immediate, written financial and programmatic commitments from the county.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted commissioners heard similar recommendations on June 3, 2021 and already identified $1 million in mental-health funds, arguing 'we are not going to keep meeting about babies' while infants and mothers die.
Joy Spencer (Equity Before Birth) stated organizations had met tirelessly with zero formal written 'yes' or operational commitments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Channel specific CBO budget requests through GM Joanne Pierce and County Manager Sowell for formal consideration during upcoming FY 2022-23 budget adoption rather than making work-session commitments.
side_b_arguments: Chair Brenda A. Howerton stated work sessions are informational only and directed CBOs to present concise, prioritized asks to GM Pierce so the Board understands exact dollar needs and funding offsets.
Commissioners Heidi Carter and Wendy Jacobs affirmed strong support for both Public Health's specific FY23 requests and breaking down departmental silos during the impending budget markup.
disagreements.resolution: Chair Howerton secured agreement from presenters to meet immediately with GM Joanne Pierce to formulate concrete budget-ready proposals.

disagreements.issue: Greater Triangle Commuter Rail Equity Priorities vs. Local Bus and Affordability Needs
disagreements.summary: Commissioners debated whether investing heavily in regional commuter rail serves low-income Durham bus riders equitably or risks leaving everyday local transit needs behind.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question the equity rationale of prioritizing regional commuter rail when low-income workers (~23% earning under $40,000 in the corridor) depend on buses and BRT has yet to be built first.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted of 9,000 new downtown families cited by business leaders fewer than 1,000 are low-income and doubted poor Durham residents could afford or access rail stops before BRT and basic bus routes are delivered.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton questioned ongoing local maintenance liabilities and whether commuter rail would crowd out buses if federal dollars fall short.
disagreements.side_b_position: Pursue commuter rail alongside bus/first-mile networks as a long-term regional economic mobility spine tying Durham residents to RTP and Wake County job centers.
side_b_arguments: TJCOG's John Hodges-Koppel pointed to 70,000 BIPOC/low-income/zero-car residents near the rail spine and cited South Florida's Tri-Rail usage by service workers as evidence buses alone cannot match rail travel times through highway congestion.

Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized public-private partnerships, 37% of Durham's legally binding affordable housing lying near the corridor, and 120,000 daily inbound commuters requiring integrated regional planning.
disagreements.resolution: GoTriangle and TJCOG committed to publishing station-level maps overlaying existing/proposed bus routes, bike racks, and park-and-ride plans for ongoing Board evaluation.

disagreements.issue: School Board Public Criticism of BOCC Over Teacher Pay ($5,000 Raises) and Affordable Housing
disagreements.summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Brenda A. Howerton rebuked public statements by School Board members blaming the BOCC for blocking teacher affordable housing and $5,000 pay raises without ever contacting commissioners.
disagreements.side_a_position: Demand direct inter-board communication and condemn public misrepresentations blaming the five women commissioners for stalling housing and teacher supplements.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted she received zero direct outreach prior to weekend remarks claiming School Board members had lobbied all five commissioners on affordable housing and teacher raises.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton stated BOCC has not refused teacher housing or youth support and called for the boards to communicate directly rather than assign blame publicly.
disagreements.side_b_position: Note earlier multi-year history underlying the School Board's perspective while continuing legal review of surplus property conveyance.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs noted the School Board chair referenced earlier historical conversations predating newer members while Interim Attorney Willie Darby awaited a legal mechanism from DPS counsel.
disagreements.resolution: No formal action; commissioners requested that elected peers cease public finger-pointing and engage the Board directly alongside legal staff.

meetings.title: BOCC - March 28th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Convening in person in the Commissioners' Chambers for the first time following pandemic remote sessions, the Board of County Commissioners opened its March 28, 2022 Regular Session with announcements celebrating Congressman David Price's federal earmarks ($250,000 for Bull City United and $8 million for the Harriet Tubman Recreation Center) and unanimously approved the March 7 and March 14 minutes (5-0). meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners convened its March 7, 2022 virtual Work Session with all five commissioners, Interim County Manager Claudia Hager, and Acting County Attorney Willie Darby present, confirming no citizen comments and no closed session. Interim Manager Hager reviewed the 14-item draft consent agenda—including an audiovisual upgrade contract for the Criminal Justice Resource Building ($72,695), a policy for Board involvement in approving ABC System general manager salaries, a $930,000 IS&T hardware/software contract amendment with Davenport Group, the $520,000 Paris Soleil public art screen wall amendment for the 318 E. meetings.title: BOCC - February 28th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the February 28, 2022 regular session with all five commissioners participating. The board read a joint resolution standing in solidarity with the people of Ukraine, unanimously approved prior meeting minutes and 11 consent agenda items, and voted 5-0 on pulled consent item 22-0103 to commit up to $3.8 million in additional debt service fund balance (bringing total county loan support to $9.765 million) plus a 15-year childcare leaseback to close a $7.1 million construction gap on the 300 East Main Street affordable housing project. Public Health Director Rod Jenkins presented declining COVID-19 metrics and recommended lifting the county indoor mask mandate effective 12:01 a.m. on March 7, 2022, and external auditors Cherry Bekaert presented an unmodified FY 2021 ACFR and Single Audit. Following boards and commissions appointments and a closed session, the board voted unanimously (5-0) to authorize Chair Howerton to sign an employment contract with incoming Durham County Manager Kimberly Sowell.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, Employee Recognition, and Resolution in Solidarity with Ukraine
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the meeting with the public charge, Commissioner Heidi Carter led the Pledge of Allegiance, and Clerk Monica Wallace read community announcements covering COVID-19 vaccination clinics, 4-H programs, Durham Creek Week, MWBE training, and board vacancies. Chair Howerton recognized General Services supervisor Charlita Felder and staff members Omar, Cedric Graham, and Julio Samillo for assisting stranded motorists on I-85 based on a constituent thank-you letter. Commissioners then jointly read a resolution drafted by Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs expressing solidarity with Ukraine and noted that the local ABC Board had already removed Russian liquor products from county ABC stores.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (February 7, 2022 Work Session and February 14, 2022 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs moved approval of the minutes while flagging information requests on page 18 related to the upcoming Monday transit plan work session so staff could provide answers ahead of the meeting. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded the motion, and the board approved both sets of minutes unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (11 of 12 Items, Excluding Item 22-0103)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton asked whether commissioners wished to pull any of the 12 consent agenda items, and Vice Chair Jacobs requested pulling item 22-0103 for public presentation by staff. The remaining 11 consent items were approved unanimously by roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0103: Additional Funding ($3.8M) and Master Development Agreement Amendment for 300 East Main Street
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County staff and Laurel Street developers Ron Stewart and Noel Henderson-James explained that lumber and supply-chain cost escalations created a $7.1 million construction funding gap on the 110-unit 300 East Main Street affordable housing project and attached childcare shell space. To close the gap, the county eliminated roughly $973,000 in developer cost reimbursements, formalized a 15-year county childcare lease ($169,500 annually with 2% escalations, valued at $2.4 million), and appropriated up to $3.8 million from the debt service fund balance, raising total county loan support from $5,965,000 to up to $9,765,000 with any value-engineering savings returned to the county. Commissioners praised the creative partnership and unanimously approved the amendment.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0130: Public Health COVID-19 Crisis Update and Lifting of Indoor Mask Mandate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported a 56.67% week-over-week decline in COVID-19 cases, a 5% test positivity rate projected to reach 4.5%, falling hospitalizations, and nearly 75% eligible vaccination coverage in Durham County. Based on new CDC community-level guidance centered on a 200-cases-per-100,000 threshold and hospital admissions, Director Jenkins announced his recommendation—coordinated with Chair Howerton and Mayor Elaine O'Neal—to lift the county indoor mask mandate at 12:01 a.m. on March 7, 2022 while continuing booster outreach and maintaining federal healthcare and transit masking rules. Commissioners asked clarifying questions regarding trigger metrics, booster campaigns, school board authority, and data dashboard updates.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0099: Presentation of FY 2021 Annual Financial Audit, ACFR, and Single Audit Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Cherry Bekaert managing partner Scott Duda and Chief Financial Officer Susan Tezai presented the FY 2021 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) and Single Audit, reporting unmodified opinions across financial statements, internal controls, and compliance with no material weaknesses or audit misstatements. Auditors noted two non-material grant compliance timing findings in medical assistance file reviews and epidemiology reporting attributed to COVID-19 delays, as well as a late submission indicator requiring a written board response to the Local Government Commission, which accepted the audit on February 1, 2022. Commissioners commended finance and county staff, and Clerk Wallace confirmed no formal vote was required to receive the report.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting County Attorney Willie Darby announced the results of four board appointment ballots cast by commissioners. Appointments were filled for the Alliance Board of Directors (1 seat), Durham Racial Equity Commission (8 seats across at-large, community-rooted organization, and youth categories), GoTriangle Transit Advisory Committee (1 seat), and the Juvenile Crime Prevention Council (1 seat).

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Attorney-Client Privilege, Contract Negotiations, and Personnel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton read three statutory justifications for entering closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation, (a)(5) for property acquisition or employment contract negotiation terms, and (a)(6) for individual public officer or employee qualifications and initial employment. The board voted 5-0 to adjourn into closed session.

agenda_items.title: Authorization of Employment Contract for Incoming County Manager Kimberly Sowell
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Upon reconvening open session at 03:30:38 with all five commissioners and Acting County Attorney Darby present, Chair Howerton announced that the board had directed staff to offer an employment contract to Kimberly Sowell as incoming Durham County Manager. Commissioners moved, seconded, and voted unanimously (5-0) to authorize the chair to sign the employment contract on the board's behalf before voting to adjourn.

meetings.title: BOCC - Annual Budget Retreat
meetings.executive_summary: The Board of County Commissioners held its full-day virtual FY 2022-23 Annual Budget Retreat with all five commissioners and Interim County Manager Claudia Hager, facilitated by Peter Inland. Staff framed policy and fiscal briefings around financial highlights, tax-base valuation projections presented by Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson, FY 2022-23 budget outlook trends, fund balance policy, the Low-Income Homeowners relief program, stormwater fees protecting Jordan Lake, and the Sequential Intercept Map with UNC School of Social Work leadership. In the afternoon wrap-up, Hager and commissioners synthesized top budget priorities—including March CIP deliberations, rural broadband via ARPA, phased mental health study investments, and multi-year ARPA step-down financing for Pre-K expansion ahead of rating-agency reviews for the planned bond referendum—without taking formal votes.

agenda_items.title: Retreat Opening, Governance Framework, and Policy Agenda Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Manager Claudia Hager welcomed all five commissioners and introduced facilitator Peter Inland, outlining the retreat schedule covering fiduciary, strategic, and generative governance. Planned sessions included financial highlights, tax valuation, FY 2022-23 budget trends, fund balance policy, the Low-Income Homeowners program, demographic trends, stormwater fees for Jordan Lake and stream protection, the Sequential Intercept Map, and commissioner priority-setting.

agenda_items.title: Annual Tax Base Projection Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson reviewed FY 2022-23 property tax base projections and explained why year-end collections typically vary by one to two percent from early estimates. He noted that while real property valuations are stable, state-assessed utility values do not arrive from the Department of Revenue until September and motor vehicle values must be projected ahead of next spring's renewals.

agenda_items.title: Afternoon Budget Prioritization Wrap-Up and Multi-Year ARPA Strategy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager synthesized the Board's priority list for the recommended FY 2022-23 budget, pointing to the March CIP presentation, rural broadband funding via ARPA, initial study funding for complex mental health investments, and a multi-year ARPA step-down model for recurring priorities such as Pre-K expansion (stepping down from $1 million to $500,000 while transitioning to county and private funding). Hager emphasized maintaining credit rating readiness for the upcoming bond referendum when evaluating recurring ARPA commitments, and thanked the budget team ahead of May departmental hearings.

meetings.title: Joint Board of County Commissioners and Board of Education Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs co-presided alongside Durham Public Schools (DPS) Board of Education Vice Chair Jovonia Lewis for the first joint BOCC–Board of Education meeting of 2022, with Commissioners Heidi Carter and Nida Allam attending while Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns were away at a conference. Both boards unanimously approved the November 16, 2021 joint meeting minutes before Interim County Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane presented the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) and roadmap toward a November 2022 General Obligation (GO) bond referendum covering DPS's $864 million 10-year facility request alongside Durham Tech, the Museum of Life and Science, and renewable energy. In the closing budget segment, Lane outlined the FY 2022-23 adoption calendar (Manager recommendation May 9, work sessions May 17–June 8, adoption June 13), BOE Vice Chair Lewis inquired about using $2.034 million in remaining ARPA ELC school-health funds, and commissioners and Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga emphasized shared workforce retention challenges and future collaboration on Durham Pre-K.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Approval of November 16, 2021 Joint Meeting Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Clerk Monica Wallace called roll for both boards at 9:01 AM, noting BOCC members Wendy Jacobs, Heidi Carter, and Nida Allam were present (Howerton and Burns at a conference) alongside BOE members Lewis, Ravin, Beyer, Sears, and Valladares. Commissioner Heidi Carter moved and BOE member Natalie Beyer seconded approval of the November 16, 2021 joint minutes, which passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: 10-Year CIP and November 2022 General Obligation Bond Referendum Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane presented plans for a November 2022 GO bond referendum addressing capital needs for DPS, Durham Technical Community College, the Museum of Life and Science, and renewable energy. Lane highlighted DPS's $864 million 10-year request driven by scope changes, Pre-K, class-size legislation, and inflation, and outlined key milestones: March CIP adoption, April market testing with voters, and a June 14 preliminary GO bond resolution.

agenda_items.title: FY 2022-23 Budget Calendar, ARPA School Health Funds, and Workforce Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the FY 2022-23 budget schedule leading to a May 9 Manager recommendation and June 13 adoption, while BOE Vice Chair Lewis requested follow-up on whether DPS could access remaining ARPA ELC school health testing ($2 million) and reopening liaison ($34,000) funds. Commissioner Heidi Carter underscored balancing school investments with community safety and transit tax/rail priorities, Superintendent Dr. Pascal Mubenga thanked BOCC for its support, and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs praised staff vacancy/SWOT analyses and requested prioritizing Durham Pre-K at the next joint meeting before closing at 10:54 AM.

votes.notes: Chair Brenda A. Howerton and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns were absent at a conference (3-0 BOCC aye). Seconded by DPS BOE member Natalie Beyer; BOE members Frederick Ravin, Natalie Beyer, and Matt Sears also voted aye and Vice Chair Jacobs declared the minutes unanimously approved.

meetings.title: BOCC - February 7, 2022 - Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the February 7, 2022 work session with all five commissioners present. Following citizen comments opposing youth detention expansion, Chair Howerton and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs defended the 36-bed replacement youth home as a court-required obligation under Raise the Age and a 2019 legal settlement while requesting a community engagement plan around the facility's assessment center. Commissioners reviewed upcoming consent agenda items—including $1.1 million for five ambulances with anti-idling technology, the $12.21 million sale of the South Parking Deck at American Tobacco Campus, and Memorial Stadium scoreboard upgrades—and scrutinized GoTriangle's FY 2021 Transit Progress Report, demanding disaggregated light-rail consultant expense data. The board also voiced reservations over a proposed assessment- and foreclosure-backed Orphan Road Policy, discussed the $65 million 2050 Renewable Energy Plan ahead of a February 14 adoption vote, and voted unanimously (5-0) to enter closed session for personnel matters.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comments on Youth Home / Juvenile Detention
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the work session in red attire for Cancer Prevention Month and read the public charge, after which Clerk Monica Wallace announced that 78 emailed comments were received and asked future commenters to include a Durham County mailing address. Clerk Wallace read a comment from resident Brittany Thomas urging investments in youth mental health, social workers, and family supports rather than detention. Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Chair Howerton pushed back against what they called misleading advocacy claims—including an email from Carolina Jews for Justice comparing the youth home to a Nazi concentration camp—clarifying that courts determine detention placements, the facility has 36 beds rather than 60, delaying the bid would cost at least $4 million, and Raise the Age plus a 2019 legal settlement require county accommodations, while requesting a staff engagement plan for the assessment center.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Review (Ambulances, Chiller, Stadium Scoreboard, Matching Grants, and South Parking Deck Sale)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Manager Claudia Hager and department heads walked commissioners through upcoming consent items, including $99,000 for Sheriff's Office replacement tasers, Justice Center conference room AV upgrades (item 22-0489), an emergency detention center chiller replacement, a Memorial Stadium video scoreboard and sound system (item 22-0051), $1.1 million for five Ford F-550 ambulances equipped with Stealth Power anti-idling systems, $71,990 in refugee health screening funds, solar design additions at the Sheriff's Training Facility, $100,000 in Matching Grants across six community projects (item 22-0067), $254,617 for Leesville Road Firehouse modifications for the Tooth Fairy mobile dental clinic (item 22-0070), and the BPAC annual report (item 22-0071). Staff also detailed item 22-0073, the $12,210,000 private sale of the South Parking Deck at American Tobacco Campus under G.S. 160A-267, noting the county had earned roughly $7.9 million in prior lease revenue on an asset with a $9.8 million net depreciated value.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0072: Durham County Transit Progress Report (FY 2021 Tax District Annual Report)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and GoTriangle's Jennifer Hayden presented the FY 2021 Durham County Transit Tax District report, detailing $41.5 million in revenues (including $34 million in half-cent sales tax), $15.9 million in expenditures across bus stop improvements, electric buses, and operations, and $25.6 million added to the Durham Transit Tax Fund. Commissioners Burns, Jacobs, Carter, and Chair Howerton demanded disaggregated consultant expense figures from the Durham-Orange Light Rail closeout report ($86 million and $12 million categories), multi-year revenue trends, city-versus-county project splits, and a governance policy for GoTriangle-owned parcels such as the Farrington Road site.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Orphan Road Policy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and General Services Director Jay Gibson presented a draft Orphan Road Policy covering an estimated 59 unaccepted non-HOA subdivision roads (up to 8.6 miles), under which 75% of property owners along 75% of frontage could petition the county to manage repairs financed 100% by property assessments over up to 10 years, enforceable by tax foreclosure. Vice Chair Jacobs noted that county staff management and collection still impose costs on all taxpayers and questioned how the 25% of non-consenting homeowners and future UDO protections would be handled. Chair Howerton expressed discomfort with tax foreclosure provisions and stated she was not ready to vote on the proposal, while Commissioner Nida Allam asked for a concrete per-household cost example from an existing road.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0060: Renewable Energy Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Sustainability Manager Tobin Fried presented the Renewable Energy Plan ahead of a planned February 14 adoption vote, outlining efficiency upgrades, Duke Energy's Green Source Advantage program (~70% of county electricity by late 2024), on-site solar and geothermal, and fleet electrification at an estimated net cost of $65 million through 2050 ($2.5 million to $4.12 million annually through 2030). Chair Howerton pressed staff to replace broad references to equity with clear, measurable accountability metrics; Commissioners Carter and Jacobs endorsed the accelerated path toward 2030 and 2050 targets and advocated joint lobbying of Duke Energy and the Utilities Commission; and Commissioner Burns urged tracking return on investment and partnering with local clean-grid firms. Chair Howerton and Interim Manager Hager also discussed opportunities for public feedback prior to the February 14 vote and during the upcoming CIP process.

agenda_items.title: Commissioners' Directives and Commissioner Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Drew Cummings presented the 2022 Commissioners' Directives tracking sheet without board questions. During Commissioner Comments, Commissioner Burns urged applying for state $350 million rural broadband grants and a $20 million EDA Good Jobs Challenge grant while highlighting library Black History Month events; Commissioner Carter praised the local urban heat island mapping study; Vice Chair Jacobs noted federal EV grant opportunities and commended staff for locking in pricing; and Chair Howerton and Commissioner Burns previewed the upcoming NACo Legislative Conference.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (Personnel / G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6))
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted unanimously (5-0) on a motion by Commissioner Nimasheena Burns seconded by Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs to enter closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) regarding personnel matters. Upon returning to open session at 05:38:30, Chair Howerton reported that direction was given to staff with no action needed, and the board voted 5-0 to adjourn.

meetings.title: BOCC - January 24th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: In its January 24, 2022 virtual Regular Session, the Board of County Commissioners heard announcements covering USPS free at-home COVID-19 tests, Low-Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) extensions, Durham Pre-K, DCHC MPO transit plan comments removing the Durham-Orange Light Rail in favor of bus improvements, and small-business relief grants amid the Omicron wave, alongside a Cervical Cancer Awareness Month message. Later in the session, Interim County Manager Claudia Hager briefed the Board on managing Durham County's $60 million ARPA allocation strategically—prioritizing rural broadband, water/sewer infrastructure, and one-time uses to avoid a $65 million recurring fiscal cliff in 2026. Acting County Attorney Willie Darby announced board and commission appointments to the Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, Board of Adjustment, Board of Health, and Women's Commission, after which the Board voted into closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(6) and returned to report direction given to staff before adjourning 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, Small-Business COVID Outreach, and Cervical Cancer Awareness
