meetings.title: BOCC - January 10th, 2022 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the January 10, 2022 regular session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners with all five commissioners participating. The board unanimously approved the December 2021 minutes and a 17-item consent agenda that included $259,469 in NCDOT ROAP funds for GoDurham Access, an $83,960.25 USDOJ mental health expansion grant for the Criminal Justice Resource Center, and $400,000 in stopgap COVID-19 emergency food assistance. Ceremonially, the board welcomed new City-County Immigrant and Refugee Affairs Strategist Celina Mate, presented a resolution honoring Rougemont resident Linwood Hedgepeth as the first Black national president of Ruritan National, held a moment of silence for Ahmaud Arbery, and issued resolutions honoring Archbishop Desmond Tutu and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. alongside a National Mentoring Month proclamation. Public Health Director Rod Jenkins delivered an urgent Omicron surge briefing, and the board voted 5-0 to approve an interlocal agreement with the City of Durham to establish a temporary COVID-19 testing site at the Wheels location.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Commissioner Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order and read the public charge, with Commissioner Heidi Carter leading the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Wallace read community announcements covering COVID-19 vaccination hours, virtual MLK Jr. employee observance programming, Durham Pre-K 2022-2023 interest forms opening February 8, a January 12 blood drive and Engage Durham comprehensive plan meeting, Low Income Homeowners Relief (LIHR) extension through January 31, the NC Business Recovery Grant Program, and LIEAP energy assistance. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns highlighted the grand opening of the renovated W.D. Hill Community Recreation Center and weekend snow precautions, and commissioners congratulated Major Bazemore on retiring after more than 33 years with the Durham County Sheriff's Office.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (December 6, 2021 Work Session and December 13, 2021 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board considered the minutes from the December 6, 2021 work session and December 13, 2021 regular session. No edits or corrections were requested by commissioners.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0736: Introduction of City-County Immigrant and Refugee Affairs Strategist Celina Mate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief of Staff Drew Cummings introduced Celina Mate, Durham's first jointly funded City-County Immigrant and Refugee Affairs Strategist housed in the City's Neighborhood Improvement Services department alongside Linwood Best and Constance Stancil. Mate described her initial work plan, prior experience at World Relief Durham, grant-writing progress, and efforts to build community bridges and pursue official Welcoming Community designation. All five commissioners welcomed Mate and praised her early impact.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Resolution Honoring Linwood Hedgepeth
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs read the resolution dated January 3, 2022 honoring Rougemont native and retired IBM quality manager Linwood Hedgepeth for making history as the first Black President-Elect and National President in the 93-year history of Ruritan National (2020-2021). Hedgepeth reflected on leading the civic organization virtually during the COVID-19 pandemic and fundraising for St. Jude Children's Research Hospital alongside his wife Anne, and commissioners thanked the Rougemont and county Ruritan clubs for their community service.

agenda_items.title: Resolutions Honoring Archbishop Desmond Tutu and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., and National Mentoring Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton led a one-minute moment of silence following sentencing in the Ahmaud Arbery murder trial before reading a resolution honoring the life and anti-apartheid legacy of Archbishop Desmond Tutu. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns read a resolution honoring Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., followed by remarks from MLK Jr. Steering Committee Vice Chair DeWarren Langley detailing 2022 commemorative events and commissioner remarks urging passage of federal voting rights legislation. Commissioners Nida Allam and Heidi Carter jointly read a proclamation declaring January 2022 National Mentoring Month, and Langley highlighted partnering youth mentoring organizations across Durham.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (17 Items, Including Items 22-0001, 22-0007, and 22-0022)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: No items were pulled from the 17-item consent agenda. Chair Howerton highlighted item 22-0001 (Budget Ordinance Amendment No. 22BCC00055 recognizing $259,469 in NCDOT ROAP funds for GoDurham Access) and item 22-0007 (Budget Ordinance Amendment No. 22BCC00056 recognizing $83,960.25 for year one of a three-year USDOJ grant to the Criminal Justice Resource Center for mental health support expansion), while Commissioner Burns highlighted item 22-0022 providing $400,000 for COVID-19 food insecurity stopgap funding.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0033: Durham County Public Health Focus Update on COVID-19 Crisis
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported an unprecedented Omicron surge with 4,192 cases over the prior seven days, a 23.6% positivity rate, 156 recent hospitalizations concentrated among unvaccinated residents, and 48.06% vaccination coverage among Black residents compared to nearly 90% among seniors 65 and older. Jenkins noted the department ordered 8,800 home tests, supplied 1,200 rapid tests to NCCU, expected 60,000 durable masks from the state to split with DSS, and was coping with dozens of staff COVID-19 absences. Commissioners discussed N95/KN95 guidance, radio outreach, sharing supplies with Durham Public Schools, and whether to renew or redesign community-based organization contracts for equitable test and mask distribution.

agenda_items.title: Item 22-0025: Interlocal Agreement with the City of Durham for a Temporary COVID-19 Testing Site (Wheels Site)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim County Manager Claudia Hager and Public Health Director Rod Jenkins presented an interlocal agreement with the City of Durham to establish a high-capacity temporary COVID-19 testing site at the Wheels site (referenced in transcript as Norfolk Road), noting bus-route access and testing vendor OptumServe readiness following City Council approval. Commissioners praised the City-County partnership and approved the agreement unanimously.

Commissioners also received detailed informational updates on GoDurham Access paratransit ($5.4M combined system, microtransit pilots, and Treyburn vanpools) and Durham Pre-K (1,516 public seats and a $1.14M FY23 ARPA request), with Commissioner Nimasheena Burns pressing for 50% Durham Public Schools cost-sharing and tax-rate restraint. After a one-hour closed session under attorney-client privilege, the board suspended the rules and voted 5-0 to engage attorney Sonny Haynes of Womble Bond Dickinson to defend the County and Board in potential litigation by former County Manager Wendell Davis.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the virtual work session amid morning storm power outages and expressed condolences regarding recent local shootings. Vice Chair Jacobs also requested pulling the Linwood Hedgepeth resolution for same-day adoption ahead of a Saturday banquet.

disagreements.issue: Long-Term Funding Responsibility and Tax Impact of Durham Pre-K Expansion
disagreements.summary: During the Durham Pre-K quarterly update, commissioners disagreed over how to sustainably finance universal preschool expansion beyond 2026 ARPA deadlines and whether Durham Public Schools should bear half the cost.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require Durham Public Schools to fund 50% of Pre-K expansion from its ARPA/ESSER allocations and weigh Durham's higher property tax rate relative to Wake and Mecklenburg counties before committing post-2026 recurring County dollars.
side_a_arguments: ARPA funds must be obligated by 2024 and spent by 2026, creating a recurring funding cliff in 2027-2029 that could force local property tax increases when Durham's tax rate already exceeds Charlotte and Wake County.
Durham Public Schools received substantial ESSER and ARPA funds and should share 50% of expansion costs rather than placing the burden solely on the County.
Commissioners should not compare votes on unrelated issues to question board members' commitment to early childhood education.
disagreements.side_b_position: Prioritize Durham Pre-K as the County's top evidence-based investment using ARPA and local budget planning to move steadily toward the 3,268-seat universal goal.
side_b_arguments: Early childhood investment is the County's most effective systemic strategy for long-term educational equity, violence prevention, and workforce support.
With 1,516 of 3,268 target seats currently funded, the board must commit to a multi-year growth trajectory and build evaluation and prenatal-to-three capacity.
No other commissioners nodded in support when asked to commit to demanding a 50% funding match from Durham Public Schools.
disagreements.resolution: Informational discussion only with no vote taken; Interim Manager Claudia Hager committed to balancing one-time ARPA investments with long-term recurring budget strategies ahead of FY23 budget deliberations.

meetings.title: Joint City-County Committee Meeting
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the December 15, 2021 Joint City-County Committee meeting alongside Durham Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson, Council Member DeDreana Freeman, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs, and Commissioner Nida Allam, with Commissioner Heidi Carter also attending. The committee unanimously approved its October 12, 2021 minutes (3-0 on the BOCC committee roll call; 6-0 combined with City members) and received an interlocal quarterly report from General Manager Joanne Pierce on Bull City United's expansion toward 25 positions across six census tracts under the new Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) department. During the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force six-month update, commissioners and council members debated task force bylaws, missing quarterly reports, and public criticism surrounding the Youth Home. After postponing one item, the committee extended the session to receive a Durham Children's Initiative update on the community-led Early Childhood Action Plan before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Joint Committee Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the joint committee meeting and welcomed newly seated Durham Mayor Elaine O'Neal, Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson, and Council Member DeDreana Freeman alongside BOCC committee members Nida Allam, Wendy Jacobs, and Howerton. Clerk roll call noted Commissioner Heidi Carter attending in an unofficial capacity and Commissioner Nimasheena Burns listed as alternate, with City Manager Wanda Page and Interim County Manager Claudia Hager also present. One agenda item requested for removal by Charlie was postponed.

agenda_items.title: Approval of October 12, 2021 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton called for a motion to approve the minutes from the October 12, 2021 Joint City-County Committee meeting. No corrections were offered, and both the county and city delegations approved the minutes unanimously by roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: Bull City United Quarterly Update and Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Joanne Pierce presented the quarterly report under the city-county interlocal agreement, outlining the Cure Violence detect-interrupt-treat-mobilize model and Bull City United's expansion from seven positions in two census tracts (13.01 and 14.00) toward 25 total positions across six census tracts, with 16 onboarded and nine vacancies remaining. Pierce explained that Bull City United, Project BUILD, and My Brother's Keeper were consolidating into the new CISS department, highlighted an expected $250,000 federal grant and new Cure Violence Global database, and responded to elected officials' questions regarding hiring pace and outcome metrics.

agenda_items.title: Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force Six-Month / Q2 Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Task Force Co-Chairs Marcia Owens and Xavier Cason reported on work across four roundtables covering violence interruption, non-police crisis response, school resource officers, and criminal legal reform, while raising concerns about Youth Home detention spending and Bull City United director vacancies. Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Howerton criticized task force messaging and 'misinformation campaigns' outside the advisory bylaws, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs and Council Member Freeman asked about overdue quarterly reports and communication protocols, and Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson defended the task force's town halls and non-carceral focus.

agenda_items.title: Durham Children's Initiative Early Childhood Action Plan (ECAP) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After postponing the preceding scheduled item and agreeing to extend the meeting by 30 minutes past 11:00 a.m., the committee heard from Kate Elder, David Reese, Bonnie Dillon, and Joy Lampkin-Foster on Durham County's 18-month community-led Early Childhood Action Plan. Presenters and Council Member Freeman discussed opportunities for deeper city engagement, alignment with county ARPA investments, and cross-jurisdictional implementation ahead of the next joint committee meeting hosted by the City on February 8, 2022.

votes.item_title: Approval of October 12, 2021 Joint City-County Committee Minutes
votes.notes: BOCC committee roll call passed 3-0 (Allam, Jacobs, Howerton). City Council committee members DeDreana Freeman, Jillian Johnson, and Mayor Elaine O'Neal also voted Aye for a combined 6-0 joint committee tally. Mover and seconder not explicitly named in transcript audio.
votes.discussion_detail: No edits were proposed prior to the joint roll-call vote approving the October 12, 2021 committee minutes.

disagreements.issue: Scope, Bylaws, and Public Messaging of the Durham Community Safety and Wellness Task Force
disagreements.summary: During the six-month Task Force update, county commissioners and city officials clashed over whether task force members were exceeding their advisory mandate by organizing public opposition campaigns against the Youth Home and criticizing Bull City United staffing, versus fulfilling their charge to engage residents on non-carceral safety alternatives.
disagreements.side_a_position: Task Force members should adhere strictly to bylaws by submitting vetted formal recommendations to elected boards rather than running public advocacy campaigns or claiming BOCC failed to fund prevention leadership.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns and Chair Brenda A. Howerton objected to public campaigns accusing commissioners of prioritizing youth 'cages' when BOCC already funded a CISS department director, data statistician, and My Brother's Keeper initiatives.

Commissioners and Council Member DeDreana Freeman cited a missing Q1 report, unclear board-liaison notification of public forums, and the need to respect bylaws limiting official action to recommendations.
disagreements.side_b_position: Task Force town halls, public dialogue, and critiques of Youth Home detention spending and BCU oversight reflect legitimate community-led exploration of non-carceral safety strategies.
side_b_arguments: Task Force Co-chair Marcia Owens questioned expanding Bull City United into more neighborhoods before hiring a dedicated director and voiced community concern over Youth Home funding.

Mayor Pro Tem Jillian Johnson defended the task force's public town halls and focus on non-carceral recommendations, noting elected bodies retain final authority to adopt or reject proposals (while Council Member Mark-Anthony Middleton urged an inclusive approach that does not exclude law enforcement).
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; committee members concluded discussion by emphasizing clearer liaison communication and submitting written recommendations to the City Council and BOCC in 2022.

meetings.title: BOCC - December 13, 2021 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the December 13, 2021 regular session with all five commissioners participating. The board unanimously approved ten sets of past minutes (5-0), honored county communications and detention Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) award winners, and approved both the consent agenda and five pulled grant-related consent items (5-0 each). Commissioners voted 5-0 to approve Item 21-0735 implementing critical-position pay adjustments and retention bonuses funded via lapse salaries ($1.2 million recurring and $2.3 million one-time) and reviewed a preliminary FY 2022–2031 Capital Improvement Plan showing requests rising from $902 million to roughly $1.63–$1.7 billion. Despite 114 public comments and a unanimous Community Safety and Wellness Task Force request seeking a six-month delay, the board voted 5-0 after extending past 11:00 p.m. to approve $29.97 million in Limited Obligation Bonds, the Bordeaux Construction / Right Build GMP contract, and a Duke Energy easement/plat for the replacement Durham County Youth Home (Item 21-0715).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, Moment of Silence, and Approval of Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order and read the public charge, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns led the Pledge of Allegiance and later requested a moment of silence for lives lost earlier that morning, and the clerk read community announcements. Commissioners unanimously approved ten backlog sets of minutes covering May 13, 17, and 24; June 16 and 28; September 13 and 27; the November 1 work session; and the November 8 and 22 regular sessions.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Recognitions (NCACC Innovation Award, NC Dogwood Award, and PIO Communications Awards)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board recognized Public Information Office staff Deborah Craig-Ray, Matt Bigelow, Melissa Curley, Dawn Dudley, and Randy Jones for winning a 2021 NCACC Excellence and Innovation Award for DCo Talks and six state Excellence in Communications awards. Sheriff Clarence Birkhead, Detention Chief Johnny Hawkins, and commissioners also recognized Major Elijah Basemore for receiving the North Carolina Dogwood Award for launching the Detention Center's Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) program.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 21-0679, 21-0705, 21-0713, 21-0716, and 21-0728)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton pulled five consent items (21-0679, 21-0705, 21-0713, 21-0716, and 21-0728) to allow staff to present external grant and funding awards publicly. Commissioners unanimously approved the remainder of the consent agenda.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items 21-0679, 21-0705, 21-0713, 21-0716, and 21-0728 (External Grant Recognitions)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented pulled grant items including a $12,000 EMPG-S emergency management grant (21-0679), a $25,000 Duke Energy resettlement support grant via DSS (21-0716), a $10,000 DHHS Community Linkages to Care grant via Public Health (21-0705), and nearly $14,000 from Duke Energy for emergency response equipment (21-0728). Commissioners Burns and Jacobs also highlighted Early Childhood Initiative contract support and progress on 500 E. Main St. affordable housing and the Little River Regional Park master plan before approving all five items unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0738: COVID-19 Public Health Focus Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rod Jenkins reported 447 total current cases, 278 cumulative deaths, a seven-day moving average rising to 69 following Thanksgiving travel, positivity remaining under 5%, and 479,501 cumulative vaccine doses administered with over 95% of seniors 65+ having at least one dose. Jenkins also urged booster shots and preventive precautions as the Omicron variant emerged.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0735: Classification and Compensation Update on Critical Positions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry, Deidre Gonzalez, Tony Noell, and consultant Tim Newsom presented critical-position pay findings across public safety, EMS, social services, tax, and telecommunications, proposing $1.2 million in recurring market/pay-band adjustments and $2.3 million in one-time FY 2021–22 retention and longevity bonuses funded through existing lapse salaries, plus a 40-hour annual leave buyback and $6,000 sign-on/$1,000 referral bonuses. Commissioners voted unanimously to adopt the study recommendations and incentive package.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0748: FY 2022–2031 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager and Budget Director Keith Lane reviewed the preliminary FY 2022–2031 CIP requests, showing capital demands climbing from $902 million in the approved FY 2020–29 CIP to roughly $1.63–$1.7 billion. Major drivers included Durham Public Schools requests rising to $910 million and $719 million in County/Durham Tech requests including a $31 million Board of Elections facility, DTCC Allied Health ($74 million) and Life Science ($29 million) buildings, animal shelter expansion, and Memorial Stadium upgrades.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0715: Durham County Youth Home Capital Project Amendment (#22CPA00013), Construction GMP Contract, and Utility Easement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services GM Jody Miller, Perry Manns, Youth Home Director Angela Nunn, and County Attorney Willie Darby presented Capital Project Amendment #22CPA00013 appropriating $29,970,128 in Limited Obligation Bonds and a construction GMP contract with Bordeaux Construction / Right Build (base $27,570,796; total NTE $28,397,920) plus a Duke Energy easement/plat for the replacement 36-bed Youth Home and Youth Assessment Center at 2432 Broad St. After the clerk read 114 public comments and a Community Safety & Wellness Task Force request urging a six-month delay—contrasted with written support from Rep./former Judge Marcia Morey—commissioners voted 5-0 to extend the meeting until 11:20 p.m. and then voted 5-0 to approve the Youth Home financing, contract, and easement.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: County Attorney Willie Darby announced ballot appointment selections for the Audit Oversight Committee (Manuel Rojas), Durham-Wake Research and Production Service District Advisory Committee (Dewey Deadman primary; Daisy Mangus secondary), Open Space and Trails Commission (Dave Connolly; Luanda Summers), and Durham Planning Commission (Bradley Batista). The board adjourned at 04:28:25 by unanimous roll-call vote.

votes.notes: Chair Howerton commended the clerk's office for bringing the minutes backlog fully up to date.

votes.notes: Manager/staff reminded the board after the initial motion to incorporate the Duke Energy easement and plat; seconder was not separately named by the chair in audio.
votes.discussion_detail: Following 114 public comments seeking a six-month delay and extensive board remarks, commissioners approved the LOB project ordinance, Bordeaux Construction / Right Build GMP contract at 2432 Broad St., and Duke Energy utility easement/plat.

disagreements.issue: Durham County Youth Home Construction Financing and Contract (Item 21-0715) vs. Six-Month Delay for Community Alternatives
disagreements.summary: Public commenters and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force urged a six-month delay on Youth Home construction contracts to redirect funds toward community-based alternatives, while all five commissioners ultimately voted to proceed with the replacement facility alongside future prevention dialogue.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the Youth Home project ordinance and construction contract immediately to replace an outdated detention site with a trauma-informed, programming-focused Youth Assessment Center.
side_a_arguments: State law requires secure detention housing for court-remanded youth; delaying the project risks leaving youth in substandard facilities or shipping them out of county.
The new facility allocates over 27,500 square feet to therapeutic assessment, schooling, counseling, and family engagement, supported by juvenile justice leaders including Rep. Marcia Morey.
Commissioners argued the county must invest in both community prevention and humane statutorily required care rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay Youth Home financing and construction contracts for six months to evaluate non-carceral youth investments and expand community input.
side_b_arguments: All 114 written public comments read into the record and the Community Safety and Wellness Task Force urged a six-month moratorium under the principle that 'youth heal in communities, not cages.'
Opponents questioned statutory necessity for the 36-bed size and argued $29.97M in debt could better address root causes of youth justice involvement.
disagreements.resolution: The board voted 5-0 to approve Item 21-0715; Commissioner Heidi Carter also proposed a follow-up motion on future community youth-investment engagement, which Chair Howerton deferred to a subsequent meeting.

meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the November 22, 2021 regular session with all five commissioners present. The board unanimously approved prior minutes (5-0) and five of six consent agenda items (5-0), pulling Item 21-0706 for discussion. disagreements.issue: Protocol for Pulling Sheriff's Office Consent Agenda Items and Clarifying Security Roles (Item 21-0706)
disagreements.summary: Following Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs's decision to pull Item 21-0706 from consent for public discussion, Commissioner Nimasheena Burns challenged the lack of prior direct outreach to Sheriff's staff, prompting an exchange over transparency versus interagency courtesy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Commissioners should contact the Sheriff's Office directly with operational questions before pulling a consent item so Sheriff staff are not blindsided and lobby screeners are not conflated with detention officers.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns noted the Sheriff's Office received no heads-up prior to the item being pulled from consent.
Burns emphasized that private security vendors guard public entrances rather than replacing certified detention officers.
disagreements.side_b_position: Pulling the item allows transparent public explanation that the $412,303 amendment funds lobby weapons screening out of the Sheriff's existing budget rather than expanding detention custody.
side_b_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs stated she contacted Interim Manager Claudia Hager beforehand and wanted the public to clearly hear why the amendment was needed amid Sheriff staffing vacancies.
disagreements.resolution: Sheriff Clarence Birkhead confirmed the contract funded entrance screening posts due to roughly 50 detention vacancies, and all five commissioners voted 5-0 to approve Item 21-0706.

meetings.title: BOCC - November 8, 2021 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the November 8, 2021 regular session with all five commissioners present. The board unanimously approved September 9 and October 11 minutes (5-0), proclaimed National Adoption Month (Item 21-0656) and Veterans Day 2021, and passed a 17-item consent agenda without pulls (5-0). meetings.title: BOCC - November 1, 2021 Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the November 1, 2021 work session with all five commissioners present. The board heard citizen comment advocating a My Brother's Keeper Durham Advisory Board, previewed 15 consent agenda items, and received updates on Bull City United and the new Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) department (Item 21-0681), a UNC School of Government study finding lower property tax appeal rates in minority neighborhoods but no systemic bias in appeal results (Item 21-0668), the draft Non-Discrimination Ordinance, and a $300,000 Cultural Master Plan proposal. Under Item 21-0682, commissioners debated Durham Public Schools' proposed funding formula and reporting schedule in the draft BOCC–DPS Memorandum of Understanding as well as inter-board communication protocols ahead of a joint meeting. At 04:11:11, the board voted 5-0 to enter closed session for economic development, attorney-client, and personnel matters before adjourning 4-0 at 05:20:34 (Vice Chair Jacobs absent on return).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Citizen Comment, and Consent Agenda Preview (15 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy Clerk Maceo Carlton read a letter from resident DeWarren Langley urging an MBK Durham Advisory Board and local action plan for boys and young men of color. Interim Manager Claudia Hager then reviewed 15 upcoming consent agenda items (`21-0639` through `21-0665`) covering Carolina Duke Inn and duplex homeless COVID housing extensions, CJRC and DSS grants, Agriculture Building facade restoration, Memorial Stadium synthetic turf replacement, Public Health fee/grant amendments, and HVAC maintenance.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0681: Bull City United Quarterly Update and Community Intervention and Support Services (CISS) Department
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Manager Joanne Pierce reviewed the consolidation of Bull City United, Project BUILD, and My Brother's Keeper into the new CISS department, gradual hiring of 18 City-funded positions (12 violence interrupters, 5 outreach workers, 1 supervisor), FY20–21 shooting and Q1 mediation metrics, an anticipated $250,000 federal grant, and a new hospital-based violence intervention partnership with Duke. Commissioners discussed data tracking, census-tract rules, school MOUs, and outreach worker coordination with Workforce Development.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0682: Draft Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) Between BOCC and Durham Public Schools Board of Education
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, Budget Director Keith Lane, and Drew Cummings reviewed proposed 2021 updates to the 2017 BOCC–DPS MOU, recommending striking out a DPS-proposed funding formula matrix and language implying sole local operating-funding responsibility due to volatile local revenue streams and state constitutional responsibility. Commissioners debated adding Universal Pre-K language, whether to lock in fixed annual reporting dates, and sharing BOCC edits directly with School Board counterparts ahead of the joint meeting.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0668: Analysis of Property Tax Appeals for Systemic Biases
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson and UNC School of Government Professor Chris McLaughlin presented a study of roughly 10,500 Board of Equalization and Review appeals across 2016 and 2019 in Durham's 152 census block groups. While majority-minority and lower-value neighborhoods appealed less frequently (with gaps narrowing in 2019 under a compressed three-year cycle and easier online tools), appeal outcomes showed no demographic bias and countywide sales-assessment ratios remained flat across demographics.

agenda_items.title: Draft Resolution Enacting Non-Discrimination Ordinance (NDO)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant County Attorney Curtis Massey and General Manager Joanne Pierce reviewed the draft Non-Discrimination Ordinance covering public accommodations and employment, including natural hair texture/style definitions under race protections. Commissioners confirmed procedural next steps for formal enactment on November 8 and future administrative enforcement policies.

agenda_items.title: Durham Cultural Advisory Board Request for Cultural Master Plan Support
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Angela Lee, Laura Ritchie, and Yvonne Coleman of the Durham Cultural Advisory Board presented a request for $300,000 in joint City-County support to update the Cultural Master Plan, noting 47 arts/creative venues closed or displaced since 2004. Commissioners voiced conceptual support while requesting a concrete project budget, clarification on ARPA versus occupancy tax funding eligibility, and exploration of artist space in the old DSS building.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0637: Commissioner Comments, Closed Session, and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners heard state budget and redistricting updates from Deborah Craig-Ray and shared remarks on B.U. food project sign-ups, Election Day logistics, DPS school board compensation, a CJAC person-first language resolution, Sheriff 911 data requests, and Homeless Services Advisory Committee 30% AMI recommendations. At 04:11:11, the board voted 5-0 to enter closed session under G.S. 143-318.11(a)(4), (a)(3), and (a)(6), returning at 05:20:34 with no action taken and adjourning 4-0 with Jacobs absent.

disagreements.issue: BOCC–Durham Public Schools MOU: Funding Matrix Removal, Reporting Deadlines, and Board-to-Board Communication (Item 21-0682)
disagreements.summary: Reviewing DPS's proposed 2021 MOU edits, staff and commissioners supported rejecting a fixed funding matrix and local funding mandate clause while debating fixed annual reporting dates and direct commissioner-to-school-board communication ahead of the joint meeting.
disagreements.side_a_position: Strike the fixed funding formula matrix and local-responsibility clause, add explicit Universal Pre-K and fixed annual reporting deadlines to ensure accountability.
side_a_arguments: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs, and Commissioner Heidi Carter warned a strict property/sales tax formula risks automatic per-pupil cuts during downturns and obscures the State's constitutional school funding role.
Vice Chair Jacobs urged embedding Universal Pre-K language and definite annual report deadlines so previous 2017 reporting commitments do not go unfulfilled.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid overly rigid staff reporting calendar mandates and share proposed BOCC revisions directly with School Board liaisons rather than routing unilateral edits solely through staff.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns criticized lacking prior committee updates and urged commissioners to communicate suggested revisions directly with DPS board members so they are not surprised at the joint meeting.
Chair Brenda A. Howerton cautioned against writing rigid report dates into the MOU that might burden staff when DPS annual data arrives on variable schedules.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Interim Manager Hager committed to softening exact reporting-date language to an annual presentation and sharing updated draft edits with the DPS Superintendent and School Board ahead of the joint meeting.

meetings.title: BOCC - October 4, 2021 Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the full-day October 4, 2021 work session with all five commissioners present. The board heard citizen comment on My Brother's Keeper Durham, previewed 20 consent agenda items—including the Immigrant and Refugee Affairs ILA (21-0555), Green Source Advantage renewable agreements (21-0464, 21-0466), 500 E. Main St. affordable housing financing (21-0595), and Cameron Grove Cemetery conveyance (21-0609)—and reviewed the County Manager search timeline with Developmental Associates (21-0608). Commissioners also received briefings on the newly released Early Childhood Action Plan (21-0616), draft Southeast Durham Comprehensive Plan Focus Area guidance (21-059), the critical-position Classification and Compensation Study (21-0622), Made in Durham's BULLS biopharma initiative (21-0545), and Phase 2 Transit Plan survey findings (21-062). During the Tax Administration update showing Q1 2021 sales ratios dropping to 79.6%, commissioners differed over whether to plan formally for a 2025 reappraisal immediately or wait for February 2022 data and state Department of Revenue confirmation.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comment (My Brother's Keeper Durham)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the work session to order with all five commissioners present, and the clerk read a letter from DeWarren Langley urging formation of an MBK Durham Advisory Board and local boys and young men of color action plan. Interim Manager Claudia Hager and GM Joanne Pierce noted operational assessments of the merged CISS programs were underway, prompting remarks from Jacobs and Burns.

agenda_items.title: Review of 20 Consent Agenda Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager walked commissioners through 20 upcoming consent items including Duke Energy Green Source Advantage agreements (`21-0464`, `21-0466`), a $93,000 HHS minority health grant (`21-0589`), the joint City-County Immigrant and Refugee Affairs ILA (`21-0555`), temporary building screening staff (`21-0566`), Public Health COVID mitigation and school-liaison grants (`21-0584`), 500 E. Main St. affordable housing commitment (`21-0595`), BPAC youth-seat reauthorization (`21-0605`), Cameron Grove Cemetery lease/conveyance (`21-0609`), and Detention Center glass replacement (`21-0618`).

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0608: County Manager Recruitment Process Update (Developmental Associates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stephen Straus of Developmental Associates LLC presented the executive search schedule—including staff/resident open-ended surveys, Oct. 21 Neogov posting, blind candidate screening, and EQ 2.0 emotional-intelligence assessments. Commissioner Heidi Carter raised concerns about scheduling critical candidate closed sessions after late regular meetings, and commissioners agreed to explore daytime or separate-date sessions.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0616: Release of Durham County Early Childhood Action Plan (ECAP)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Early Childhood Coordinator Kate Elder, Durham Children's Initiative CEO David Reese, Bonnie Dillon, and parent advisor Humberto Trejo presented Durham's newly released Early Childhood Action Plan shaped by 150 leaders and 1,200+ caregivers. Commissioners praised the inclusive process and discussed potential ARPA funding for family direct support, pre-K/childcare expansion, and culturally affirming mental health services.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-059: Comprehensive Plan Draft Southeast Durham Focus Area Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Director Sara Young, Senior Planner Kayla Seibel, and Scott Whitman presented draft interim guidance covering place types—including Future Growth Area east of Kemp/Virgil Roads pending fire station capacity, Mixed Residential, 15-Minute Neighborhood, and Neighborhood Services Area—alongside 24 draft policies opposing proffered age restrictions and strengthening environmental and multimodal access. Commissioner Carter also asked staff to examine school-capacity adequacy standards during the countywide comprehensive plan update.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0622: Classification and Compensation Study of Critical Positions Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, Deidre Gonzalez, and HR Director Kathy Everett-Perry outlined the scope, peer-jurisdiction benchmarking methodology, and target public-safety/compliance departments for the critical-positions pay study ahead of formal recommendations returning in November.

agenda_items.title: Tax Administration Update: Reappraisal Timing (2025 vs. 2026) and Farragut Software Conversion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson, Deputy Assessor Starlin Beatty, and Appraisal Manager Keyar Doyle reported that Farragut CAMA/billing software modules were on schedule for late 2021 and spring 2022 launch, while Durham's Q1 2021 sales ratio dropped to 79.6%—below NC's 85% statutory trigger—likely forcing mandatory advancement to a Jan. 1, 2025 reappraisal. Commissioners debated whether to commit immediately to 2025 or wait for February 2022 market data and April 2022 state DOR notice.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-0545: Made in Durham Annual Reporting Update and BULLS Life Sciences Initiative
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Board Chair Dr. Victor Dzau, Executive Director Casey Steinbacher, Durham Tech President J.B. Buxton, Dr. Kara Battle, and Chamber CEO Geoff Durham updated commissioners on Made in Durham's 30-partner Opportunity Youth Collaborative, DPS referral app, five-woman pre-pilot cohort supported by $10,000 Oak Foundation stipends, upcoming 16-student winter pilot, and five-year biopharma manufacturing talent-pipeline scaling plan.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-062: Durham County Transit Plan Phase 2 Survey and Governance Study Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman presented over 2,300 Phase 2 survey responses (roughly half people of color and one-third regular transit riders via Engagement Ambassadors) comparing Options A (expanded bus service), B (Bus Rapid Transit), and C (Commuter Rail), noting rider prioritization of frequent 15-minute, late-night, and Sunday bus service alongside a commuter-rail cost-sharing gap (20% Durham + 67% Wake) and parallel governance study. Commissioners questioned on-demand microtransit, regional funding equity, and fare-free options before adjourning 5-0 at 05:37:15.

disagreements.issue: Property Tax Reappraisal Schedule: Immediate Commitment to 2025 vs. Waiting for 2022 State Data Under Current 2026 Plan
disagreements.summary: Following Tax Administration's report that Q1 2021 sales ratios dropped to 79.6% (below the 85% statutory trigger) while Farragut software conversion remained on schedule, commissioners disagreed on whether to move toward formally scheduling a 2025 reappraisal now or await state Department of Revenue confirmation under the February 2021 compromise delaying to 2026.
disagreements.side_a_position: Prepare and consider formally scheduling a 2025 general reappraisal rather than waiting until 2026–2027, minimizing cumulative homeowner sticker shock and maintaining shorter assessment cycles.
side_a_arguments: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs warned a seven-year gap before 2026–2027 exposes homeowners to severe property tax jumps even under a revenue-neutral rate, while shorter 3- to 4-year cycles improve equity.
Commissioner Heidi Carter welcomed Tax Administration's readiness to conduct a 2025 reappraisal ahead of the earlier 2026 schedule.
disagreements.side_b_position: Respect the February 2021 compromise setting 2026 and avoid changing the board's reappraisal date repeatedly until February 2022 trends and April 2022 NCDOR notice clarify whether advancement to 2025 is legally mandated.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns urged colleagues not to pressure Tax Administrator Dwane Brinson again after the board already compromised from 2027 down to 2026 in February.
Interim Manager Claudia Hager recommended returning in February 2022 with additional sales-ratio data and software conversion progress rather than revising the formal schedule prematurely.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken at the work session; Chair Howerton and commissioners agreed to await Tax Administration's February 2022 follow-up update and April 2022 NCDOR statutory notice.

meetings.title: BOCC - September 27, 2021 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 27, 2021 regular session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners, with all five seated commissioners participating. The board unanimously approved prior minutes, issued proclamations for Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week, Fox Family Foundation 30th Anniversary Week, and National Community Planning Month, and approved 11 consent agenda items while pulling Item 21-0575 ('Hacking into History' Restrictive Covenant Project) for public presentation and a separate 5-0 vote. Following the close of a 24-hour public comment window, commissioners voted 5-0 to approve the rezoning of 2104 and 2112 Ellis Road (Case Z2000042) to Commercial General with Development Plan (CG(D)) and adopt its statement of consistency. The board also reviewed a comprehensive American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding framework and draft evaluation rubric for Durham County's $62.4 million allocation and announced multiple boards and commissions appointments.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Commissioner Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order, read the public charge, and led the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Toomer read announcements regarding the Durham Emergency Rental Assistance Program (ERAP) pausing intake on October 4 with 3,000 pending applications and $953,000 remaining, municipal primary early voting through October 2, an October 13 virtual job fair, and MED Week (October 4–8). Chair Howerton highlighted Fidelity's announcement of 1,500 new RTP jobs and Mark Milligan's '1000 Black Men' mentorship effort, while Commissioners Allam, Jacobs, and Burns shared updates on Open Space matching grants, the Low-Income Housing Tax Relief Program (up to $750 for 10-year residents at or below 30% AMI), a Merck workforce hiring event, and $57.7 million in unclaimed state funds for Durham County residents.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (August 2 Work Session and August 23 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board reviewed the minutes for the August 2, 2021 work session and August 23, 2021 regular session. No corrections or edits were requested prior to the roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0572: Proclamation Recognizing Minority Enterprise Development (MED) Week 2021
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns read the proclamation declaring October 4–8, 2021 as Minority Enterprise Development Week under the theme 'Thriving Through Adversity,' citing pandemic impacts on minority- and women-owned businesses. Purchasing Manager Susan Perry noted the procurement division was now 100% staffed and congratulated MWBE Coordinator Keisha Davis on receiving the City's Diversity Advocate of the Year Award, while Davis outlined free virtual MED Week events.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0592: Proclamation for Fox Family Foundation 30th Anniversary Week
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioner Heidi Carter read the proclamation recognizing the week of September 27, 2021 as Fox Family Foundation 30th Anniversary Week, noting nearly $7.4 million in grant awards to 73 Durham County nonprofits since 1991. Foundation President David Prescher accepted the proclamation and emphasized continuing operating support and nonprofit collaboration across Durham.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item: Proclamation for National Community Planning Month 2021
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs read the proclamation declaring October 2021 as National Community Planning Month in support of the City-County Planning Department and resident planners. Planning Director Sara Young and Senior Planner Danny Cultra thanked volunteers and residents, and Commissioner Carter praised community engagement around the Comprehensive Plan update.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (11 Items, Excluding Item 21-0575)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Vice Chair Jacobs requested pulling Item 21-0575 ('Hacking into History' Restrictive Covenant Project) to the end of the agenda so staff could present its community significance, which Chair Howerton placed at the end of the agenda after Commissioner Burns noted it had been discussed at a prior work session. The remaining 11 consent agenda items were approved together by roll-call vote.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Item 21-0593: Zoning Map Change 2104 & 2112 Ellis Road (Case Z2000042)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the September 13 public hearing and 24-hour comment window, Clerk Toomer reported no additional email comments were received. After Commissioner Allam thanked Planning Commissioner Nate Baker for follow-up information and Vice Chair Jacobs confirmed 80–90 feet of woodlands along NC 147, 75 feet along Ellis Road, and 30-foot residential UDO buffers with applicant attorney Patrick Byker, the board closed the public hearing and approved both the CG(D) rezoning ordinance and the NCGS 160D-605 statement of consistency.

agenda_items.title: Other Business Item 21-0612: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Funding Update and Draft Evaluation Rubric
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, General Manager Jodi Miller, and General Manager Deborah Craig-Ray presented an update on Durham County's $62.4 million ARPA allocation (subject to December 2024 obligation and December 2026 expenditure deadlines), an upcoming online and mailed survey for unincorporated areas, and a draft evaluation rubric covering eligibility, compliance, strategic plan alignment, complexity/timing, community benefit, collaboration, equity, fiscal and environmental sustainability, and performance evaluation. Commissioners praised the rubric's clarity ahead of an October approval vote, urged staff to evaluate underfunded county priorities (such as the BULLS Initiative, Durham Pre-K, ECAP, and expanding low-income tax relief to 60% AMI), and discussed whether the 'complexity' criterion reflected timing risk rather than penalizing ambitious projects.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item 21-0575: Durham County 'Hacking into History' Restrictive Covenant Project Contract
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Register of Deeds Sharon Davis and JT Tabron presented the $50,000 public-private partnership with NCCU, DataWorks, and the Yinsom Group (Tia Hall) using Zooniverse and community forums to identify, map, and examine racially restrictive covenants in Durham public records, as well as emerging efforts to locate slave deeds and cemeteries. Commissioners commended the project and Commissioner Burns urged featuring it prominently on the county website before the board approved the contract unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting County Attorney Willie Darby announced citizen appointments to the Audit Oversight Committee (Nicole McCoy), Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission (Tyler Dewey, Milton Kendall, Kia Mostafa/Monsta), Citizen Advisory Committee (Seth Kendall), Community Child Protection/Child Fatality Prevention Team (Johnny Frederick, James Groves, Christie Mela, John Morris), Discovery Durham Tourism Development Authority (Carlos Rubio), Triangle Transit Advisory Committee (Kendall Bora, Kathleen Plaska), and Historic Preservation Commission (Katie).

meetings.title: BOCC - September 13, 2021 Regular Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 13, 2021 regular session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners, with all five commissioners present. The board unanimously approved August 9 minutes and 16 consent agenda items, recognized IS&T for its fifth consecutive Top 10 Digital Counties award, proclaimed World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day, and honored retiring Lincoln Community Health Center CEO Philip Harewood. Commissioners held a public hearing on rezoning 2104 and 2112 Ellis Road (Case Z2000042) for a self-storage facility—debating housing supply and proximity to a proposed commuter rail station before leaving the hearing open 24 hours and deferring the vote to September 27. The board also heard a Delta-variant COVID-19 briefing from Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins and debated $10.1 million in ARPA and emergency food security funding recommendations presented by Food Security Coordinator Mary Oxendine and Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Commissioner Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton called the meeting to order and read the public charge, and Commissioner Burns led the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Toomer announced weekend dementia caregiver daycare services through Durham Center for Senior Life and walk-in COVID-19 vaccination hours including third doses for immunocompromised residents. Vice Chair Jacobs and Commissioner Allam publicized a September 15 redistricting public meeting at Durham Tech, Straight Talk Support Group's transitional housing fundraiser, and early voting starting September 16, while Chair Howerton recognized 9/11 first responders.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (August 9, 2021 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Commissioners reviewed the August 9, 2021 regular session minutes with no edits or comments offered. The board approved the minutes unanimously by roll call.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items: Top 10 Digital County Award (21-0496), World Alzheimer's Day (21-057X), and Philip Harewood Retirement Resolution
agenda_items.discussion_summary: CIO Greg Morrow accepted recognition for Durham County's fifth straight Top 10 Digital Counties ranking despite COVID-19 and malware challenges. Commissioner Carter read a proclamation designating September 21, 2021 as World Alzheimer's and Dementia Awareness Day (accepted by Dementia Inclusive Inc. board member Janine Gordon), and Vice Chair Jacobs read a resolution honoring retiring Lincoln Community Health Center CEO Philip Harewood for 28 years of service, joined by Lincoln board chair Dr. Rosemary Jackson and Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (16 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton noted that the 16 consent items had been reviewed during the September 9 work session and no items were pulled for separate discussion. The board unanimously approved all 16 consent agenda items.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Item 21-0531: Zoning Map Change 2104 & 2112 Ellis Road (Case Z2000042)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Senior Planner Danny Cultra presented Stackhouse Development LLC's request to rezone 4.86 acres at 2104 and 2112 Ellis Road from RR/RS-20 to Commercial General with Development Plan (CG(D)) for a climate-controlled self-storage facility, noting a 9-3 Planning Commission recommendation and a new 100-year stormwater commitment. Resident Todd Paton submitted a written comment opposing the rezoning in favor of multi-family housing near a proposed regional passenger rail stop, while applicant attorney Patrick Byker, Robert Schunk, and Ellis Crossing developer Eric Rifkin argued the narrow 200-foot-wide parcel with right-in/right-out median access is unsuited for residential traffic and serves adjacent RTP life-science labs and Ellis Crossing residents. Following commissioner questions, the hearing remained open 24 hours through September 14 with a vote scheduled for September 27.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Held open 24 hours / Vote deferred to Sept. 27

agenda_items.title: Other Business Item 21-0569: Public Health Director Update on COVID-19 Crisis
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins reported 761 new cases over seven days, a 6.9% lab positivity rate, 66.9% eligible (12+) vaccination coverage, and strong gains from the $100 vaccine incentive program before it ended August 31, while noting unvaccinated residents were 5.5 times more likely to contract COVID-19 and African American women represented the highest recent case demographic. Commissioners discussed ~23% COVID ICU occupancy, upcoming October compensation recommendations for hard-to-recruit nursing and public safety staff amid $20,000 UNC Health signing bonuses, and Commissioner Burns's allegation that state grantee Andrew Herrera had failed to pay roughly 10 Black community-based organizations for June and July.

agenda_items.title: Other Business Item 21-0541: County Food Security Initiatives Update and ARPA Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Food Security Coordinator Mary Oxendine and Cooperative Extension Director Donna Rewalt reviewed over $2 million in county pandemic food investments (including Eat NC and $264,000 in nonprofit grants) and outlined $8.6 million in urgent recommendations ($1.3M for food security capacity grants, continuing 800/week produce boxes, and $4.5M for DPS kitchen equipment) plus $1.5 million in longer-term initiatives (Double Bucks extension, Thriving Community Fund BIPOC/women food-business grants, disadvantaged farmer grants, community engagement, and a food system assessment). Commissioners Burns and Carter questioned whether Black farmers held GAP/GHP certifications and whether DPS should fund kitchen equipment from its $146M in ESSER funds, while Interim Manager Hager and Vice Chair Jacobs stressed that proposals must go through the formal RFP and ARPA evaluation rubric before any funding decisions.

votes.notes: Mover and seconder not explicitly identified by name in transcript audio.
votes.discussion_detail: No comments or edits were offered on the August 9, 2021 regular session minutes prior to the roll-call vote.

disagreements.issue: 2104 & 2112 Ellis Road Rezoning (Case Z2000042): Self-Storage vs. Multi-Family Housing & Transit-Oriented Development
disagreements.summary: Resident Todd Paton and commissioners debated whether rezoning residentially zoned land along Ellis Road to Commercial General for a self-storage facility undermined Durham's urgent multi-family housing needs and future commuter rail transit-oriented development.
disagreements.side_a_position: Preserve residential zoning for multi-family housing and transit-oriented development near the proposed regional passenger rail stop rather than approving another self-storage facility.
side_a_arguments: Written commenter Todd Paton argued Durham faces skyrocketing rents and needs 40,000 new housing units, making a 100+ unit apartment complex the highest and best use.
Commissioner Heidi Carter noted it felt counterintuitive to upzone residential land to commercial given Durham's housing shortage and proximity to a proposed commuter rail station.
Commissioner Nida Allam requested transportation staff input on potential impacts on the planned regional passenger rail line.
disagreements.side_b_position: Approve CG(D) zoning for climate-controlled self-storage because site geometry and median traffic restrictions make residential use unviable and RTP firms and nearby apartments need local storage.
side_b_arguments: Applicant attorney Patrick Byker and Robert Schunk stated the 4.86-acre lot is only 200 feet wide with right-in/right-out median restrictions on Ellis Road, which would force excessive residential U-turns.
Byker noted the site is over a half-mile walk outside the core transit-station area and would serve RTP life-science startups and CROs needing off-site climate-controlled storage.
Ellis Crossing developer Eric Rifkin testified that his 1,800-unit mixed-use project across the street supports the facility as a needed amenity for residents.
disagreements.resolution: The public hearing was left open for 24 hours (through September 14) for transportation staff follow-up and additional comment; the board unanimously approved the rezoning 5-0 on September 27.

disagreements.issue: Food Security $10.1M ARPA Proposals: Urgent Stop-Gap Relief vs. Process Rigor, BIPOC Farmer Access, and DPS ESSER Overlap
disagreements.summary: Commissioners and staff debated how to balance urgent $8.6 million food-security and school kitchen equipment funding requests against limited ARPA dollars, uniform procurement rules, and concerns over whether Black farmers and businesses could actually qualify.
disagreements.side_a_position: Subject all $10.1M in food security proposals to the county's uniform ARPA rubric, RFP competition, disaggregated equity verification, and scrutiny of school vs. county funding sources.
side_a_arguments: Commissioner Nimasheena Burns questioned how Black farmers could benefit when only one Black farmer in the county is GAP/GHP certified, and urged checking whether DPS should pay for its $4.5M kitchen equipment needs from its $146M in ESSER funds.

Chair Brenda Howerton called for disaggregated data rather than broad promises that funds will help Black residents, stressing the board must allow the County Manager to evaluate all competing requests strategically.

Interim Manager Claudia Hager and Vice Chair Wendy Jacobs emphasized that $62.4M in ARPA cannot cover every ask and all proposals must pass compliance, RFP, and rubric vetting alongside upcoming housing proposals.
disagreements.side_b_position: Prioritize immediate stop-gap emergency food grants and produce boxes quickly, potentially via fund balance or FEMA reimbursement, while using RFPs and non-GAP-restricted grants to reach BIPOC partners.
side_b_arguments: Commissioner Heidi Carter argued 'stop-gap' emergency food grants for existing distributors like the Food Security Task Force and Congregations in Action should come forward expeditiously, even using fund balance subject to reimbursement.

Mary Oxendine clarified that GAP certification is only required for selling to schools—not for the proposed produce box or farmer grants—and offered to return in the emergency-operations channel to prevent a lapse in produce boxes.

DPS Child Nutrition Director Jim Keaton explained that child nutrition operates as a self-funded enterprise fund strained by lower virtual-school meal reimbursements and $15/hour county-aligned wages.
disagreements.resolution: No funding vote was taken; Chair Howerton directed Interim Manager Hager and staff to review all requests under the county's compliance and rubric framework and schedule follow-up one-on-one and board discussions.

meetings.title: BOCC - September 9, 2021 Regular Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the September 9, 2021 work session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners, starting at 10:36 AM following a Durham Tech dedication event, with all five commissioners participating. The board heard citizen comment on an eviction emergency, previewed 14 consent items—including utility repairs, a $50,000 Greater Durham Black Chamber of Commerce contract, $1.65M in mental health carryover, and a $2.4M co-located Fire/EMS Station 18 ILA—and voted 5-0 after suspending the rules to approve the Bahama Fire Station rezoning (Case Z2000046) and its consistency statement. Commissioners also heard an Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (AWAC) presentation supporting Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (TNVR) ordinance changes, reviewed 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan scenarios with DCHC MPO, examined a $21M–$31M Board of Elections space-needs assessment, previewed ARPA engagement and rubric plans, and voted 5-0 to suspend the rules and make a Dangerous Dog Appeal Board reappointment.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order and Citizen Comments on Eviction Crisis
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the work session at 10:36 AM following a Durham Tech dedication event and read the public charge. Clerk Monica Toomer read a citizen comment from Larissa Sidel warning of an acute eviction emergency (citing 82 eviction hearings the previous Friday) and urging the county to distribute ERAP funds directly to tenants or through nonprofits such as Legal Aid when landlords refuse to participate.

agenda_items.title: Review of Consent Agenda Items (14 Items Including Station 18 ILA and Mental Health Carryover)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager walked through 14 consent items for the September 13 agenda, including the Building Bridges jail opioid-treatment grant (21-0522), McFarland Farm conservation easement (21-0526), Triangle Wastewater Treatment Plant and collection system repair amendments (21-0530, 21-0533, 21-0534, 21-0539, 21-0542), a $20 million Chinn Road pump station grant application (21-0540), Durham Pre-K funding (21-0536), a $50,000 Greater Durham Black Chamber of Commerce contract (21-0537), Alliance Behavioral Health $1.65M carryover funding including $650,000 for MOORS youth mobile crisis care, a $318,750 Governor's Highway Safety grant (21-0550), and a late-added $2.4M co-located Fire/EMS Station 18 ILA on Herndon Road. Commissioner Burns sought measurable deliverables by January for the Black Chamber contract, and Vice Chair Jacobs requested data on residents served by MOORS and tying utility capacity costs to developers.

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 21-0561: Zoning Map Change for Bahama Fire Station (Case Z2000046)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the August 23 public hearing and 24-hour comment window, Clerk Toomer reported no additional public comments received. The board closed the public hearing, voted 5-0 to suspend the rules, voted 5-0 to adopt the ordinance rezoning 1426 Bahama Road from CN and RS-20/MLR-A to Commercial Neighborhood with a Text-Only Development Plan (CN(D)/MLR-A) prohibiting on-site alcohol uses, and voted 5-0 to adopt the NCGS 160D-605 statement of consistency.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 5-0 (suspend rules, rezoning, and consistency statement)

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 21-0521: Animal Welfare Advisory Committee (AWAC) Community Cat Management / TNVR Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: AWAC spokesperson Jan Paul presented an 18-month study of Durham County's estimated 30,000 feral cats, concluding that current trap-and-euthanize policies fail to reduce populations, strain APS and Animal Services budgets and staff, and lag behind 64 NC counties using Trap-Neuter-Vaccinate-Return (TNVR), while noting state wildlife experts found no threatened bird species endangered by cats in Durham. Commissioners Jacobs, Burns, and Carter strongly endorsed directing the County Attorney's Office to draft ordinance amendments permitting TNVR; Chair Howerton declined to entertain a motion due to severe time pressure and directed legal staff and management to follow up with ordinance proposals.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / No vote (staff directed to draft ordinance)

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 21-0538: DCHC MPO 2050 Metropolitan Transportation Plan (MTP) Alternatives Analysis
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Manager Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO Senior Planner Andy Henry reviewed 2050 regional growth forecasts (52% Durham population growth and 85% employment growth) and compared Plans & Trends, Shared Leadership, and Altogether scenarios—with Altogether extending commuter rail to Mebane, adding BRT corridors, converting downtown NC 147 to a four-lane boulevard, and shifting funding from highway widening to transit and complete streets. Because state highway-centric funding (90% to roads) left carbon emissions rising +16% overall, Henry noted the MPO board directed staff to prepare two competing October drafts (a traditional highway-weighted option and a transit/equity/climate-weighted option). Commissioners urged prioritizing transit-dependent riders, Treyburn/RTP job access, bus shelter upgrades, and bus driver pay/childcare.

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 21-0518: Board of Elections Space Needs & Programming Assessment Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Assistant General Manager Perry Manns, Elections Director Derek Bowens, and RND Architects principal Charles Nicholson detailed severe operational, security, and fire-code deficiencies across the Board of Elections' split Judicial Annex (4,281 sq. ft.) and leased South Austin Avenue warehouse (10,400 net sq. ft. lacking climate control, adequate exits, and observer visibility), documenting a 13,000 net sq. ft. deficit against a 43,000 gross sq. ft. need. They presented three preliminary options—a $31M new build by 2025, a $21M+ leased flex space fit-up by August 2023, or a phased lease/renovation—for CIP evaluation, and Vice Chair Jacobs asked staff to also consider purchasing and retrofitting an existing building.

agenda_items.title: Discussion Item 21-0546: American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager, Jodi Miller, and Deborah Craig-Ray reviewed Durham County's $62.4 million ARPA allocation ($5.1M earmarked for FY22 COVID costs), 300+ survey responses and 80 community proposals from summer city-county engagement, upcoming Phase 2 outreach to unincorporated areas starting September 30, and an 8-category draft evaluation rubric ahead of a deeper review on September 27. Commissioners clarified future county RFP submission pathways and agreed to email rubric feedback.

agenda_items.title: Item 21-059X: Dangerous Dog Appeal Board Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: At the close of the work session, the board voted 5-0 to suspend its rules and voted 5-0 to appoint a member (referred to in audio as 'Mo' / 'Motriro') to an additional three-year term on the Dangerous Dog Appeal Board. Staff also noted commissioners could review directives online and agreed to confirm whether Acting County Attorney Willie Darby had sufficient guidance on drafting the TNVR ordinance prior to adjournment.

meetings.title: BOCC Regular Session for Aug. 23 (full audio)
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton presided over the August 23, 2021 regular session of the Durham Board of County Commissioners (full audio recording), with all five commissioners present. The board unanimously approved July 12 minutes and 11 consent agenda items, proclaimed September 2021 as National Recovery Month, and recognized three National Association of Counties (NACo) Achievement Awards won by the Board of Elections, Public Health/OES, and Tax Administration. Commissioners held a public hearing on rezoning the old Bahama Fire Station at 1426 Bahama Road (Case Z2000046) and kept it open 24 hours, voted 5-0 to approve a $125,000 economic development incentive for Smart Wires Inc., heard a Delta-variant COVID-19 briefing from Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins and interim manager Claudia Hager's employee vaccine incentive rollout, announced board appointments, and met in closed session before adjourning.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, and Commissioner Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Brenda A. Howerton opened the August 23, 2021 regular session at 7:00 PM, read the public charge, and Commissioner Allam led the Pledge of Allegiance. Clerk Monica Toomer read community announcements including an August 31 MWBE outreach session for 300 East Main Street, Durham Center for Senior Life dementia care management, NCDOT fall litter sweep, the bilingual Nurturing Durham website, Durham Youth Ambassadors, and municipal primary early voting starting September 16. Commissioners Allam and Jacobs highlighted a state court ruling restoring voting rights to over 50,000 North Carolinians on felony probation/parole and urged community donations and volunteers for up to 90 Afghan refugees arriving in Durham in September.

agenda_items.title: Approval of Minutes (July 12, 2021 Regular Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board considered the July 12, 2021 regular session minutes with no edits or corrections. Vice Chair Jacobs moved and Commissioner Burns seconded approval, passing 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0459: Proclamation for National Recovery Month (September 2021)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Howerton read the proclamation declaring September 2021 as National Recovery Month under the theme 'Recovery is for Everyone,' highlighting national mental health and substance-use treatment gaps. Dr. Lonnie Hall accepted the proclamation on behalf of the Recovery Community of Durham, and Vice Chair Jacobs and Chair Howerton emphasized reducing stigma and expanding support amid rising pandemic overdoses.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0520: Recognition of Three NACo Achievement Awards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager introduced three NACo Achievement Award-winning initiatives achieved amid both COVID-19 and a malware attack: the Board of Elections polling wait-time/operations app, Public Health and OES's COVID-19 Vaccine Distribution Dashboard, and Tax Administration's Jabber remote call center, 99.9%-satisfaction live chat, and long-term tax deferral program. Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins, Tax Administrator Dwayne Brinson, CIO Greg Morrow, and OES's Ari Shine accepted recognition and thanked cross-departmental teams.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (11 Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With no items requested to be pulled and at Vice Chair Jacobs's suggestion to spare Interim Manager Hager's voice, the board waived reading the 11 consent agenda items and approved them unanimously 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Item 21-0505: Zoning Map Change for Bahama Fire Station (Case Z2000046)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning Manager Michael Stock presented the Bahama Volunteer Fire Rescue Company's request to rezone two parcels totaling 0.76 acres at 1426 Bahama Road from CN and RS-20/MLR-A to Commercial Neighborhood with a text-only development plan (CN(D)/MLR-A) barring bars, nightclubs, or on-site alcohol consumption (Planning Commission recommended 10-0). Stock explained to Chair Howerton that combining the parcels reduces non-conformity, and Fire Chief Len Needham testified the department seeks to sell the old station to help buy a fire truck without debt while protecting the surrounding village. The public hearing was kept open 24 hours until August 24, with a vote scheduled for the September 9 work session.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Held open 24 hours / Vote deferred to Sept. 9

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Item 21-0511: Economic Development Incentive Allocation for Smart Wires Inc. ($125,000)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following the August 9 public hearing and 24-hour comment window, Clerk Toomer reported no comments received. Commissioner Carter moved and Commissioner Allam seconded allocating $125,000 to Smart Wires Inc. and authorizing Interim Manager Hager to execute the agreement incorporating the job-creation and investment conditions in the briefing sheet (as confirmed by Vice Chair Jacobs), passing 5-0.

agenda_items.title: Other Business: Durham County Public Health COVID-19 Response Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins reported a surging Delta wave (118 seven-day moving average, 8.1% lab positivity, 793 active cases, and African Americans accounting for 47.83% of August cases), highlighted over 25,000 vaccine incentive gift cards ($100 first dose / $25 driver) driving a 37% vaccination increase, announced a September 1 pause on broad outreach to rest staff and launch third-dose boosters for immunocompromised residents, and noted unvaccinated residents faced six times the attack rate (1,580 vs. 251 per 100,000). Commissioners urged clear public criteria on immunocompromised eligibility, welcomed Interim Manager Hager's county employee policy ($250 and two bonus days off if vaccinated by October 4, or weekly testing), and inquired about pediatric clusters (<5).

agenda_items.title: Boards and Commissions Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Acting County Attorney Willie Darby announced appointments to the Dangerous Dog Appeal Board (Brian Mulligan, corrected from 'Miriam' by Vice Chair Jacobs), Durham County Convention Center Authority (Miriam De La Hunt Andrews), Juvenile Crime Prevention Council (LaKeisha Blake, Joseph Jackson III, Brandon Morsey), and TJCOG Water Resource Collaborative (Michael Koenig).

agenda_items.title: Closed Session (G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5), (a)(6)) and Adjournment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The board voted 5-0 to enter closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) and (a)(6) regarding property acquisition/contract negotiations, employment contract terms, and individual personnel matters, after Chair Howerton reminded the public that the September work session would be held Thursday, September 9 at 9:00 AM due to Labor Day and Rosh Hashanah. Returning to open session at 02:18:19, the board reported giving direction to staff and adjourned 5-0.

votes.item_title: Approval of Minutes (July 12, 2021 Regular Session)
votes.discussion_detail: The board approved the July 12, 2021 regular session minutes unanimously with no edits.

votes.item_title: Item 21-0511: Economic Development Incentive Allocation for Smart Wires Inc. ($125,000)
votes.notes: Chair verbally misspoke '145 thousand' when restating the motion after Commissioner Carter moved $125,000; the item and motion specified $125,000.
votes.discussion_detail: After confirming no 24-hour public comments were received and verifying that performance conditions from the briefing sheet are incorporated into the agreement, the board approved $125,000 in economic development funds for Smart Wires Inc.

votes.item_title: Motion to Adjourn into Closed Session (N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5), (a)(6))
votes.notes: Returned to open session at 02:18:19 with direction given to staff.
votes.discussion_detail: The board adjourned into closed session pursuant to N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(5) and (a)(6) to instruct staff on property/employment contract negotiations and consider personnel qualifications/performance.

Howerton, with all five commissioners present) captures the board's recognition of National Recovery Month and three NACo Achievement Awards for Elections, Public Health/OES, and Tax Administration. agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0459: Proclamation for National Recovery Month (September 2021)

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Item 21-0520: Recognition of Three NACo Achievement Awards
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Interim Manager Claudia Hager recognized three NACo Achievement Awards earned despite COVID-19 and a malware attack: Board of Elections (election-day tracking app), Public Health and OES (COVID-19 Vaccine Distribution Dashboard), and Tax Administration (Jabber remote call center, 99.9%-satisfaction live chat, and tax deferral program), with remarks from Rodney Jenkins, Dwayne Brinson, CIO Greg Morrow, and OES's Ari Shine.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (11 Items)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing Item 21-0505: Zoning Map Change for Bahama Fire Station (Case Z2000046)

agenda_items.title: Other Business: Durham County Public Health COVID-19 Response Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Health Director Rodney Jenkins reported a surging Delta wave (118 seven-day moving average, 8.1% positivity, 793 active cases, and 47.83% of August cases among African American residents), highlighted 25,000+ vaccine incentive cards ($100 first dose / $25 driver), and announced third-dose boosters for immunocompromised residents and a September 1 pause on broad outreach.
